The lecture of this chapter (figures built as it is explained)

We begin this chapter with a question the earlier chapters leave open: what a body does to the support it presses on. In chapter 5 we loaded a beam with forces and moments, in chapter 11 we wrote the equilibrium equations and boundary conditions of an elastic body, and in chapter 12 we assembled beams from finite elements. In all of this the supports and loads were given. Here we compute them: how a foundation sinks, and how a force arises where two bodies touch.

The words of the title tell what we will do, and figure 25.1 shows them. A contact (kontakt, stik) is the place where two bodies touch and pass a force to each other, as a ball touches a ring. Hertz contact is named after Heinrich Hertz, who solved how two rounded bodies are squeezed when pressed together (history in section 25.6). The expression rolling bearing (kotalni ležaj) is made of two words: a bearing (ležaj) is the part of a machine that carries a rotating shaft and passes its force to the housing, and rolling means that balls or rollers roll between the inner and the outer ring instead of the shaft sliding in the housing. A ball touches each ring only over a small area, so the contact is decisive here.

The contact decides two things, which figure 25.2 shows. The first is strength: a steel ball of diameter 12.7 mm pressed with a force of 100 N on a flat steel plate touches the plate in a circle of radius about 0.16 mm (for steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), computed in section 25.6). If we spread the force over the whole cross-section of the ball, an area about 1500 times larger would carry it. The mean pressure in the contact circle is therefore about 1500 times larger than over the cross-section, and at its centre it reaches \(1772\) MPa. The calculation holds as long as the steel stays elastic. A steel with the yield stress \(220\) MPa would start to yield under the ball already at a force of \(0{,}80\) N. The balls and rings of bearings are therefore made of hardened steel, which in bearings carries pressures above \(1380\) MPa in continuous service (section 25.6).

The second is stiffness: a bearing with nine balls of the same diameter, fitted between the rings without play, is a spring that is not linear. The graph of its force against the approach of the rings is not a straight line, its stiffness is the slope of the tangent and grows with the force, because the contact patches of the balls grow with the force. The frequency at which the shafts and machines carried by the bearing vibrate depends on this stiffness, just as a mass on a spring vibrates with the natural angular frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\) (definition 9.4). Since the bearing is not a linear spring, this equation holds only for small vibrations about the loaded state, with \(k\) the slope of the tangent in that state. At \(1000\) N and a change of the force by \(100\) N the change of the displacement computed along the tangent differs from the true one by less than \(2\,\%\), and for vibrations during which balls are unloaded the equation does not hold (section 25.8).

The chapter promises three things, and figure 25.3 shows them in a row. First, we describe the foundation by ever more accurate models: first a row of independent springs under a beam, then a solid elastic half-space that sinks also around the loaded point, and then the contact of two rounded bodies, where we compute the size of the contact area, the pressure and the approach of the bodies. Second, from this we compute how a bearing distributes its load over the balls and what its stiffness is. Third, we show how a bearing enters a calculation by the finite element method, and connect the chapter to those before it, also to the vibration of chapter 9. Where a result cannot be proved in this book, we cite it with its source and say that it is cited.

We start with the simplest foundation, the one we know from rails on sleepers.

25.1 A beam on an elastic foundation

A rail lies on sleepers, and the sleepers lie on gravel. When a wheel rolls onto the rail, the rail bends and sinks into the foundation, and the foundation pushes it back up. How far does the rail sink under the wheel, where is the bending moment largest, and how far from the wheel is the effect still felt? This section answers these questions with the simplest model of a foundation. The chapter will then replace the foundation step by step with a more real one: first with a half-space, which sinks also around the loaded point, then with the contact of two rounded bodies, and finally with a rolling bearing, where the foundation is a ring on which steel balls roll.

A foundation (podlaga) is what lies under the beam and carries it. It is elastic because it returns to its original state when unloaded, like a spring. The model carries Winkler's name, and Zimmermann simplified his calculation for rails (VK, PDF p. 81, TIMO, PDF p. 370).

From history

When railways were built, people asked how a rail bends under a wheel. Winkler took the rail as a continuous beam on rigid supports (TIMO, PDF p. 370). A sleeper, however, is not a rigid support: the gravel under it gives way. Zimmermann prepared tables that simplified Winkler's calculation of a beam on an elastic foundation, and applied the theory to the deflection of sleepers. In his picture the rail lies on elastic supports, and at the usual distances between sleepers the vertical load is spread over several sleepers, so the separate elastic supports can be replaced by an equivalent continuous elastic foundation (TIMO, PDF p. 370). The source gives only the initial H. and no full name.

The story showed a step that we shall take ourselves: a row of elastic supports is replaced by a foundation that is elastic at every point. Why this makes sense was told by Zimmermann, and how well it works we shall test with numbers at the end of the section. First we set up the model.

Take the beam of chapter 5, steel, 20 mm wide and 40 mm high, with \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m\(^2\) (theorem 5.35). The axis \(x\) runs along the beam, the axis \(y\) points up, and the deflection \(v(x)\) is the displacement of the axis from its straight position, measured upward. We lay the beam on a row of springs so close together that we cannot tell them apart.

Let us draw the figure part by part. First the ground, a hatched surface, and above it a straight line showing where the axis of the beam would lie if nothing acted on it. On the ground we put the springs, each with one end on the ground and the other on the beam. The springs stand side by side and do not influence one another: this is the essence of the model. The beam has a shape that we shall compute: it is lowest under the force, then rises above the line and gradually dies out. The force \(P\) presses from above downward, so the arrow ends at the point where it acts, like every push. The deflection is the distance between the straight position and the beam. Last the force of the foundation: a spring that the beam has compressed pushes the beam upward, so the arrow ends on the beam. The length of the arrow is proportional to the deflection and is longest under the force.

We state the model also as a definition, since it gets its name and its numbers there.

Definition 25.1 Elastic or Winkler foundation (elastična podlaga)

Let \(k > 0\) be a number in N/m\(^2\), called the foundation modulus (modul podlage). A foundation with modulus \(k\) acts on the beam of chapter 5, which has axis \(x\) and deflection \(v(x)\) upward, with a force per unit length

\[f(x) = -k\,v(x) \tag{25.1}\]

in the direction of the axis \(y\). The function \(f\) takes the number \(v(x)\) and returns the number \(f(x)\), at each point of the axis separately. The force of the foundation on the piece of the axis between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} f\,\mathrm{d}t\). The model has six idealizations. The foundation is linear: the force is proportional to the deflection. Every point is independent: \(f(x)\) depends only on \(v(x)\) and not on the deflection of neighbouring points. The foundation acts on both sides: where \(v > 0\) it pulls the beam down, it does not only push. The foundation transmits no longitudinal forces (no friction). The modulus \(k\) is constant along the beam. The deflection is small, within the limits of the Euler-Bernoulli beam model (\(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\), chapter 5).

Source: COOK §8.8 (PDF p. 301, read): the model requires that the foundation resists only the displacement normal to its surface, with a pressure proportional to the displacement, and that the surrounding foundation is "unaffected". VK §3.7 (PDF p. 81, read) calls \(k\) the foundation modulus and measures it in force per area per displacement, COOK writes it \(\beta\) (pressure \(p = \beta\,w\)). Our \(k\) is force per length per displacement, that is the modulus of VK or COOK multiplied by the width of the face of the beam that lies on the foundation, as in COOK, who takes \(\mathrm{d}A = b\,\mathrm{d}x\) for a beam. The list of idealizations and their limits are ours.

The unit of \(k\) is N/m\(^2\): a force per unit length in N/m, divided by a deflection in metres. The choice already made by section 9.4.7 of chapter 9 is \(k = 1{,}0\cdot 10^{6}\) N/m\(^2\). At a deflection of 1 mm the foundation gives \(1000\) N/m, which on a face 20 mm wide is a pressure of 50 kPa. A row of springs of stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}}\) at distance \(s\) has \(k = K_{\mathrm{t}}/s\), as with the sleepers of the story. Why the idealizations of the definition are acceptable here, when they fail and what they cost, we say with numbers once we have the solution.

Symbols are occupied in several places of the book. The letter \(k\) is the thermal conductivity in chapter 14, the shear factor in chapter 5, the stiffness of a spring in chapters 9 and 10. Here \(k\) is always the foundation modulus. The letter \(\beta\) is as in section 9.4.7: \(\beta = (k/(4\,EI))^{1/4}\). The force on the beam is written \(P\) as in chapter 9, because \(F\) appears later in the chapter for the contact of bodies.

First we derive the equation that the deflection satisfies. Let us draw a piece of the beam between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) and everything that acts on it.

Let us draw figure 25.5. The piece is the part of the axis from \(x_1\) to \(x_2\), which we imagine cut off from the rest. Below it is the foundation with its springs. From above presses the external load \(q\) in N/m, drawn downward. The force of the foundation \(-k\,v\) points upward, because we drew a place where \(v < 0\). The piece is cut off, so we also draw the forces that held it: the shear force \(V(x_2)\) on the right face points in the direction \(+y\), on the left face it is opposite by lemma 5.10, \(-V(x_1)\). At the bottom are the ends of the piece, \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), with the distance between them.

The sum of the forces on the piece is zero. We add up the forces of the springs over the piece: the sum \(-k\,v(t_{\mathrm{i}})\,\Delta t_{\mathrm{i}}\) over a partition of the piece is a Riemann sum of the continuous function \(-k\,v\), and its limit is the integral. The load \(q - k\,v\) is continuous, because \(v\) is continuous. Lemma 5.10 gives for this piece

\[V(x_2) - V(x_1) = -\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}\big(q(t) - k\,v(t)\big)\,\mathrm{d}t . \tag{25.2}\]

On the right is the load that the piece carries, springs included, on the left the change of the shear force across the piece. The equation holds for every piece, not only a short one. What follows is the equation for \(v\) at every point.

Theorem 25.2 Equation of a beam on a foundation (enačba nosilca na podlagi)

Let the beam be prismatic and satisfy the assumptions of theorem 5.35, and let the foundation be as in definition 25.1 with modulus \(k\) along the interval \((a, b)\). On \((a, b)\) let there be no point forces, couples and distributed moment (\(m = 0\)), let the load \(q\) be continuous and \(v\) four times continuously differentiable. Then equation (25.2) holds for the piece between \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), all \(a < x_1 < x_2 < b\), if and only if

\[EI\,v'''' + k\,v = q \quad \text{on } (a, b) . \tag{25.3}\]
Proof

We must show that the difference of the two sides of equation (25.2) is the integral of one continuous function over the piece, and then use that a continuous function with zero integral over every piece vanishes everywhere.

  1. By theorem 5.35 \(M = EI\,v''\), and by corollary 5.11 the shear force is \(V = -M' - m = -M'\), since \(m = 0\). Hence \(V = -EI\,v'''\).
  2. Insert the shear forces at the ends of the piece and the load with the foundation force into (25.2) and multiply by \(-1\): \(EI\,\big(v'''(x_2) - v'''(x_1)\big) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2}(q - k\,v)\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  3. The function \(v''''\) is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.55, part 1), over the piece, \(EI\,\big(v'''(x_2) - v'''(x_1)\big) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} EI\,v''''\,\mathrm{d}t\).
  4. Let \(f = EI\,v'''' + k\,v - q\), a continuous function. By steps 2 and 3, (25.2) for the piece \([x_1, x_2]\) is equal to \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_1}^{x_2} f\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\).
  5. If (25.3) holds, \(f = 0\), so the integral is zero for every piece and (25.2) holds.
  6. Conversely let (25.2) hold for every piece. Choose \(x_0 \in (a, b)\) and \(G(x) = \int_{\mathrm{x}_0}^{x} f\,\mathrm{d}t\). By step 4, \(G = 0\) everywhere on \((a, b)\). The function \(G\) is differentiable with derivative \(f\) (theorem 3.55, part 2), because \(f\) is continuous, and it is zero everywhere, so \(f = G' = 0\).

Source: The equilibrium of the piece is lemma 5.10. The same equation follows from example 3 under theorem 5.70, where the term \(\tfrac12\,k\,v^2\) means the energy of the springs. COOK §8.8 (PDF p. 301, read) takes \(U = \tfrac12\int\beta\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}A\) (8.8-1) for the energy of the foundation, for a beam with \(\mathrm{d}A = b\,\mathrm{d}x\), which is our term with \(k = \beta\,b\), VK (3.65)-(3.67) (PDF pp. 81-82, read) uses the same model for a plate. The proof with a finite piece is not from a source.

We obtained the equation from the equilibrium of a piece, and the route of chapter 5 gives it from energy. A spring per unit length has energy \(\tfrac12\,k\,v^2\) (like a spring of stiffness \(k\) and displacement \(v\)), its derivative with respect to the deflection is the force \(k\,v\), and the Euler-Lagrange equation gives the same term \(k\,v\) in the equation. The two routes agree, which is a test of the model.

Let us test the theorem on numbers. Let the beam have its own weight \(q = -61{,}21\) N/m (section 5.1.3, chapter 5) and let the deflection be constant, \(v_0 = q/k = -0{,}0612\) mm. Then \(v_0'''' = 0\) and equation (25.3) says \(0 + k\,v_0 = q\), which holds. By equation (25.2), \(V(x_2) - V(x_1) = 0\) and \(-\int(q - k\,v_0)\,\mathrm{d}t = 0\), since the springs carry exactly the weight, \(k\,v_0 = q\).

The theorem rejects a different deflection. Let \(v_1 = -0{,}1\) mm be constant. Then \(v_1'''' = 0\), but \(k\,v_1 = -100\) N/m and not \(q = -61{,}21\) N/m. The springs push up with \(100\) N/m, the weight pulls down with \(61{,}21\) N/m, and \(38{,}79\) N/m upward remains. On a piece 1 m long this is \(38{,}79\) N, while the shear force does not change at a constant deflection, \(V(x_2) - V(x_1) = 0\). Equation (25.2) does not hold, the piece would accelerate upward: a deflection of \(-0{,}1\) mm with no other forces is not an equilibrium.

Now we solve the most important case: a long beam with one force. A rail under a wheel is such a case, the beam is much longer than the region where it bends. We take it to be infinite so that the end does not matter, and later in the section we check how long a real one must be.

Equation (25.3) at \(q = 0\) is linear with constant coefficients, of the kind solved in section 9.4.7. There the four solutions are \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\beta x}\cos\beta x\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{\pm\beta x}\sin\beta x\) (figure 9.47), and four constants are to be fixed by conditions that we set up now. Under the force the conditions are given by lemma 5.44: \(v\), \(v'\) and \(M\) are continuous, and the shear force jumps by \(-F_{\mathrm{y}} = P\). Far from the force the deflection must stay bounded, because the beam is not loaded there.

Theorem 25.3 Infinite beam under a point force (neskončen nosilec s točkovno silo)

Let the beam be prismatic with \(EI\) and a foundation \(k\) along the whole axis, \(\beta = (k/(4\,EI))^{1/4}\). At the point \(x = 0\) let a force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -P\) (\(P > 0\), downward) act, and no other loads. Let \(v\) be four times continuously differentiable on \(x \neq 0\), let it solve (25.3) with \(q = 0\) on each side, let it be bounded on \(\mathbb{R}\) and let it satisfy the conditions of lemma 5.44 at \(x = 0\). Then there is exactly one such function and

\[v(x) = -\frac{P\beta}{2k}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta |x|}\big(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta |x|\big) . \tag{25.4}\]
Proof

On each side we write the general solution, boundedness removes two constants on each side, and the conditions under the force fix the remaining four.

  1. The equation is \(v'''' + 4\beta^4 v = 0\), because \(k = 4\,EI\,\beta^4\). By section 9.4.7 (theorem 9.44 and corollary 9.45) all real solutions on \(x > 0\) are \(v = \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x) + \mathrm{e}^{\beta x}(a\cos\beta x + b\sin\beta x)\), and on \(x < 0\) they are \(v = \mathrm{e}^{\beta x}(C\cos\beta x + D\sin\beta x) + \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(a'\cos\beta x + b'\sin\beta x)\).
  2. Let \((a, b) \neq (0, 0)\) and \(r = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2} > 0\). There is an angle \(\varphi\) with \(a\cos\beta x + b\sin\beta x = r\cos(\beta x - \varphi)\). At the points \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (\varphi + 2\pi n)/\beta\) (for \(n\) so large that \(x_{\mathrm{n}} > 0\)) the second term equals \(r\,\mathrm{e}^{\beta x_{\mathrm{n}}}\), which grows beyond every bound with \(n\), while the first term is at most \(|A| + |B|\) in absolute value. The function \(v\) is not bounded. Boundedness on \(x > 0\) therefore requires \(a = b = 0\).
  3. On \(x < 0\) the same argument at the points \(x_{\mathrm{n}} = (\varphi' - 2\pi n)/\beta \to -\infty\) gives \(a' = b' = 0\). What remains is \(v = \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x)\) for \(x > 0\) and \(v = \mathrm{e}^{\beta x}(C\cos\beta x + D\sin\beta x)\) for \(x < 0\).
  4. The derivatives at \(x = 0\) (checked with SymPy): from the right \(v = A\), \(v' = \beta(B - A)\), \(v'' = -2B\beta^2\), \(v''' = 2\beta^3(A + B)\). From the left \(v = C\), \(v' = \beta(C + D)\), \(v'' = 2D\beta^2\), \(v''' = 2\beta^3(D - C)\).
  5. Continuity of \(v\) gives \(C = A\). The moment \(M = EI\,v''\) is continuous, so \(-2B = 2D\), \(D = -B\). The slope \(v'\) is continuous: \(B - A = C + D = A - B\), so \(B = A\) and \(D = -A\).
  6. The shear force is \(V = -EI\,v'''\) and it jumps by \(V(0^+) - V(0^-) = -2\,EI\,\beta^3\big((A + B) - (D - C)\big) = -2\,EI\,\beta^3\cdot 4A = -8\,EI\,\beta^3 A\), where we inserted \(B = A\), \(D = -A\), \(C = A\). The jump must be \(P\), so \(A = -P/(8\,EI\,\beta^3)\). Since \(EI\,\beta^3 = k/(4\beta)\), \(A = -P\beta/(2k)\).
  7. For \(x > 0\), \(v = A\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta x)\), and for \(x < 0\), \(v = A\,\mathrm{e}^{\beta x}(\cos\beta x - \sin\beta x)\). Because \(\cos\beta x = \cos\beta|x|\) and \(\sin\beta x = -\sin\beta|x|\), on \(x < 0\) this equals \(A\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta|x|}(\cos\beta|x| + \sin\beta|x|)\). This is (25.4).
  8. The constants are determined uniquely (steps 2 to 6). Steps 5 and 6 are equivalent to the four conditions under the force, so the function of step 7 satisfies them all. It is bounded: \(|v| \le \sqrt{2}\,|A|\), because \(|\cos t + \sin t| \le \sqrt{2}\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta|x|} \le 1\).

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 370, read on the page image) treats the rail as an infinitely long beam on a foundation with modulus \(K\) and gives the maximum moment \(M_{\max} = \tfrac{P}{4}\sqrt[4]{4EI/K}\) (equation (b)). This is our \(M(0) = P/(4\beta)\) below the theorem, since \(\beta = (K/(4EI))^{1/4}\). The proof with boundedness and with lemma 5.44 is not from a source.

Figure 25.6 shows the theorem. Let us draw the first panel. The horizontal axis is \(t = \beta x\), a dimensionless distance measured in units of \(1/\beta = 0{,}538\) m, and it is the same in all three panels. The unit \(1/\beta\) is natural because \(k/(4\,EI)\) has unit \(\mathrm{m}^{-4}\), so \(\beta\) has unit \(\mathrm{m}^{-1}\). Every length built from \(EI\) and \(k\) is therefore \(1/\beta\) times a number. The deflection is the curve \(v/|v(0)|\) against \(t\). It is lowest under the force and decays fast: at \(t = \pi\), that is at \(x = 1{,}69\) m, only \(\mathrm{e}^{-\pi} = 0{,}0432\) of the largest deflection is left. At \(P = 10\) kN, \(v(0) = -P\beta/(2k) = -9{,}298\) mm. Since \(EI\,v''\) is the bending moment, the second derivative of equation (25.4) gives \(M(x) = \dfrac{P}{4\beta}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta|x|}\big(\cos\beta x - \sin\beta|x|\big)\). This is the moment in the third panel. It is largest under the force, \(M(0) = P/(4\beta) = 1344{,}4\) N m. Its zero is at \(t = \pi/4\), marked on the axis, so at \(x = 0{,}422\) m. Between \(t = \pi/4\) and \(t = 5\pi/4\) the moment is negative, and its smallest value is \(-0{,}208\,M(0)\) at \(t = \pi/2\).

A test of the model on numbers: the largest bending stress, from the moment \(M(0)\), is \(M(0)\cdot(h/2)/I = 1344{,}4\cdot 0{,}02/(1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}) = 252\) MPa, above the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa (definition 2.7, the value for our steel from chapter 3). At \(P = 10\) kN the linear model therefore no longer holds. Since the stress is proportional to \(P\), it holds up to \(P = 8{,}73\) kN. We keep the example because the numbers are clear, and the ratios in the figure do not depend on \(P\). The slope stays within the limits of the model: the largest \(v'\) is \(0{,}0111\) at \(t = \pi/4\), which gives \(v'^2 = 1{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\), and the limit \(v'^2 \le 10^{-2}\) of chapter 5 is met.

Now we estimate the cost of the other idealizations of definition 25.1 too. For each we say why it is acceptable here, when it fails and what it costs.

  • Linearity and constant \(k\). The force of the foundation is described by one number \(k\), the same under the whole beam. Why: at a small deflection every smooth force law is close to its tangent, and \(k\) is its slope. It fails when the foundation stiffens under a larger load or varies along the beam. Cost: the solution depends on \(k\) through \(\beta \propto k^{1/4}\), so the largest deflection is \(|v(0)| = P\beta/(2k) \propto k^{-3/4}\) and the largest moment is \(M(0) = P/(4\beta) \propto k^{-1/4}\). If the true \(k\) is twice as large, the deflection is smaller by the factor \(2^{3/4} = 1{,}68\), the moment and the stress only by the factor \(2^{1/4} = 1{,}19\).
  • Independent points. Each spring feels only the deflection above it. Why: in Zimmermann's model every sleeper has its own elastic support, and for Hertz's plate on water (below) the pressure of the water at each point depends only on the depth there. It fails for a solid foundation, such as the ground or a steel ring, which sinks also around the loaded point. Section 25.4 shows that the surface of a half-space under a point force sinks also far from it, in proportion to \(1/r\), while the Winkler foundation sinks only under the load. How much this changes the deflection of the beam we do not compute in this chapter.
  • Acting on both sides. The foundation pulls where \(v > 0\). Why: this holds for a beam attached to the foundation, and for every beam as long as the pull nowhere exceeds the pressure of its own weight. It fails for a beam that only lies on the foundation, at a larger force. Cost: below we compute that for our beam the foundation does not pull as long as \(P < 1524\) N.
  • No friction. The force of the foundation on the bottom face of the piece is vertical. Why: the load is vertical, and along the axis the bottom face moves only because the cross section turns, by \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -y\,v'\) at \(y = -h/2\), which at \(P = 10\) kN is at most \(0{,}02 \cdot 0{,}0111\) m \(= 0{,}22\) mm. It fails for a beam whose bottom is glued to the foundation or pressed into it. Cost: friction, which by definition 8.2 equals \(\mu\) times the pressure in sliding and is smaller at rest, would give on the bottom face, \(h/2\) below the axis, a distributed moment \(m\) with \(|m| \le \mu\,k\,|v|\,h/2\), and the equation would be \(EI\,v'''' + k\,v = q - m'\). Since \(v\) changes over lengths of the order \(1/\beta\), the term \(m'\) compared with the force of the foundation \(k\,|v|\) is of the order \(\mu\,\beta h/2 = 0{,}037\,\mu\), at \(\mu \le 1\) about 4 % or less.

The theorem has the hypothesis of boundedness. What happens without it? The function \(w = \cosh\beta x\,\cos\beta x\) is smooth on the whole axis and solves \(w'''' + 4\beta^4 w = 0\), because it is the real part of \(\cosh\big((1 + \mathrm{i})\beta x\big)\), whose fourth derivative is \((1 + \mathrm{i})^4\beta^4 = -4\beta^4\) times the same function. Being smooth, it has no jumps at \(x = 0\) and changes none of the four conditions under the force. So \(v + \epsilon\,w\) is, for every \(\epsilon\), another solution that meets all hypotheses of the theorem except boundedness.

Let us draw figure 25.7 for \(\epsilon = 1\) µm. The horizontal axis is again \(t = \beta x\), from the force to \(t = 4\pi\), that is to \(x = 6{,}76\) m. The force \(P\) presses at \(t = 0\). The blue curve is the bounded solution \(v\) of the theorem: under the force it is \(-9{,}30\) mm, and from \(t \approx 5{,}5\) on it cannot be told from the axis at the scale of the figure. The orange curve is \(v + \epsilon\,w\). Up to \(t = 2\pi\) it differs from the blue one by less than \(0{,}27\) mm, so we draw it only from there. At \(t = 2\pi\), \(x = 3{,}38\) m, \(\epsilon\,w = \epsilon\cosh 2\pi = 0{,}268\) mm. Then the orange curve swings \(9{,}6\) mm below the axis, deeper than the beam under the force, though nothing acts there, and at \(t = 4\pi\), \(x = 6{,}76\) m, it is already \(143\) mm above the axis. The dashed curve is \(\tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\,\mathrm{e}^{t}\), the growing part of \(\epsilon\cosh t = \tfrac{\epsilon}{2}\big(\mathrm{e}^{t} + \mathrm{e}^{-t}\big)\). At the points \(t = 2\pi n\), where \(\cos t = 1\), the orange curve touches it (the difference is \(v\), at \(t = 2\pi\) only \(0{,}017\) mm). These are the points \(x_{\mathrm{n}}\) of step 2 of the proof of theorem 25.3 with \(a = \tfrac12\), \(b = 0\) and \(\varphi = 0\). The hypothesis of boundedness is no decoration: without it there is no uniqueness. Of the two solutions the blue one is right, because far from the force the beam is not loaded and cannot bend more and more there.

Equilibrium says that the foundation must carry the whole force \(P\). Let us check that our solution gives this.

Lemma 25.4 Reaction of the foundation (reakcija podlage)

For the deflection (25.4) the total force of the foundation on the beam equals the force: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(-k\,v)\,\mathrm{d}x = P\), where \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\) is the sum of the integrals over \((-\infty, 0]\) and \([0, \infty)\).

Proof

By definition 9.21 the integral to infinity is the limit of integrals to \(T\), and the integral over \((-\infty, 0]\) is the limit of integrals from \(-T\) to \(0\). The function \(v\) is even, so both integrals are equal and it suffices to compute the integral over \(x > 0\).

  1. The derivative of \(-\tfrac1\beta\,\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\cos\beta x\) is \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\cos\beta x + \mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}\sin\beta x\) (rules for a product and a composite function, lemma 1.82).
  2. By the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.55, part 1), the area under the curve from \(0\) to \(T\) is \(\int_0^T\mathrm{e}^{-\beta x}(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac1\beta\big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\beta T}\cos\beta T\big)\).
  3. Since \(|\mathrm{e}^{-\beta T}\cos\beta T| \le \mathrm{e}^{-\beta T}\), which tends to zero, the limit is \(1/\beta\).
  4. The integral is the area under the curve of figure 25.6, multiplied by \(-k\). Both halves together: \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(-k\,v)\,\mathrm{d}x = k\,\dfrac{P\beta}{2k}\cdot\dfrac{2}{\beta} = P\).

Source: The computation is not from a source.

Let us show the lemma on figure 25.8. The horizontal axis is now \(x\) in metres, and the force \(P = 10\) kN presses at \(x = 0\). The blue curve is the force of the foundation per unit length, \(-k\,v(x)\), from the deflection (25.4). Where the beam is below its straight position, it is positive and the foundation pushes the beam up, most strongly under the force, with \(k\,|v(0)| = 9298\) N/m. The force of the foundation on a piece of the axis is the integral of this curve, that is the area under it. The grey area between \(x = -1{,}267\) m and \(1{,}267\) m is \(10{,}67\) kN, more than \(P\). Further from the force, between \(1{,}267\) m and \(2{,}956\) m on each side, the beam is above its straight position and the foundation pulls it down: the orange strips are \(0{,}70\) kN together, and we subtract this force. The strips still further from the force, too thin for the figure, add \(0{,}03\) kN. What remains is \(10{,}67 - 0{,}70 + 0{,}03 = 10{,}00\) kN \(= P\), as the lemma says.

The lemma also tells how far the effect of the force reaches. The dashed rectangle has the height \(k\,|v(0)|\), as if the foundation pushed everywhere as hard as under the force. To carry the force \(P\) its area must be \(P\), so its width is \(P/(k\,|v(0)|) = 2/\beta = 1{,}076\) m. The true curve falls away from the force, so the foundation carries the same force over a longer stretch: the grey area reaches to \(\pm 1{,}267\) m, that is \(\pm 3\pi/(4\beta)\), and the effect of the force reaches a few units of \(1/\beta = 0{,}54\) m.

One thing about the theorem surprised us: the function in (25.4) changes sign. What does this mean for the foundation? Hertz found the same pattern for another foundation.

From history

At the beginning of 1883 Hertz was occupied with the bending of an infinite plate floating on water and loaded normally at one point. He found that under the force the plate bends downward, but at a certain distance from the force the deflection changes sign and the plate rises, at a still larger distance it goes down again, and so on. The surface is therefore wavy, and the height of the waves quickly decreases with the distance from the force. He arrived at the paradoxical conclusion that a plate heavier than water can be kept afloat by loading it at its centre. The explanation is that the bending turns the plate into a shell, which presses out of the water more than the weight of the plate (TIMO, PDF p. 288, read).

Hertz's plate on water has the same pattern as our beam: a deflection under the force, then a sign that alternates, and an amplitude that decreases quickly. Water is a foundation of our kind for the plate: when the plate sinks by an additional depth \(w\), the buoyancy grows by \(\rho_{\mathrm{w}}\,g\,w\) per unit area, so in proportion to the displacement (this inference is ours, not the source's). The pattern is therefore not a property of our number or material, but of the law that the force is proportional to the deflection. Let us look at it on the beam.

Lemma 25.5 The foundation pulls the beam back (podlaga vleče nosilec nazaj)

For the deflection (25.4), \(v(x) > 0\) if and only if \(\beta|x|\) lies in one of the intervals \(\big(\tfrac{3\pi}{4} + 2j\pi,\ \tfrac{7\pi}{4} + 2j\pi\big)\), \(j = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) There the foundation pulls the beam down with a force \(-k\,v < 0\). The largest pull is at \(\beta|x| = \pi\) and equals \(k\,|v(0)|\,\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}\).

Proof

We must show where the function \(g(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-t}(\cos t + \sin t)\) has negative values for \(t \ge 0\) and where it is smallest.

  1. Since \(v = -\frac{P\beta}{2k}\,g(\beta|x|)\) and \(P\beta/(2k) > 0\), \(v > 0\) exactly where \(g(\beta|x|) < 0\).
  2. We have \(\cos t + \sin t = \sqrt{2}\,\sin(t + \pi/4)\), because \(\sin(t + \pi/4) = (\sin t + \cos t)/\sqrt{2}\). This expression is zero at \(t + \pi/4 = n\pi\), that is at \(t = 3\pi/4,\ 7\pi/4,\ 11\pi/4,\ \dots\)
  3. The factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-t}\) is positive, so \(g\) is negative exactly where \(\sin(t + \pi/4) < 0\), that is on the intervals \((3\pi/4 + 2j\pi,\ 7\pi/4 + 2j\pi)\). There \(v > 0\).
  4. The derivative is \(g' = -\mathrm{e}^{-t}(\cos t + \sin t) + \mathrm{e}^{-t}(\cos t - \sin t) = -2\,\mathrm{e}^{-t}\sin t\), zero at \(t = n\pi\), and \(g(n\pi) = (-1)^n\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi}\). The negative values of \(g\) have local minima at odd \(n\) with value \(-\mathrm{e}^{-n\pi}\), which decreases in absolute value with \(n\). The largest pull is therefore at \(t = \pi\): \(v = |v(0)|\,\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}\) and \(-k\,v = -k\,|v(0)|\,\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}\).

Source: The computation is not from a source. Hertz's paradox for a plate on water shows the alternation of sign (TIMO, PDF p. 288).

Let us look at figure 25.6. The deflection in the first panel rises above the axis at \(t = 3\pi/4\), but at the scale of the panel it is hardly visible. The second panel therefore shows the same deflection magnified 20 times, only to the right of the force. The zeros \(3\pi/4\) and \(7\pi/4\) are marked on the axis, and between them is the shaded region where \(v > 0\). At \(k = 1{,}0\cdot 10^6\) N/m\(^2\) this region lies, for every force, between \(x = 1{,}267\) m and \(2{,}956\) m, of length \(\pi/\beta = 1{,}689\) m. At \(P = 10\) kN the highest point is \(0{,}4018\) mm above the axis at \(x = 1{,}689\) m. There the foundation pulls the beam down with the force \(k\cdot 0{,}4018\) mm \(= 401{,}8\) N/m. The next region starts at \(11\pi/(4\beta) = 4{,}646\) m, and at its highest point it is \(\mathrm{e}^{-2\pi} = 0{,}0019\) times as high as the first.

Would the beam's own weight remove this? The lemma holds for a beam without weight. The weight \(\rho g A = 61{,}21\) N/m (chapter 5) lowers the beam by a further \(0{,}0612\) mm, so at \(t = \pi\) the total deflection is still \(+0{,}4018 - 0{,}0612 = +0{,}3406\) mm, and the foundation together with the weight still pulls, with \(340{,}6\) N/m. The pull at \(t = \pi\) equals \(P\beta\,\mathrm{e}^{-\pi}/2\), and the weight exceeds it only when it is smaller than \(61{,}21\) N/m, that is at \(P < 1524\) N. At a force of 10 kN the pull is 6,6 times the weight.

A foundation that pulls is not a foundation on which the beam only lies. The ground under a sleeper cannot pull. At \(P = 10\) kN the solution would ask it to pull between \(x = 1{,}27\) m and \(2{,}96\) m, with the beam's own weight between \(1{,}29\) m and \(2{,}61\) m, so a beam that only lies there would lift off the ground around that place. The real problem then has two parts: where the beam touches, the foundation acts as a spring, elsewhere the force is zero, and the boundary between them is unknown. We set up the contact conditions in section 25.5, but a beam that lifts off the foundation is not solved in this chapter. The model solved here is therefore correct for a foundation that is attached to the beam and can pull (a beam bolted to springs). For a foundation that only supports the beam it is correct as long as the total force of the foundation, that is the force that carries the weight plus \(-k\,v\), is not negative, so at \(P < 1524\) N.

What remains is a beam of finite length. Its ends are free: the shear force and the moment are zero there.

Corollary 25.6 A finite beam on a foundation (končni nosilec na podlagi)

Let the beam of length \(L\) be prismatic with \(EI\) and a foundation \(k\) along the whole length \([-L/2, L/2]\), \(\beta = (k/(4\,EI))^{1/4}\). Let the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = -P\) (\(P > 0\), downwards) act at the point \(x = 0\), and let there be no other loads. We seek a function \(v\) that is four times continuously differentiable separately on \([-L/2, 0]\) and on \([0, L/2]\) (with one-sided derivatives at the endpoints), solves (25.3) with \(q = 0\) on each side, meets the conditions of lemma 5.44 at \(x = 0\) and has free ends, \(V = M = 0\), that is \(v'' = v''' = 0\) at \(x = \pm L/2\). Then there is only one such function. It is even, and for \(x \ge 0\) it equals

\[v = c_1\cosh\beta x\cos\beta x + c_2\sinh\beta x\sin\beta x + c_3\cosh\beta x\sin\beta x + c_4\sinh\beta x\cos\beta x , \tag{25.5}\]

where the constants are the unique solution of the four linear equations \(v'(0) = 0\), \(-EI\,v'''(0^+) = P/2\), \(v''(L/2) = 0\), \(v'''(L/2) = 0\). The foundation carries the whole force: \(\int_{-\mathrm{L}/2}^{L/2}(-k\,v)\,\mathrm{d}x = P\).

Proof

We prove uniqueness with energy, get the symmetry from uniqueness, then write the system for the constants, show that a solution of the system gives a solution of the problem, and check the reaction.

  1. Let \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) be two solutions. The difference \(u = v_1 - v_2\) solves \(EI\,u'''' + k\,u = 0\) on each side of the force. The conditions under the force are the same for \(v_1\) and \(v_2\): \(v\), \(v'\) and \(v''\) are continuous, and \(v'''\) jumps by \(-P/EI\), because \(V = -EI\,v'''\). So \(u\), \(u'\), \(u''\) and \(u'''\) have equal limits from the left and from the right at \(x = 0\). At the ends \(u'' = u''' = 0\).
  2. Multiply the equation by \(u\) and integrate separately over \([-L/2, 0]\) and over \([0, L/2]\). Integrating by parts twice (corollary 3.56), on each half \(\int EI\,u''''u\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[EI\,u'''u - EI\,u''u'\big] + \int EI\,u''^2\,\mathrm{d}x\). The boundary terms at the ends \(\pm L/2\) are zero because \(u'' = u''' = 0\). The terms at \(x = 0\) from the two halves cancel, because the limits of \(u\), \(u'\), \(u''\), \(u'''\) from the left and from the right are equal (step 1). The sum of the two halves is \(\int_{-\mathrm{L}/2}^{L/2}\big(EI\,u''^2 + k\,u^2\big)\,\mathrm{d}x = 0\).
  3. The integrals over the two halves are non-negative and their sum is zero, so each is zero. On each half the integrand is continuous and non-negative and its integral is zero, so it is zero everywhere. Hence \(u = 0\) and the solution is unique.
  4. The mirror image \(x \mapsto v(-x)\) solves the same problem, because the load, the foundation and the conditions do not change under reflection. By uniqueness \(v(-x) = v(x)\).
  5. The functions \(\cosh t\cos t\), \(\sinh t\sin t\), \(\cosh t\sin t\), \(\sinh t\cos t\) are real and imaginary parts of \(\cosh\big((1 + \mathrm{i})t\big)\) and \(\sinh\big((1 + \mathrm{i})t\big)\), which solve \(y'''' = -4y\). Their initial data \((y, y', y'', y''')\) at \(t = 0\) are \((1, 0, 0, 0)\), \((0, 0, 2, 0)\), \((0, 1, 0, 2)\) and \((0, 1, 0, -2)\) (checked with SymPy), so they are linearly independent. By theorem 9.41 every solution on \(x > 0\) is determined by its initial data, so (25.5) is the general solution.
  6. The derivatives at \(x = 0\) are \(v'(0) = \beta(c_3 + c_4)\) and \(v'''(0) = 2\beta^3(c_3 - c_4)\). Evenness gives \(v'(0) = 0\), and \(V(0^+) = P/2\), because \(V\) jumps by \(P\) and \(V\) is odd. So \(c_4 = -c_3\) and \(-EI\cdot 4\beta^3 c_3 = P/2\), that is \(c_3 = -P\beta/(2k)\).
  7. Let the constants satisfy \(c_4 = -c_3\), \(c_3 = -P\beta/(2k)\) and the conditions \(v''(L/2) = v'''(L/2) = 0\). Then the even extension, \(v(x) = v(-x)\) for \(x < 0\), is a solution of the problem. On \(x < 0\) it solves the equation, because the equation contains only the even derivative \(v''''\). The functions \(v\) and \(v''\) are even, so their limits from the left and from the right at \(x = 0\) are equal. The function \(v'\) is odd with \(v'(0^+) = \beta(c_3 + c_4) = 0\), so \(v'(0^-) = 0\) too. The shear force \(V = -EI\,v'''\) is odd with \(V(0^+) = -EI\cdot 4\beta^3 c_3 = P/2\), so it jumps by \(P/2 - (-P/2) = P = -F_{\mathrm{y}}\), as lemma 5.44 requires. At the left end \(v''(-L/2) = v''(L/2) = 0\) and \(v'''(-L/2) = -v'''(L/2) = 0\).
  8. The two conditions at the end \(x = L/2\) give two linear equations for \(c_1\) and \(c_2\), and their matrix does not depend on \(P\). The matrix is invertible. Otherwise the system at \(P = 0\), where \(c_3 = c_4 = 0\), would have a solution \((c_1, c_2) \neq (0, 0)\). By step 7 its even extension would be a solution of the problem with \(P = 0\), not zero by the independence of the functions (step 5). The function \(v = 0\) is also a solution of the problem with \(P = 0\), which steps 1 to 3 exclude. So the system has exactly one solution, and by step 7 it gives a solution of the problem.
  9. On each side of the force \(-k\,v\)\( = EI\,v''''\). The integral over \([-L/2, 0)\) and \((0, L/2]\) gives \(EI\,\big(v'''(0^-) - v'''(-L/2)\big) + EI\,\big(v'''(L/2) - v'''(0^+)\big)\). The terms at the ends are zero, what remains is \(-EI\,\big(v'''(0^+) - v'''(0^-)\big) = V(0^+) - V(0^-) = P\).

Source: The proof with energy and four conditions is not from a source. Section 9.4.7 only found the four solutions and promised that the constants are fixed by the conditions at the ends, here we do it.

Let us compute an example: the same beam, \(P = 10\) kN, length \(L = 4\) m and \(L = 1\) m. The first means \(\beta L = 7{,}438\), the second \(\beta L = 1{,}860\).

Let us draw figure 25.9. The zero line is the position without load. On it lies the grey curve of the infinite beam from figure 25.6. The blue curve is the beam of length 4 m: near the middle it almost coincides with the grey one, and at the ends it rises above the zero line. The orange curve is the beam of length 1 m: its middle is considerably lower than for the infinite beam. Both follow equation (25.5) with the constants from the system of the corollary. For comparison the dashed lines show the deflection \(-P/(kL)\) of a beam that does not bend at all and lies on the springs like a rigid board: \(-2{,}5\) mm at \(L = 4\) m and \(-10\) mm at \(L = 1\) m.

The system of the corollary gives the following. At \(L = 4\) m the deflection under the force is \(-9{,}3142\) mm, the infinite beam has \(-9{,}2979\) mm (ratio \(1{,}0018\)). The ends rise by \(0{,}7554\) mm above the zero line. The infinite beam behaves in the same way: the end is at \(x = L/2 = 2\) m, in the region from \(1{,}267\) m to \(2{,}956\) m, where the infinite beam lies above the zero line (figure 25.6). The end of the beam with \(L = 1\) m is at \(x = 0{,}5\) m, before this region, and lies below the zero line. The total force of the foundation is \(10\,000{,}00\) N, as the corollary says. At \(L = 1\) m the deflection under the force is \(-11{,}371\) mm, that is \(22{,}3\) % more than for the infinite beam, and the ends sink by \(7{,}960\) mm. The beam is neither a rigid board nor an infinite beam: the deflection of the board, \(-10\) mm, is 12 % smaller than the true \(-11{,}371\) mm, because the beam does bend after all, and the infinite beam has \(-9{,}298\) mm because it has no ends that could sink.

The factor \(\mathrm{e}^{-\beta L/2}\), by which the envelope of the solution decays towards the end of the beam, is \(0{,}0243\) at \(L = 4\) m and \(0{,}3946\) at \(L = 1\) m. In the first case the middle differs from the infinite beam by \(0{,}18\) %, in the second by \(22\) %. These are two computed points, not a general limit.

The question from the story remains: how good is the replacement of springs by a continuous foundation? We also computed the same beam of length 4 m with \(P = 10\) kN on sleepers. The springs of stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = k\,s\) are at distance \(s\), and the force acts midway between two sleepers. The computation was done with the finite elements of chapter 12 (the matrix of lemma 12.4) with nodes at the sleepers, at the ends and under the force. The force of the spring at a sleeper is a nodal force, and between the nodes the beam carries no load, so the true deflection of the sleeper model is a polynomial of degree three on each element (\(EI\,v'''' = 0\)), which the finite elements capture exactly (as in theorem 12.13). So there is no element error: the table shows the exact deflections of the sleeper model. A check confirms this, since four elements between neighbouring nodes give the same deflections to six decimal places in millimetres.

The upper panel of figure 25.10 shows the sparsest row of sleepers. On the ground we put four sleepers at a spacing \(s = 1\) m, each as a spring of stiffness \(K_{\mathrm{t}} = k\,s = 10^6\) N/m, because it replaces one metre of continuous foundation. The thin grey line is the position of the axis without load. The force \(P\) acts in the middle, \(0{,}5\) m from both middle sleepers. The thick grey curve is the same beam on a continuous foundation, which sinks by \(9{,}31\) mm under the force. The orange curve is the beam on the sleepers, which sinks by \(12{,}00\) mm. The two foundations are equally stiff in total, four springs of \(10^6\) N/m like \(4\) m of foundation with \(k = 10^6\) N/m\(^2\), and both give a rigid board the deflection \(P/(4\cdot 10^6\ \mathrm{N/m}) = 2{,}5\) mm. They differ only in where they support: the continuous foundation supports the beam also under the force, while on the sleepers nothing supports it between the two middle sleepers, and there it bends more.

The test shows when the continuous foundation holds. The lower panel of figure 25.10 draws the table. On the horizontal axis is \(\beta s\), the spacing in units of \(1/\beta\), on the vertical one the deflection under the force, from 9 mm upward. The dashed line is the continuous foundation, \(9{,}314\) mm, and the five points are the rows of the table. At a spacing of \(0{,}25\) m, which is below half of \(1/\beta = 0{,}538\) m, the difference is \(0{,}08\) % and the point lies on the dashed line. At a spacing of \(0{,}5\) m, about \(1/\beta\), the difference is already \(1{,}4\) %, and with four sleepers on \(4\) m (\(\beta s = 1{,}86\)) it is \(29\) %: there the deflection is \(12{,}0\) mm and the continuous model underestimates it by \(22\) %, since it would give \(9{,}3\) mm. Zimmermann's step from the story therefore holds for the usual closely spaced sleepers and not for four sleepers on a beam.

We have thus derived, solved and tested the model. The solution shows that the effect of the force dies out over a distance of a few \(1/\beta\), that the foundation carries the whole force, and that the sign of the deflection alternates, so the foundation sometimes pulls the beam. The last is the key for the rest of the chapter: a foundation in which every point is independent cannot represent a body that sinks also around the loaded point, and it does not know when contact would break. In the next sections we therefore replace the Winkler foundation by a half-space.

25.2 The foundation in vibration and in the finite element method

In section 25.1 we laid a beam on a foundation that has its own spring under every point: a deflection \(v\) produces a force \(k\,v\) per unit length, and neighbouring points do not know each other. There we computed rest. This section answers two questions the book has promised. The first (chapter 13): how does the foundation change the modes of vibration of a beam, their shapes and frequencies? The second (chapter 12): where do we put the foundation in a finite element model, so that for a beam on a foundation the same holds as for a beam without it, and what happens if we put it in by a shortcut?

The model stays the one of section 25.1. The foundation is Winkler's (definition 25.1): a force \(k\,v\) per unit length, every point independent, springs pull as well as push. For vibration we add one more idealization and name it: the foundation has no mass, only the beam has inertia. COOK (PDF p. 301) remarks for a beam on a Winkler foundation that in dynamics the foundation also contributes mass. We do not include this mass, because the Winkler model does not say how much of it there is. The effect would be, for a foundation of mass \(0{,}1\,\rho A\) per unit length, an equation with \(\rho A + 0{,}1\,\rho A\) in front of \(w_{\mathrm{tt}}\), so every frequency drops by the factor \(1/\sqrt{1{,}1}\), the first from \(425{,}03\) to \(405{,}25\) 1/s (about \(5\) %), while the shapes stay the same. Neglecting it is therefore justified as long as the foundation mass is much smaller than the beam mass. The beam is steel, section \(20 \times 40\) mm, \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\) N m\(^2\), \(\rho A = 6{,}24\) kg/m (chapter 5), the foundation has \(k = 1{,}0 \cdot 10^6\) N/m\(^2\) as in section 25.1. The letter \(k\) has several meanings in the book. In this section it is always the foundation modulus. We write the mode index \(j\), although theorem 13.46 writes it \(k\).

25.2.1 Modes of a beam on a foundation

We start with what we know: a simply supported beam of length \(L = 2\) m has, by theorem 13.46, the modes \(\sin(j\pi x/L)\) and frequencies \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}0} = (j\pi/L)^2\sqrt{EI/(\rho A)}\). The question: what happens to them when the beam lies on a foundation?

Let us draw figure 25.11, the left part first. The foundation of the first mode consists of the lower horizontal line, the ground, and springs fixed to it, which carry the beam from below. The first mode is one half-wave of a sine above the grey rest position of the beam, with deflection zero at both supports. The springs follow the shape: under the middle they stretch most, near the supports least. Under the second mode the springs on one half stretch and on the other compress, since the deflection there has the opposite sign, and the middle of the beam is at rest. The third mode has two zeros inside the beam, so its springs are stretched, compressed and stretched again in turn. In all three cases the force of the spring at every point is proportional to the deflection at that point. This will decide everything.

Before proving it, let us say what we look for. The beam vibrates when the deflection at every point is \(w(x, t) = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\), and such a pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of vibration (definition 13.6) if it satisfies the equation of motion and the support conditions. The equation of motion of a beam on a foundation must first be derived, since theorem 13.37 does not contain the foundation. That is the first step of the proof.

Theorem 25.7 Modes of a simply supported beam on a foundation (načini prosto podprtega nosilca na podlagi)

Let a uniform beam with constant \(EI\), \(\rho A\) and length \(L\) be simply supported at both ends (definition 13.39), let it lie on a Winkler foundation of modulus \(k > 0\) (definition 25.1) without mass, and let no other load act on it. Then:

  1. The equation of motion, in which the term \(k\,w\) belongs to the springs of the foundation, is
    \[\rho A\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} + EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} + k\,w = 0 \quad \text{on } (0, L) , \tag{25.6}\]
    and the support conditions are \(w = w_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\) at \(x = 0\) and \(x = L\), as for a beam without the foundation.
  2. A pair \((\omega, \varphi)\) with \(\omega > 0\) is a mode of vibration exactly when \(\varphi\) is a nonzero multiple of \(\sin(j\pi x/L)\) with an integer \(j \ge 1\) and
    \[\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}^2 + \frac{k}{\rho A} , \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{j}0} = \frac{(j\pi)^2}{L^2}\sqrt{\frac{EI}{\rho A}} . \tag{25.7}\]
  3. For every \(j\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}} > \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}} > \sqrt{k/(\rho A)}\). The difference \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}} - \omega_{\mathrm{j}0} = \dfrac{k/(\rho A)}{\omega_{\mathrm{j}} + \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}}\) is smaller than \(\dfrac{k}{2\rho A\,\omega_{\mathrm{j}0}}\) and tends to zero as \(j \to \infty\).
Proof

We must show that the foundation adds to the equation one term without derivatives, that this term only shifts the frequency, and that the shapes stay sines.

  1. By section 25.1 the foundation has energy \(\tfrac12\int_0^L k\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), that is the energy \(\tfrac12 k\,w^2\) of a spring per unit length, and this energy contains no derivatives. The action is the action (13.41) decreased by \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2}\tfrac12\int_0^L k\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\). At \(w + \alpha\eta\) the derivative of this term with respect to \(\alpha\) at \(0\) is \(-\int\!\int k\,w\,\eta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}t\), so \(B_1\) of the proof of theorem 13.37 gains this term, and the function \(R\) of step 5 of that proof becomes \(R = -\rho A\,w_{\mathrm{tt}} - EI\,w_{\mathrm{xxxx}} - k\,w + q\) with \(q = 0\). The term \(k\,w\,\eta\) has no boundary contributions, so the natural conditions and the support conditions stay unchanged. The rest of the proof (the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations) is as for theorem 13.37 and gives equation (25.6). This is claim 1.
  2. Take a mode \((\omega, \varphi)\), \(w = \varphi(x)\cos\omega t\). As in step 2 of the proof of theorem 13.40, \(\big(EI\,\varphi'''' + k\,\varphi - \rho A\,\omega^2\varphi\big)\cos\omega t = 0\), so at \(t = 0\)
    \[EI\,\varphi'''' = (\rho A\,\omega^2 - k)\,\varphi \quad \text{on } [0, L] , \qquad \varphi(0) = \varphi''(0) = \varphi(L) = \varphi''(L) = 0 .\]
  3. Multiply the equation by \(\varphi\) and integrate. Integrating by parts twice (corollary 3.56) gives \(\int_0^L\varphi\varphi''''\,\mathrm{d}x = \big[\varphi\varphi''' - \varphi'\varphi''\big]_0^L + \int_0^L(\varphi'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the bracket is zero because \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi''\) vanish at both ends. Hence \(EI\int_0^L(\varphi'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x = (\rho A\,\omega^2 - k)\int_0^L\varphi^2\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  4. The integral \(\int\varphi^2\) is positive, since \(\varphi^2\) is continuous, nonnegative and not everywhere zero (lemma 6.10, item 3). If \(\int(\varphi'')^2\) were \(0\), then \(\varphi''\) would be zero everywhere (the same lemma), \(\varphi\) would be linear with \(\varphi(0) = \varphi(L) = 0\), so \(\varphi = 0\), which it is not. So the left side of step 3 is positive and \(\rho A\,\omega^2 - k > 0\): no frequency lies below the dashed line of figure 25.11. By step 3 inertia, \(\rho A\,\omega^2\int\varphi^2\), balances both forces that pull the beam back, bending and the springs, so \(\rho A\,\omega^2\) is larger than \(k\) alone. Let \(\Omega = \sqrt{\omega^2 - k/(\rho A)} > 0\).
  5. The equation of step 2 is now \(\varphi'''' = \beta^4\varphi\) with \(\beta^4 = \rho A\,\Omega^2/EI\), and the simply supported beam without a foundation has the same conditions. By theorem 13.40, \((\Omega, \varphi)\) is a mode of the beam without the foundation, so by theorem 13.46 \(\varphi\) is a multiple of \(\sin(j\pi x/L)\) and \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}\), the grey line. From the definition of \(\Omega\) it follows that \(\omega^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}^2 + k/(\rho A)\).
  6. Conversely: for \(\varphi = \sin(j\pi x/L)\) we have \(\varphi'''' = (j\pi/L)^4\varphi\), so \(EI\,\varphi'''' + k\,\varphi = \big(EI\,(j\pi/L)^4 + k\big)\varphi = \rho A\,(\omega_{\mathrm{j}0}^2 + k/(\rho A))\varphi = \rho A\,\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2\varphi\), since \(EI\,(j\pi/L)^4 = \rho A\,\omega_{\mathrm{j}0}^2\) by equation (13.51). The support conditions hold since \(\varphi'' = -(j\pi/L)^2\varphi\). With step 2 read backwards, \(w = \varphi\cos\omega_{\mathrm{j}} t\) solves equation (25.6). This is claim 2.
  7. Claim 3: \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) is a sum of two positive numbers, so it is larger than each of them. The difference of squares \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}^2 = k/(\rho A)\) is the area of the band between the squares with sides \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}0}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}}\). The band consists of two strips of width \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}} - \omega_{\mathrm{j}0}\), of lengths \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}0}\), so its area is \((\omega_{\mathrm{j}} - \omega_{\mathrm{j}0})(\omega_{\mathrm{j}} + \omega_{\mathrm{j}0})\), which gives the formula. Since \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}} + \omega_{\mathrm{j}0} > 2\omega_{\mathrm{j}0}\), the width of the band is smaller than \(k/(2\rho A\,\omega_{\mathrm{j}0})\). Since \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}0} = j^2\omega_{10}\) grows beyond every bound, this estimate tends to zero: a band of the same area around an ever larger square is ever thinner.

Source: COOK (PDF p. 301): the foundation adds a term \(\tfrac12 k\,w^2\) to the energy, the foundation matrix has the form of the mass matrix. CK example 13.2 (PDF pp. 411 to 413) for the modes of a beam without a foundation. The proof in steps is not from the sources, it combines theorem 13.37, theorem 13.40 and theorem 13.46.

The proof showed three things. The foundation adds to the equation a term \(k\,w\) without derivatives (step 1). For a sine this term is proportional to the sine itself, so the shape stays (step 6). So only the square of the frequency changes, by the constant number \(k/(\rho A)\) (step 5). The reason for both is the same: the spring under a point pulls back in proportion to the deflection at that point, and for a sine the bending force of the beam per unit length, \(EI\,\varphi''''\), is proportional to the deflection too.

Let us draw figure 25.12. Step 3 of the proof says that for a mode \(\rho A\,\omega^2\int\varphi^2 = EI\int(\varphi'')^2 + k\int\varphi^2\). We divide by \(\rho A\int\varphi^2\) and get \(\omega^2\) as a sum of two parts, which we draw as a bar. The vertical axis is \(\omega^2\) in units of \(10^5\) 1/s\(^2\). For the first mode, \(\varphi = \sin(\pi x/L)\), the lower, orange part is the contribution of the springs, \(k/(\rho A) = 1{,}603\). It is the same for every mode, since a spring pulls back in proportion to the deflection. On it we put the blue part, the contribution of bending, \(EI\int(\varphi'')^2/(\rho A\int\varphi^2) = \omega_{10}^2 = 0{,}204\). The bar ends at \(\omega_1^2 = 1{,}807\). For the second mode the orange part is the same and the blue one is \(\omega_{20}^2 = 3{,}264\), sixteen times larger: the waves are half as long, so \(\varphi''\) is four times larger at the same deflection and \((\varphi'')^2\) sixteen times. The bar reaches \(\omega_2^2 = 4{,}866\). The dashed line is at the height \(k/(\rho A)\), which the orange part alone already reaches. The blue part is never negative, since \((\varphi'')^2 \ge 0\), and it is positive, since \(\varphi\) is not linear (step 4), so every bar ends above the dashed line. The third, dashed bar shows what a frequency below the line would mean, for example \(\omega^2 = 1{,}0\): the blue part would have to be \(-0{,}603\), which is impossible with \(EI\int(\varphi'')^2 \ge 0\).

Let us draw figure 25.13, which shows claim 3 as areas. For the first mode we draw a grey square with side \(\omega_{10} = 142{,}82\) 1/s and around it, with the same lower left corner, an orange square with side \(\omega_1 = 425{,}03\) 1/s. The areas of the squares are \(\omega_{10}^2\) and \(\omega_1^2\), so the band between them has the area \(\omega_1^2 - \omega_{10}^2 = k/(\rho A) = 1{,}603 \cdot 10^5\) 1/s\(^2\) (equation (25.7)). The width of the band is the frequency shift, \(282{,}21\) 1/s. We draw the same in the same scale for the second and the third mode. All three bands have the same area, but the squares grow like \(j^2\), so the band gets ever thinner: the widths are \(126{,}30\) and \(60{,}90\) 1/s. The band of the third mode is \(\omega_3 + \omega_{30} = 2631{,}66\) 1/s long, and width times length is again \(1{,}603 \cdot 10^5\) 1/s\(^2\).

Let us look at the numbers on the right part of the figure. The vertical axis is the circular frequency \(\omega\) and the dashed line on it is \(\sqrt{k/(\rho A)} = 400{,}32\) 1/s, the lowest frequency the foundation allows (claim 3). For each mode there are two horizontal lines: the grey one is the frequency without the foundation, the orange one with it, the arrow between them is the shift. For the first mode the frequency jumps from \(142{,}82\) to \(425{,}03\) 1/s, that is \(2{,}98\) times, for the second from \(571{,}28\) to \(697{,}58\) 1/s (\(1{,}22\) times), for the third from \(1285{,}38\) to \(1346{,}28\) 1/s (\(1{,}047\) times) and for the fourth from \(2285{,}13\) to \(2319{,}93\) 1/s (\(1{,}015\) times). The numbers are written for the first two. By claim 3 the shift is less than \(k/(2\rho A\,\omega_{\mathrm{j}0})\), and it falls because the beam has greater own stiffness at higher modes: at \(j = 4\), \(\omega_{40}^2 = 5{,}22 \cdot 10^6\) 1/s\(^2\) and \(k/(\rho A) = 1{,}60 \cdot 10^5\) 1/s\(^2\), so the foundation adds only \(3\) % of the square. For the first mode, \(\omega_{10}^2 = 2{,}04 \cdot 10^4\) 1/s\(^2\) and the foundation adds almost eight times this (\(7{,}9\) times).

A foundation that changes along the length. The theorem is not as general as it looks. If the foundation is not uniform, for example if \(k = 0\) under the left half of the beam and \(k > 0\) under the right, the sine is no longer a mode.

Let us draw figure 25.14. The beam is simply supported and vibrates as \(\sin(\pi x/L)\). Under the left half there are no springs, under the right half there are. The two points \(x = L/4\) and \(x = 3L/4\) are marked, since we will compare the multiplier there. For \(\varphi = \sin(\pi x/L)\) we would have \(EI\,\varphi'''' + k(x)\varphi = \big(EI\,(\pi/L)^4 + k(x)\big)\varphi\) and the multiplier would be different at \(x = L/4\) than at \(x = 3L/4\), where \(\varphi \ne 0\). The equation \(= \rho A\,\omega^2\varphi\) with a single \(\omega\) cannot hold. The proof used a constant \(k\) in step 6: a constant multiplier is what the sine preserves.

A beam without supports. The same procedure holds for a free beam lying only on the foundation. The rigid translation \(\varphi = 1\) and the rigid rotation \(\varphi = x - L/2\) have frequency zero without the foundation (\(\varphi'''' = 0\)). With it, each has \(\omega^2 = k/(\rho A)\), that is \(\omega = 400{,}32\) 1/s or \(63{,}7\) Hz: the beam bounces on the springs. This is the dashed line in figure 25.11. In the finite element model (the next part) it shows as the two lowest natural frequencies of a free beam \(L = 4\) m: \(400{,}32\) and \(400{,}32\) 1/s, and the third is \(408{,}42\) 1/s (num-02.out, item 4). The third is the first bending mode: the free beam without the foundation has \(\omega = (4{,}7300/L)^2\sqrt{EI/(\rho A)} = 80{,}9\) 1/s (figure 13.83) and \(\sqrt{80{,}9^2 + 400{,}32^2} = 408{,}4\) 1/s.

25.2.2 The foundation in the finite element model

In chapter 12 we divided the beam into elements. Each element is an interval \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) of length \(h\), has four unknowns \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (v_1, \varphi_1, v_2, \varphi_2)^\T\) and a deflection \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) from Hermite functions (definition 12.3). The bending energy gives the stiffness matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 12.4), the kinetic energy the consistent mass matrix \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 12.43). What does the energy of the foundation springs give?

Let us draw figure 25.15, the left part first. The ground is below the element and springs are fixed to it, one for every point of the element, all with the same stiffness \(k\) per unit length, as in section 25.1. The dashed line is the rest position of the upper end. The displacement \(v_1\) is the downward displacement of node 1 without rotation, node 2 stays at rest. The blue deflection is then \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = v_1H_1\) and the length \(h\) is the length of the element between the nodes \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) and \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\). The constant \(k\) is the same under all points. The springs are compressed differently: under node 1 by \(v_1\), under node 2 by nothing.

A spring per unit length has energy \(\tfrac12 k\,v^2\), so the energy of the foundation under the element is an integral over a finite piece \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\), and not a sum over small parts. By step 1 of the proof of the next lemma it is a quadratic form in \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). Before computing it, let us look at the shortcut we see on the right panel: we replace the foundation by two nodal springs, each of stiffness \(kh/2\) (label). The total stiffness is the same, \(kh\), which is the same trick as the lumped mass of a beam, where the mass \(\rho A h\) was divided in halves at the ends (definition 12.44). On the right are the same ground, the same rest position, the same element of length \(h\), the same deflection and the same displacement, but the springs are only at the ends. COOK (PDF p. 301) calls such discrete springs "awkward and error-prone", because their stiffnesses depend on the spacing of the nodes.

Lemma 25.8 Foundation matrix of a beam element (matrika podlage elementa nosilca)

Let \([x_{\mathrm{a}}, x_{\mathrm{b}}]\) be a finite element of a beam of length \(h\) (definition 12.3) on a Winkler foundation of constant modulus \(k\). Then:

  1. The energy of the foundation under the element is \(U_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}} = \tfrac12\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\,\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) with
    \[\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}} = k\int_{\mathrm{x}_\mathrm{a}}^{x_{\mathrm{b}}}\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{k h}{420}\begin{pmatrix} 156 & 22h & 54 & -13h \\ 22h & 4h^2 & 13h & -3h^2 \\ 54 & 13h & 156 & -22h \\ -13h & -3h^2 & -22h & 4h^2 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{25.8}\]
  2. \(\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}} = \dfrac{k}{\rho A}\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\), where \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the consistent mass matrix (12.47) of the element with constant \(\rho A\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\) is symmetric and positive definite. A displacement of the element as a whole, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (1, 0, 1, 0)^\T\), has \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = k h\), and a rotation about the middle, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (-h/2, 1, h/2, 1)^\T\), has \(k h^3/12\).
  4. For a beam with \(n\) elements and selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) (theorem 12.9), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}} = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) is the matrix for which \(\vek d^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\vek d = \int_0^L k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) at \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} d_{\mathrm{I}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\), and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}} = \dfrac{k}{\rho A}\,\mat M\) with \(\mat M\) from equation (12.50) when \(k\) and \(\rho A\) are the same on all elements. For the energy form \(B(w, z) = \int_0^L EI\,w''z''\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L k\,w\,z\,\mathrm{d}x\) we have \((\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{p}})_{\mathrm{IJ}} = B(H_{\mathrm{J}}, H_{\mathrm{I}})\).
Proof

We must show that the foundation energy is a quadratic form with this matrix, that the matrix is indeed the mass matrix times a constant, that it has these properties and that it assembles like the others.

  1. Since \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), \(v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\) \(= \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) (lemma 1.102). The column \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) does not depend on \(x\), so by linearity of the integral (lemma 6.10) \(\tfrac12\int k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\big(k\int\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat H_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x\big)\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\). This is the first expression of claim 1.
  2. The entries \(k\int H_{\mathrm{i}}H_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) are the same integrals that SymPy computed in step 4 of the proof of lemma 12.43, with \(k\) instead of \(\rho A\): for example \(k\int H_1^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \tfrac{13}{35}\,kh = \tfrac{156}{420}\,kh\). All ten different entries are in matrix (25.8) and SymPy shows \(\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}} - (k/\rho A)\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}} = \mat 0\) (num-02.py, item 1). This is claim 2.
  3. Symmetry and positive definiteness: by claim 2, \(\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\) is a positive multiple of \(\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\), which has both properties by lemma 12.43. For \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = (1, 0, 1, 0)^\T\) we get \(\tfrac{kh}{420}(156 + 54 + 54 + 156) = kh\) and for \((-h/2, 1, h/2, 1)^\T\), by step 7 of lemma 12.43, \(\tfrac{k}{\rho A}\cdot\rho A h^3/12 = kh^3/12\).
  4. As in step 1 of the proof of theorem 12.9, \(\vek d^\T\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\vek d = \vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{e}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{e}}}k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) and the sum over \(e\) gives \(\int_0^L k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\) by lemma 6.10 (item 1). Since \(\mat M = \sum_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}} = (k/\rho A)\,\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\) for every \(e\), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}} = (k/\rho A)\,\mat M\).
  5. For \(B\): the entry \((I, J)\) of \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\) is \(\int_0^L k\,H_{\mathrm{J}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) (step 3 of the proof of theorem 12.9 with \(k\,H_{\mathrm{J}} H_{\mathrm{I}}\) in place of \(EI\,H_{\mathrm{J}}''H_{\mathrm{I}}''\)), and \(\mat K\) is by item 2 of that theorem \(\int EI\,H_{\mathrm{J}}''H_{\mathrm{I}}''\,\mathrm{d}x\). The sum is \(B(H_{\mathrm{J}}, H_{\mathrm{I}})\).

Source: COOK §8.8 (PDF p. 301): "Matrix [\(k_\psi\)] has the same form as the mass matrix [m] used in dynamics" for a beam on a Winkler foundation, and the energy \(\tfrac12 k w^2\). Steps 1 to 5 are not from the source, they follow lemma 12.43.

Let us draw figure 25.16. On the left the element is moved down by one unit as a whole, so all springs are compressed equally and twice the energy, \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\), equals \(kh\), the stiffness \(k\) per unit length times the length \(h\). On the right the element turns about its middle: the left half goes up and the right half goes down. The springs are therefore stretched on the left and compressed on the right, by \(h/2\) at the ends, and twice their energy is \(kh^3/12\).

Let us draw figure 25.17. The beam is divided into three elements, each with its own deflection \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\). Below them is the square of the deflection, and the area under it per element, multiplied by \(k\), is twice the foundation energy \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}^\T\mat k_{\mathrm{p},\mathrm{e}}\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) of that element. The sum of the three areas is twice the foundation energy of the whole beam, \(\int_0^L k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the selection matrices \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) only put each element in its place.

Let us draw figure 25.18. On the left the element moves downward, node 1 with velocity \(\dot v_1\), node 2 at rest, and the velocities in between follow \(H_1\). On the right is the same element on springs, displaced by \(v_1\) at node 1 and by the same \(H_1\) in between. Under the left one is the square of the velocity \(\dot v_1^2H_1^2\), which the kinetic energy multiplies by \(\rho A\) and integrates. Under the right one is the square of the displacement \(v_1^2H_1^2\), which the foundation energy multiplies by \(k\) and integrates. The two curves are the same, the area under each is \(\tfrac{13}{35}h\), so the entry \((1, 1)\) of the mass matrix is \(\tfrac{13}{35}\rho A h\) and that of the foundation matrix is \(\tfrac{13}{35}kh\). The only difference is the factor \(k/(\rho A)\).

The lemma says something we do not expect: the foundation matrix is the mass matrix multiplied by a constant. The reason is in steps 1 and 2: both the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\int\rho A\,\dot v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\) and the foundation energy \(\tfrac12\int k\,v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\) are integrals of the square of the field without derivatives, so they have the same quadratic forms. In the bending energy the integrand is the square of the second derivative and the matrix is different.

Let us test it on one element with \(h = 1\) m and \(k = 10^6\) N/m\(^2\). Figure 25.19 shows what energy the foundation gives in different states of the element.

On the left, the axes show the position \(x\) from \(x_{\mathrm{a}}\) to \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\) and vertically the square of the deflection. The blue curve is \(v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\) at \(v_1 = 1\): at node 1 it is \(1\), at node 2 zero, between them it falls as \(H_1^2\). The orange line is \(v_{\mathrm{h}}^2\) as two nodal springs see it: the deflection is \(1\) at node 1 and \(0\) at node 2, and what happens between is not asked. The areas under them, \(\tfrac{13}{35}h\) and \(\tfrac12 h\), are the \((1, 1)\) entries of the consistent and the nodal matrix in units of \(k\), and they are different. On the right (axes, blue curve) the element is only rotated at node 1: the deflection is zero at both nodes, so the nodal model sees nothing, but in reality the springs in between are stretched and the area is \(h^3/105\).

The numbers at \(h = 1\) m, twice the energy in N m (num-02.out, item 2b):

state of the element \(\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\) consistent matrix nodal springs ratio nodal / consistent
\(v_1 = 1\) m, rest \(0\) \(3{,}714 \cdot 10^5\) \(5{,}000 \cdot 10^5\) \(1{,}346\)
\(v_1 = v_2 = 1\) m \(1{,}000 \cdot 10^6\) \(1{,}000 \cdot 10^6\) \(1\)
\(v_1 = 1\) m, \(v_2 = -1\) m \(4{,}857 \cdot 10^5\) \(1{,}000 \cdot 10^6\) \(2{,}059\)
\(\varphi_1 = 1\), rest \(0\) \(9{,}524 \cdot 10^3\) \(0\) \(0\)

Of the states in the table, the nodal model agrees with the consistent matrix only for a displacement of the element as a whole (second row), in the others it gives a different energy, and in both directions: more for unequal displacements, zero for a rotation. This will be decisive for the bound in the next part.

The lemma holds for the foundation and also immediately gives a discrete version of theorem 25.7.

Corollary 25.9 Frequencies of the model with a foundation (frekvence modela s podlago)

Let a simply supported beam be made of \(n\) Hermite elements with the consistent mass matrix \(\mat M\), let \(\mat K\) be the bending stiffness matrix of the free unknowns (theorem 12.9) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}}\) the foundation matrix (lemma 25.8), all with the displacements of nodes 0 and \(n\) removed. Then the pairs \((\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{p}},\ \mat M)\) and \((\mat K,\ \mat M)\) have the same eigenvectors and eigenvalues \(\lambda^h_{\mathrm{r}} + k/(\rho A)\) and \(\lambda^h_{\mathrm{r}}\) (definition 10.13), where \(\lambda^h_{\mathrm{r}} = (\omega^h_{\mathrm{r}0})^2\). So \((\omega^h_{\mathrm{r}})^2 = (\omega^h_{\mathrm{r}0})^2 + k/(\rho A)\) and

\[\omega^h_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{\omega_{\mathrm{r}0}^2 + \frac{k}{\rho A}}\]

for every \(r = 1, \dots, N\), where \(N\) is the number of free unknowns and \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) the natural frequency of theorem 25.7.

Proof

We must show that the foundation matrix is a multiple of the mass matrix, then use corollary 13.83.

  1. By item 4 of lemma 25.8, \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}} = (k/\rho A)\,\mat M\) on all unknowns. Removing the same row and the same column keeps the relation \(\mat K_{\mathrm{p}} = (k/\rho A)\,\mat M\) on the free unknowns too.
  2. \((\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{p}})\vek d = \lambda\mat M\vek d\) is equivalent to \(\mat K\vek d = (\lambda - k/\rho A)\,\mat M\vek d\) by step 1, so \(\vek d\) is an eigenvector of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) with value \(\lambda - k/\rho A\), and conversely. The eigenvectors are the same, the eigenvalues differ by \(k/\rho A\).
  3. By corollary 13.83, \(\lambda^h_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}0}\) for \(r = 1, \dots, N\) for a simply supported beam. We add \(k/\rho A\) to both sides: \((\omega^h_{\mathrm{r}})^2 \ge \omega_{\mathrm{r}0}^2 + k/\rho A = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) by equation (25.7).

Source: The proof in steps is not from the sources, it follows lemma 25.8 and corollary 13.83.

Let us draw figure 25.20. On the left is the axis of the eigenvalues \(\lambda = \omega^2\) in units of \(10^5\) 1/s\(^2\). The grey dots are the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) of the model with \(n = 2\), that is without the foundation: \(0{,}206\), \(4{,}021\) and \(25{,}402\). The orange dots are the eigenvalues with the foundation, \(1{,}808\), \(5{,}623\) and \(27{,}005\). All three arrows have the same length, \(k/(\rho A) = 1{,}603\), because the foundation adds the same amount to every eigenvalue. On the right are the bars for the second mode. The lower one is the exact one, with the grey part \(\omega_{20}^2 = 3{,}264\) and the orange part \(k/(\rho A)\). The upper one is the model one, with the grey part \((\omega^h_{20})^2 = 4{,}021\) and the same orange part. The difference between the ends of the grey parts, \(0{,}757\), is the same as between the ends of the whole bars, so the model bar stays longer with the foundation too.

The numbers for the beam of figure 25.11, \(L = 2\) m, are in the table (num-02.out, items 3 and 3b). All are in 1/s.

\(n\) model \(\omega_1\) \(\omega_2\) \(\omega_3\)
exact values with the foundation \(425{,}03\) \(697{,}58\) \(1346{,}28\)
2 without the foundation \(143{,}38\) \(634{,}08\) \(1593{,}80\)
2 consistent foundation \(425{,}22\) \(749{,}87\) \(1643{,}31\)
4 consistent foundation \(425{,}05\) \(699{,}43\) \(1368{,}72\)
8 consistent foundation \(425{,}03\) \(697{,}70\) \(1347{,}86\)

At \(n = 2\), \(\sqrt{143{,}38^2 + 400{,}32^2} = 425{,}22\) and \(\sqrt{634{,}08^2 + 400{,}32^2} = 749{,}87\), exactly what the corollary says. All consistent frequencies are above the exact ones, as they must be. The error grows with the order of the mode: at \(n = 2\) it is \(0{,}045\) % for the first and \(7{,}5\) % for the second mode, since a mesh of two elements describes the second half-wave shape badly. At \(n = 8\) the third error is \(0{,}12\) %.

Nodal springs give something else, and not always higher. At \(n = 2\) and nodal springs the frequencies are \(417{,}98\), \(634{,}08\) and \(1637{,}65\) 1/s. The first and the second are below the exact \(425{,}03\) and \(697{,}58\), which the corollary excludes for the consistent model. The second, \(634{,}08\) 1/s, is exactly the frequency of the model without the foundation: in the second mode the middle node has deflection zero, so the nodal spring does not feel it and the foundation does nothing. The consistent foundation raises the same frequency of the model to \(749{,}87\) 1/s (corollary 25.9), and the exact frequency of the beam on the foundation is \(697{,}58\) 1/s (theorem 25.7), \(63{,}5\) 1/s above the nodal model. At \(n = 4\) and \(8\) all three are above the exact ones. So at a coarse mesh the model with nodal springs can have a frequency below the true one, which the consistent one cannot. The reason is in the table of figure 25.19: the nodal model has another energy of the foundation, larger for some fields and smaller for others than the true one, so it is neither an upper nor a lower bound.

25.2.3 The deflection under a force in the consistent finite element model is always too small

The free beam of section 25.1, of length \(L = 4\) m or \(L = 1\) m, on a foundation with \(k = 10^6\) N/m\(^2\), loaded in the middle by a force \(P = 10\) kN, has a deflection under the force of \(9{,}3142\) mm and \(11{,}3713\) mm (corollary 25.6, \(\beta L = 7{,}438\) and \(1{,}860\)). The model with the consistent foundation matrix gives at \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16\) elements (num-02.out, item 2):

\(L\) \(n = 2\) \(n = 4\) \(n = 8\) \(n = 16\) exact
4 m \(7{,}1744\) \(8{,}9281\) \(9{,}2855\) \(9{,}3123\) \(9{,}3142\)
1 m \(11{,}3290\) \(11{,}3687\) \(11{,}3712\) \(11{,}3713\) \(11{,}3713\)
