(all in mm). At \(L = 4\) m the values are always below the exact one, the error is \(23\) %, \(4{,}1\) %, \(0{,}31\) % and \(0{,}02\) %. At \(L = 1\) m the last value looks equal to the exact one, but only to four decimals. With a more accurate computation (num-02.out, item 5) the exact value is \(11{,}371348\) mm and \(n = 8, 16, 32\) give \(11{,}371184\), \(11{,}371338\) and \(11{,}371348\) mm, so still below or equal up to rounding, and the difference falls by a factor of \(16\) when \(n\) doubles (\(1{,}6 \cdot 10^{-4}\), \(1{,}0 \cdot 10^{-5}\), \(6{,}4 \cdot 10^{-7}\) mm). The factor \(16\) is measured, not proved.

Let us draw figure 25.21. On the right part is the axis of the number of elements \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16\) and vertically the deflection. The dashed line is the exact value \(9{,}3142\) mm. The blue line connects the values of the consistent model: it rises from below and approaches the dashed one. We add the orange line of the model with nodal springs, which at \(L = 4\) m is also below the dashed line and still lower, but approaches it as well. On the left part is the same for \(L = 1\) m (axes, the exact value, the blue line): the blue rises from below again, but the orange starts above the dashed line, at \(11{,}9944\) mm, and falls: \(11{,}5234\), \(11{,}4089\), \(11{,}3807\) mm. So at \(L = 1\) m the nodal model is above the exact value for all four meshes.

Why is the blue line always below the dashed one? The model allows only fields that are piecewise cubic polynomials, which is a subspace of all admissible fields. A restriction to fewer fields stiffens the beam, a stiffer beam bends less under the same force than the exact one, so the deflection under the force is too small. This is the idea of theorem 6.34, and the corollary below proves it.

Let us draw figure 25.22. On the left is the set of all admissible fields and inside it the smaller set of piecewise cubic fields that the model allows. The exact deflection \(v\) is in the large set, the model deflection \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) in the small one. On the right the beam is loaded by the same force: the exact deflection is larger, the model deflection smaller, since the model cannot choose from all fields.

Corollary 25.10 The deflection under the force is a lower bound for a consistent foundation (poves pod silo je pri konsistentni podlagi spodnja meja)

Let a free beam with constant \(EI\) lie on a Winkler foundation with constant \(k > 0\) and be loaded by point forces \(P_1, \dots, P_{\mathrm{m}}\) at points \(x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{m}}\) that are nodes of a mesh of \(n\) Hermite elements, forces and deflection measured in the same direction (definition 25.1). Let \(v\) be the exact deflection and \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) the deflection given by the model with the consistent foundation matrix (lemma 25.8), \((\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{p}})\vek d = \vek f\). Then

\[\sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^m P_{\mathrm{i}}\,v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_{\mathrm{i}}) \le \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^m P_{\mathrm{i}}\,v(x_{\mathrm{i}}) , \tag{25.9}\]

that is, the work of the forces on the model is not larger than on the exact field. For one force, \(P\,v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1) \le P\,v(x_1)\), so \(|v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1)| \le |v(x_1)|\).

Proof

We must show that the model is the Ritz solution for the energy form \(B\) and that the exact solution is in the weak form with the same form, then use theorem 6.34.

  1. The form \(B(w, z) = \int_0^L EI\,w''z''\,\mathrm{d}x + \int_0^L k\,w\,z\,\mathrm{d}x\) is symmetric and bilinear. It is positive: \(B(w, w)\) is the sum of the bending part \(\int EI\,(w'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x \ge 0\) and the foundation part \(\int k\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), so \(B(w, w) \ge \int k\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}x > 0\) for continuous \(w \ne 0\) (lemma 6.10, item 3), since \(k > 0\). This holds also for a free beam without supports: a rigid displacement has no bending part, but the foundation feels it. The load \(\ell(w) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} P_{\mathrm{i}}\,w(x_{\mathrm{i}})\) is linear and does not depend on the deformation.
  2. The exact deflection \(v\) solves \(EI\,v'''' + k\,v = 0\) on every piece between neighbouring forces and ends, \(v\), \(v'\) and \(v''\) are continuous, the free ends have \(v'' = v''' = 0\), and at the point \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(EI\,\big(v'''(x_{\mathrm{i}}^+) - v'''(x_{\mathrm{i}}^-)\big) = P_{\mathrm{i}}\) (lemma 5.44, \(V = -EI\,v'''\), \(V\) jumps by \(-P_{\mathrm{i}}\)). For any admissible \(w\) (continuous \(w\) and \(w'\)), on every piece by lemma 6.13 \(\int EI\,v''''w = \big[EI\,v'''w - EI\,v''w'\big] + \int EI\,v''w''\).
  3. We add over the pieces. The terms with \(v''w'\) cancel at interior points (continuity) and are zero at the ends. The terms \(EI\,v'''w\) give at every \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) the sum \(-EI\,[v''']\,w(x_{\mathrm{i}}) = -P_{\mathrm{i}}\,w(x_{\mathrm{i}})\), and are zero at the ends. So \(0 = \int(EI\,v'''' + k\,v)\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = -\ell(w) + B(v, w)\), that is \(B(v, w) = \ell(w)\) for every admissible \(w\): the weak form.
  4. The Hermite functions \(H_{\mathrm{I}}\) are admissible fields (continuous with continuous slope, step 1 of the proof of corollary 13.83). By item 5 of lemma 25.8, \((\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{p}})_{\mathrm{IJ}} = B(H_{\mathrm{J}}, H_{\mathrm{I}})\), and \(f_{\mathrm{I}} = \ell(H_{\mathrm{I}})\): the force \(P_{\mathrm{i}}\) is picked up by the function \(H_{\mathrm{I}}\) of node \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) for displacement (\(H_{\mathrm{I}}(x_{\mathrm{i}}) = 1\), other nodal values \(0\), lemma 12.8), so \(f_{\mathrm{I}} = P_{\mathrm{i}}\) for this \(I\) and zero elsewhere. These are the Ritz equations \(\sum_{\mathrm{J}} B(H_{\mathrm{J}}, H_{\mathrm{I}})\,d_{\mathrm{J}} = \ell(H_{\mathrm{I}})\) for the space \(\{H_{\mathrm{I}}\}\) with \(\psi_0 = 0\) (definition 6.32), so \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is the Ritz solution.
  5. By item 2 of theorem 6.34, \(\ell(v_{\mathrm{h}}) \le \ell(v)\), which is equation (25.9). For one force this is \(P\,v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1) \le P\,v(x_1)\). Both sides are nonnegative: \(P\,v(x_1) = \ell(v) = B(v, v)\) by step 3 with \(w = v\), and \(P\,v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1) = \ell(v_{\mathrm{h}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} d_{\mathrm{I}}\,\ell(H_{\mathrm{I}}) = \sum_{\mathrm{I}, \mathrm{J}} d_{\mathrm{I}}\,B(H_{\mathrm{J}}, H_{\mathrm{I}})\,d_{\mathrm{J}} = B(v_{\mathrm{h}}, v_{\mathrm{h}})\) by the Ritz equations of step 4. So \(v(x_1)\) and \(v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1)\) have the sign of the force \(P \ne 0\) or are zero, and the inequality gives \(|v_{\mathrm{h}}(x_1)| \le |v(x_1)|\).

Source: Theorem 6.34 (BATHE (4.89) to (4.91), PDF p. 258, COOK PDF p. 164: "either exact or too stiff"). COOK (PDF p. 302): "convergence occurs with mesh refinement, but a rather fine mesh may be needed to determine bending moments accurately". The proof in steps is not from the sources.

Let us draw figure 25.23. On the left the free beam is displaced as a whole by \(w = 1\) mm, so all springs are compressed equally. There is no bending, \(w'' = 0\), so the bar has only the orange foundation part, \(\int_0^L k\,w^2\,\mathrm{d}x = kL\,w^2 = 4{,}00\) N m. Without the foundation this bar would be empty and the form would be zero for the rigid displacement. On the right the beam is bent as \(w = \cos(2\pi x/L)\) mm, and the springs are compressed and stretched by different amounts. The bar has the blue bending part \(0{,}255\) N m and on top of it the orange foundation part \(2{,}00\) N m. The bending part is never negative, so the bar is at least as tall as its orange part, and that part is positive for every \(w \ne 0\).

Let us draw figure 25.24. At the top is the beam, which the force at \(x_1\) divides into two pieces, and above it an admissible field \(w\), which the proof chooses arbitrarily. On every piece, integration by parts gives the boundary terms \(EI\,v'''w\) and \(-EI\,v''w'\) at both ends of the piece. In the middle is the graph of \(EI\,v'''\): at \(x_1\) its value from the left is \(-5\) kN and from the right \(+5\) kN, and the jump is \(10\) kN, that is \(P\). The left piece gives at \(x_1\) the term \(EI\,v'''(x_1^-)\,w(x_1)\), the right piece, for which \(x_1\) is the left end, gives \(-EI\,v'''(x_1^+)\,w(x_1)\). The sum is \(-P\,w(x_1)\). At the bottom is the graph of \(EI\,v''\), which does not jump at \(x_1\): both pieces give the term \(EI\,v''(x_1)\,w'(x_1)\) with opposite signs, so they cancel. At the ends both \(EI\,v''\) and \(EI\,v'''\) are zero and there are no boundary terms.

The proof showed that with lemma 25.8 the model is a Ritz solution, so the theorem on energy holds. The bound is for the work of the forces, not for the deflection at every point separately. For two forces, \(P_1 = +10\) kN in the middle and \(P_2 = -10\) kN (upward) at a quarter of the free beam \(L = 4\) m, the work on the exact field is \(169{,}90\) N m, on the model with \(n = 4\) elements \(165{,}55\) and with \(n = 8\) \(169{,}50\) N m, all below the exact (num-02.out, item 7). The individual deflection is also below the exact one in absolute value for these numbers (\(8{,}09\) against \(8{,}31\) mm and \(8{,}46\) against \(8{,}68\) mm at \(n = 4\)), but the theorem does not require this and does not prove it.

Where the bound does not hold: nodal springs. With nodal springs the foundation matrix is not the matrix of the form \(B\) (the energy is different, table of figure 25.19), the model is not a Ritz one and the theorem does not hold. The proof would stop at step 4. The result confirms it: at \(L = 1\) m the deflection is \(11{,}9944\) mm at \(n = 2\), \(5{,}5\) % above the exact \(11{,}3713\) mm, and stays above the exact one for all four meshes (figure 25.21, left side). At \(L = 4\) m it is also below the exact (\(4{,}96\), \(8{,}19\), \(9{,}24\), \(9{,}31\) mm), but the theorem does not guarantee this, since it says nothing about the nodal model. The reason the proof fails is in the table of figure 25.19: for a rotation without displacement the nodal model does not feel the foundation, and for unequal displacements it feels it more strongly, \(2{,}059\) times for opposite displacements, so there is no comparison in either direction.

The mesh must be fine enough for the true deflection. For an infinitely long beam on a foundation the distance from the force to the largest lift is \(\pi/\beta = 1{,}69\) m, half the wavelength \(2\pi/\beta\) (section 25.1, \(\beta = 1{,}8596\) 1/m, minimum of the deflection at \(\beta x = \pi\)). Over this distance the deflection passes from its largest downward value to the lift, and the mesh must describe this shape. The free beam with \(L = 4\) m has its end already \(2\) m from the force, so its end lifts most (NumPy), and the length \(\pi/\beta\) stays the scale on which the deflection changes shape. With \(L = 4\) m and \(n = 8\), \(h = 0{,}5\) m, that is \(\beta h = 0{,}93\), and the error is \(0{,}31\) %, and at \(L = 1\) m and \(n = 2\) (\(h = 0{,}5\) m) \(0{,}37\) %. At \(h = 1\) m (\(n = 4\), \(L = 4\) m), \(\beta h = 1{,}86\) and the error is \(4{,}1\) %. These are two measured cases, not a rule.

Let us draw figure 25.25. The curve is the deflection of the infinitely long beam under the force: it is largest under the force, then decreases through zero and the beam lifts a little on the other side. The distance from the force to the largest lift is \(\pi/\beta\). Below is the mesh with \(h = 0{,}5\) m, and about \(3{,}4\) elements fit into this distance.

This section gave two results we need further on. The first: the foundation in the finite element model is a matrix obtained from the same energy as the others and, for constant \(k\) and \(\rho A\), it is the mass matrix multiplied by \(k/(\rho A)\), so the vibration on a foundation in the model is the same vibration as without it, shifted in the square of the frequency. The second: the shortcut with nodal springs gives, for a uniform foundation, at some meshes frequencies below the true ones and a deflection above the true one, which the consistent model does not do. The bearing in section 25.9 acts at a point, not along the length, so a spring at a node is there the right model and not a shortcut.

25.3 A line force on a half-plane: the Flamant solution

The spring model of section 25.1 counted the sinking of each point separately. A real foundation does not act so: where we press it, the surroundings sink too. We answer how first for the simplest load that the contact of a cylinder with a plane really has, a force spread along a long straight line (force \(F'\) on the surface). A cylinder lying on a plane presses along its line of contact, and if the cylinder is much longer than the depth to which the field matters, the field in a cross-section does not change along the line. The question of this section is therefore: what stresses and displacements does a force \(F'\) per unit length of a line produce in an elastic body that it presses on its flat surface? We need the answer in section 25.5, where we build the contact of two cylinders from it.

The body we take is a prism with axis \(z\) whose cross-section is the half-plane (half-plane (polravnina)) \(y \geq 0\): all points of the \(x\), \(y\) plane on one side of the line \(y = 0\). The name says that we cut the plane in half and kept one half. The axis \(y\) points into the body, the surface is the line \(y = 0\). The material is homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic with \(E\) and \(\nu\), the strains are small, the surface is smooth without friction. The field does not depend on \(z\) and the displacement in the direction \(z\) is zero, so the state is plane strain (definition 11.32) and by corollary 11.38 it is described by the constants \(E^* = E/(1 - \nu^2)\) and \(\nu^* = \nu/(1 - \nu)\) of theorem 11.33. The star is the same as in the plane problem of chapter 11. The same number, \(E/(1 - \nu^2)\), will appear again in section 25.5 as the contact modulus of a body against a rigid opponent, but there \(E^*\) describes a pair of bodies. For the steel of the book (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)) it is \(E^* = 215{,}38\) GPa and \(\nu^* = 0{,}4286\). Let \(F' = 100\) N/mm, as if a cylinder of length \(10\) mm pressed with a force of \(1000\) N.

A force per unit length has the unit N/m, not N. Since in the plane problem the whole load lies on a line along \(z\), we write it \(F'\) so as not to confuse it with the force \(F\) in a point of section 25.4. A stress is a force per area, N/m\(^2\). The problem is linear, so the stress is proportional to \(F'\), and the factor multiplying \(F'\) has the unit 1/m. This factor depends on the distance \(r\) from the line, on the angle and on \(E\) and \(\nu\). Of these only \(E\) has newtons in its unit, so \(E\) cannot appear in the factor, and the stress must be \(F'/r\) times a function of the angle (and of \(\nu\)). Equilibrium says the same: the length of an arc of radius \(r\) is proportional to \(r\) and its force must be \(F'\) for every \(r\), so the stress on the arc is proportional to \(1/r\).

Let us draw figure 25.26. First the surface, a horizontal line with hatching above it: the body is below. Through its point \(O\) we draw the axis \(y\) down into the body and the axis \(x\) along the surface. In \(O\) the force \(F'\) presses down, so the arrow ends in \(O\), like every push. A point of the body is described by the distance \(r\) and the angle \(\theta\) that the radius makes with the axis \(y\), that is with the line of the force. The body occupies \(-\pi/2 \leq \theta \leq \pi/2\), the surface is at \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\). Around \(O\) we draw a half-disc of radius \(a\), which is part of the body. The rest of the body acts on it with stresses on the arc, and for the equilibrium of the half-disc they must give zero together with the force \(F'\). So we get a condition for a force in a point where the stress is not defined.

Definition 25.11 Line force on a half-plane (linijska sila na polravnini)

Let the body be the half-plane \(y > 0\) of an isotropic linearly elastic material in plane strain, without body force, and let \(F' > 0\) be a number with the unit N/m. A stress field \(\ten\sigma\) with continuous second derivatives on \(\{y > 0\}\) that extends continuously to the surface \(y = 0\) at \(x \neq 0\) is the stress field of the line force \(F'\) in \(O\) if:

  1. it satisfies the equilibrium equations and the compatibility condition of the plane problem (theorem 11.40) at every point of the body, also on the arc,
  2. the surface is free outside \(O\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) at \(y = 0\), \(x \neq 0\),
  3. for every \(a > 0\) the force that the part of the body outside the half-disc \(r < a\) exerts on it through the arc \(r = a\) equals \((0, -F')\) per unit length, which is opposite to the force \(F'\) pressing in \(O\).

The second condition says that outside \(O\) the surface is free. The third condition is the equilibrium of the half-disc: if the stress stayed bounded as \(r \to 0\), the force on the arc, which has length \(\pi a\), would go to zero as \(a \to 0\) and could not balance \(F'\). The stress must therefore go beyond every bound in \(O\), which is a measure of the model, not a fault (see below the theorem).

Where do we look for the function? The stress is \(F'/r\) times a function of the angle \(\theta\), and the Airy function is twice an integral of the stress over length, so it has the form \(\varphi = r f(\theta)\). Let us show what such a form gives.

Lemma 25.12 The Airy function \(r f(\theta)\) (Airyjeva funkcija \(r f(\theta)\))

Let \(f\) be a four times continuously differentiable function of the angle on \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\) and \(\varphi = r f(\theta)\) on the half-plane \(y > 0\). Then:

  1. \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = (f + f'')/r\), where the stresses are given by (11.70),
  2. \(\nabla^4\varphi = (f'''' + 2f'' + f)/r^3\), so \(\varphi\) is biharmonic exactly when \(f'''' + 2f'' + f = 0\),
  3. all such \(f\) are \(f = C_1\cos\theta + C_2\sin\theta + C_3\,\theta\cos\theta + C_4\,\theta\sin\theta\), and for them \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = (2C_4\cos\theta - 2C_3\sin\theta)/r\).
Proof

We must show three claims. We use lemma 11.50 and corollary 11.18 without derivatives in \(z\).

  1. For \(\varphi = r f(\theta)\) we have \(\partial\varphi/\partial r = f\), \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial r^2 = 0\) and \(\partial^2\varphi/\partial\theta^2 = r f''\). By (11.70), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = f/r + r f''/r^2 = (f + f'')/r\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 0\). Next, \(\frac1r\,\partial\varphi/\partial\theta = f'\), which does not depend on \(r\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\partial f'/\partial r = 0\).
  2. By corollary 11.18, \(\nabla^2\varphi = 0 + f/r + f''/r = (f + f'')/r\). For \(g(\theta)/r\) we have \(\partial^2/\partial r^2 = 2g/r^3\), \(\frac1r\,\partial/\partial r = -g/r^3\) and \(\frac{1}{r^2}\,\partial^2/\partial\theta^2 = g''/r^3\), so \(\nabla^2(g/r) = (g + g'')/r^3\). With \(g = f + f''\) we get \(\nabla^4\varphi = (f + 2f'' + f'''')/r^3\).
  3. We solve the equation \(f'''' + 2f'' + f = 0\).
    • Its characteristic polynomial is \((s^2 + 1)^2\) with the double roots \(\pm\mathrm{i}\).
    • By theorem 9.44 every solution has the form \((p + q\theta)\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta} + (\bar p + \bar q\theta)\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}\).
    • By corollary 9.45 the real solutions are the linear combinations of \(\cos\theta\), \(\sin\theta\), \(\theta\cos\theta\), \(\theta\sin\theta\).
    • For \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) we have \(f + f'' = 0\).
    • For \(\theta\cos\theta\), \(f'' = -2\sin\theta - \theta\cos\theta\), so \(f + f'' = -2\sin\theta\).
    • For \(\theta\sin\theta\), \(f'' = 2\cos\theta - \theta\sin\theta\), so \(f + f'' = 2\cos\theta\).
    • With claim 1 the expression for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) follows.

Source: SADD (8.4.31)-(8.4.32) (PDF p. 199-200) and BARBER (12.2)-(12.3) (PDF p. 186) take from the general Michell solution the terms with the stress \(1/r\). The proof is ours.

Figure 25.27 shows three possible distributions on the half-disc of radius \(a\) below the surface. The lemma says something surprising: with this form \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) are zero for every \(f\). The stress has only a radial component, so the solution is called the simple radial distribution (BARBER PDF p. 187). The surface is the line \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), its normal is \(\pm\boldsymbol e_\theta\), and the stress vector on it is \(\pm(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta}\boldsymbol e_\theta) = \boldsymbol 0\), so the surface is free by itself. What remains is the force: \(C_3\) gives a stress \(\propto \sin\theta\), which is odd in \(\theta\) and would give the horizontal force \(-\pi C_3\) (03-check.py, C3), while condition 3 of the definition requires a vertical force, so \(C_3 = 0\). The terms with \(C_1\), \(C_2\) give \(\varphi = C_1\,r\cos\theta + C_2\,r\sin\theta = C_1 y + C_2 x\), which is linear and has all stresses zero.

Theorem 25.13 The Flamant solution (Flamantova rešitev)

Let the half-plane \(y > 0\) be as in definition 25.11 and \(F' > 0\). The function \(\varphi = -\dfrac{F'}{\pi}\,r\theta\sin\theta\) (\(r\) and \(\theta\) as in figure 25.26) is biharmonic and its stresses are the stress field of the line force \(F'\). More precisely:

  1. \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -\dfrac{2F'\cos\theta}{\pi r}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\), so the stresses on the arc all point radially. In Cartesian components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\dfrac{2F'\,y^3}{\pi\,(x^2 + y^2)^2}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -\dfrac{2F'\,x^2 y}{\pi\,(x^2 + y^2)^2}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\dfrac{2F'\,x y^2}{\pi\,(x^2 + y^2)^2}\).
  2. The surface is free outside \(O\), and on every half circle \(r = a\) the resultant of the stresses equals \((0, -F')\).
  3. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is constant, \(-2F'/(\pi d)\), on the circle \(r = d\cos\theta\) that touches the surface in \(O\), with diameter \(d\).
  4. Under the force (\(x = 0\)), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2F'/(\pi y)\), and on the line at depth \(a\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(x)/\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(0) = (1 + x^2/a^2)^{-2}\).
Proof

We must show that \(\varphi\) satisfies lemma 25.12 with a determined \(C_4\) and that the claims follow.

  1. We take \(f = C_4\,\theta\sin\theta\), so \(f'''' + 2f'' + f = 0\) by lemma 25.12, claim 3, and \(\varphi\) is biharmonic. By claim 1 of the lemma \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) and by claim 3 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 2C_4\cos\theta/r\), so the stresses on the arc are indeed all radial. By theorem 11.40, claims 1 and 3 (without body force, \(V = 0\), \(\varphi\) has continuous derivatives up to the fourth order on \(y > 0\), where \(r > 0\)), the stresses satisfy equilibrium and the compatibility condition. This is the first condition of definition 25.11.
  2. The arc \(r = a\) has the outer normal \(\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}} = (\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\) in the components \(x\), \(y\) and the force per unit length of arc \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\,\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}}\), since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). The arc between the angles \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) has length \(a(\theta_2 - \theta_1)\), so the resultant over the arc is an integral over the angle with the factor \(a\), \(\big(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin\theta\,a\,\mathrm{d}\theta,\ \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\cos\theta\,a\,\mathrm{d}\theta\big)\). With \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 2C_4\cos\theta/r\) the first component is zero, since the integrand is odd, and the second is \(2C_4\int\cos^2\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = \pi C_4\). The requirement \(\pi C_4 = -F'\) gives \(C_4 = -F'/\pi\), and with it \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -2F'\cos\theta/(\pi r)\). This is the first part of claim 1 and the third condition of the definition.
  3. The surface at \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\): in Cartesian components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\cos^2\theta\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin\theta\cos\theta\) (transformation of stress, theorem 2.53, since \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) are zero). At \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) has the factor \(\cos\theta = 0\) and \(\cos^2\theta = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero at \(r > 0\). This is the second condition of the definition and the first part of claim 2.
  4. Since for a point at distance \(r\) and angle \(\theta\) \(x = r\sin\theta\) and \(y = r\cos\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2F'\cos^3\theta/(\pi r) = -2F'y^3/(\pi r^4)\) and likewise \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin^2\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). This is the rest of claim 1 (checked in SymPy, num-03.py, S4).
  5. On the circle \(r = d\cos\theta\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -2F'\cos\theta/(\pi d\cos\theta) = -2F'/(\pi d)\), claim 3. At \(x = 0\), \(r = y\) and \(\theta = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = -2F'/(\pi y)\). At \(y = a\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}(x) = -\dfrac{2F'}{\pi a}\,\dfrac{1}{(1 + x^2/a^2)^2}\), claim 4.

Source: SADD §8.4.7, (8.4.34)-(8.4.36) (PDF p. 199-201): the same stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}} = -2Y\sin\theta/(\pi r)\) with the angle measured from the surface (crop 8.4.35 read), and "lines of constant radial stress are circles tangent to the surface" (PDF p. 201). BARBER §12.2-12.3, (12.2)-(12.7), (12.11) (PDF p. 186-188). Neither source discusses uniqueness on the pages cited, see the text below the theorem.

The proof showed that the stress of the theorem satisfies all three conditions of the definition. What does it say? Figure 25.28 shows two panels.

In the left panel there is the surface with the force \(F'\) in \(O\). Through the point \(O\) we draw three circles, all touching the surface in \(O\), with a vertical diameter \(d = 1\), \(2\), \(4\) mm. By claim 3 the stress on each is constant, and the values are \(63{,}66\), \(31{,}83\) and \(15{,}92\) MPa in compression: half for a twice larger diameter. This is the same law \(\sigma \propto 1/r\) as in the motivation. The right panel shows the profile of the stress on the line at depth \(a\): it is largest under the force, at \(x = a\) it is \(\tfrac14\), at \(x = 2a\) only \(0{,}04\) and at \(x = 5a\) only \(0{,}0015\) of the largest value (SymPy and NumPy, num-03.py, N7). The vertical stress on this line is thus gathered under the force, in a strip a few \(a\) wide. The stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) itself, however, falls only like \(1/r\) (claim 1): at the point \(x = 5a\), \(y = a\) it is still \(1/26 = 0{,}038\) of the value under the force at depth \(a\), only there it points almost horizontally, so its vertical part is small (03-check.py, C5).

Under the force. Figure 25.29 shows the stress by depth: the horizontal axis is the depth \(y\) in mm, the vertical axis the stress in MPa. The compressive stress \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}| = 2F'/(\pi y)\) is \(63{,}7\) MPa at \(y = 1\) mm, \(636{,}6\) MPa at \(0{,}1\) mm and \(6366\) MPa at \(0{,}01\) mm (num-03.py, N2). It goes beyond every bound as \(y \to 0\). This is not a fault of the solution but a measure of the model: a force on a line means a force on zero area. The linear theory assumes that all derivatives of the displacements are below about \(0{,}001\) in size (section 3.2.1, assumption 4). Under the force \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero, so by Hooke's law of plane strain (theorem 11.33) the derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}/E^*\). The bound \(0{,}001\) at \(E^* = 215{,}4\) GPa thus means a stress of at most \(215{,}4\) MPa, and at \(F' = 100\) N/mm this holds for \(y \geq 2F'/(\pi\cdot 215{,}4\ \mathrm{MPa}) = 0{,}30\) mm. Closer than that the solution does not hold. What a real contact does we see in section 25.5: the force spreads over a strip of finite width.

Is the solution the only one? We proved that the field is a solution, not that it is the only one. By definition 25.11 it is not the only one either, as figure 25.30 shows. Take the uniform stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = s\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\) with any number \(s\) acting on the sides of the dashed box. Its Airy function \(s\,y^2/2\) is biharmonic, so it satisfies equilibrium and compatibility. It leaves the surface free, since \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) are zero. On the half-disc it gives the force \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} s\sin\theta\,a\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 0\) in the direction \(x\) and zero in the direction \(y\) (03-check.py, C2). Added to Flamant's (plus), it gives another field to the right of the equals sign that satisfies all three conditions of the definition. It is the stress of a horizontal tension or compression at infinity, not a consequence of the force in \(O\). The uniqueness theorem of the boundary value problem (theorem 11.4) holds for bounded bodies and regular data, and a half-plane with a point force is neither, so we cannot use it here, and we do not prove uniqueness under extra conditions at infinity. We proved only this much: among the functions of the form \(r f(\theta)\) only this one gives the stress field of a line force (lemma 25.12 and the paragraph after it).

The displacements follow from the stresses through Hooke's law and the relation between displacements and strains.

Lemma 25.14 Displacements of the Flamant solution (pomiki pri Flamantovi rešitvi)

Let the stress field be that of theorem 25.13 and \(E^*\), \(\nu^*\) as above. The displacement field in local components

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{r}} &= -\frac{F'}{\pi E^*}\Big(2\cos\theta\,\ln r + (1 - \nu^*)\,\theta\sin\theta\Big) , \\ u_\theta &= \frac{F'}{\pi E^*}\Big(2\sin\theta\,\ln r - (1 - \nu^*)\,\theta\cos\theta + (1 + \nu^*)\sin\theta\Big) \end{aligned} \tag{25.10}\]

has strains that by Hooke's law of plane strain give the stresses of theorem 25.13. Every other displacement field with the same strains differs from it by a rigid displacement \((A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta,\ -A\sin\theta + B\cos\theta + W r)\) with constants \(A\), \(B\), \(W\). The field (25.10) has \(u_\theta = 0\) on the line of the force \(\theta = 0\). On the surface (\(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), \(r = |x|\)) it has:

  1. the horizontal displacement of size \(\dfrac{(1 - \nu^*)F'}{2E^*}\) toward \(O\), \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{(1 - \nu^*)F'}{2E^*}\), equal at all \(r\),
  2. the vertical displacement (into the body) \(w(x) = -\dfrac{F'}{\pi E^*}\big(2\ln|x| + 1 + \nu^*\big)\),
  3. the difference of displacements \(w(x_1) - w(x_2) = \dfrac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\ln\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}\) does not depend on the rigid displacement.
Proof

We must show that (25.10) gives the right strains, that it is the only form, and claims 1 to 3. We get the strains in cylindrical coordinates from corollary 11.21 and the stresses from corollary 11.27.

  1. By theorem 11.33 plane strain has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu^*\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E^*\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (\sigma_{\theta\theta} - \nu^*\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})/E^*\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = (1 + \nu^*)\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}/E^*\). With \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) we get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}/E^* = -2F'\cos\theta/(\pi E^* r)\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = -\nu^*\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}/E^* = 2\nu^* F'\cos\theta/(\pi E^* r)\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\).
  2. From \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}}\) it follows that \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{2F'\cos\theta}{\pi E^*}\ln r + f(\theta)\) with a so far unknown function \(f\). From \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (u_{\mathrm{r}} + \partial u_\theta/\partial\theta)/r\) it follows that \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = 2\nu^*F'\cos\theta/(\pi E^*) - u_{\mathrm{r}}\). With an integral over \(\theta\), where \(\Phi(\theta)\) is a primitive function of \(f\), \(u_\theta = \dfrac{2F'\sin\theta}{\pi E^*}\big(\ln r + \nu^*\big) - \Phi(\theta) + g(r)\) with an unknown function \(g\).
  3. We use the condition \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\).
    • By corollary 11.21 we multiply it by \(2r\) and insert: \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial\theta + r\,\partial u_\theta/\partial r - u_\theta = 0\).
    • The terms with \(\ln r\) cancel and what remains is \(f' + \Phi + c\sin\theta + (r g' - g) = 0\) with \(c = 2(1 - \nu^*)F'/(\pi E^*)\).
    • The first three terms depend only on \(\theta\), the last only on \(r\), so each is constant: \(r g' - g = -K\), \(g = K + W r\), and \(f' + \Phi + c\sin\theta = K\).
  4. We solve the last equation for \(f\) and \(\Phi\).
    • The derivative of the last equation with respect to \(\theta\) gives \(f'' + f = -c\cos\theta\).
    • The function \(-\tfrac{c}{2}\,\theta\sin\theta\) solves it, since \((\theta\sin\theta)'' + \theta\sin\theta = 2\cos\theta\).
    • The difference of two solutions solves \(h'' + h = 0\), so by theorem 9.44 it is \(A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\).
    • Hence \(f = -\tfrac c2\,\theta\sin\theta + A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\), and from \(f' + \Phi + c\sin\theta = K\) follows \(\Phi\), which agrees with \(f\) (\(\Phi' = f\) is checked by differentiation).
    • Inserted in step 2, \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_\theta\) are as (25.10), only with the terms \(A\cos\theta + B\sin\theta\) in \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(-A\sin\theta + B\cos\theta + Wr\) in \(u_\theta\).
    • These terms are a rigid displacement: a shift \((B, A)\) in the directions \(x\), \(y\) and a rotation \(W\) (their strains are zero, SymPy, S9).
    • For (25.10), \(A = B = W = 0\) and \(K\) is already included. Since \(\sin 0 = 0\), \(u_\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = 0\).
  5. On the surface \(\cos\theta = 0\), \(\sin\theta = \pm1\), \(\theta\sin\theta = \pi/2\) and \(\theta\cos\theta = 0\). Hence \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{(1 - \nu^*)F'}{2E^*}\) on both sides. The basis vector \(\boldsymbol e_{\mathrm{r}}\) points along the surface away from \(O\), so the displacement is toward \(O\), and nothing depends on \(r\). This is claim 1.
  6. At the surface \(\theta = \pm\pi/2\), \(\boldsymbol e_\theta = (0, \mp1)\) in the components \(x\), \(y\) and \(u_\theta = \pm\dfrac{F'}{\pi E^*}(2\ln r + 1 + \nu^*)\), so the vertical displacement is \(-\dfrac{F'}{\pi E^*}(2\ln r + 1 + \nu^*)\) on both sides. This is claim 2, its difference is claim 3, since the rigid displacement cancels in the difference.

Source: SADD (8.4.37)-(8.4.43) (PDF p. 201-203), crop (8.4.43) read: the same expressions with the angle measured from the surface and for plane stress (\(E\), \(\nu\) in place of \(E^*\), \(\nu^*\) by corollary 11.38). SADD (8.4.44), (8.4.45) (PDF p. 203): all points of the surface move horizontally the same amount toward the force, "an unexpected result". BARBER (12.12), (12.13) (PDF p. 188) the same expression in other notation. We checked the result in SymPy (num-03.py, S6 to S9).

The proof showed that the displacement field is unique up to a rigid displacement and has a simple form on the surface. Figure 25.31 shows it.

In the left panel there is the surface with the force \(F'\), and below it a grid of points, in each a displacement is drawn (\(0{,}28\) cm per unit). Near the force the displacements point down, and along the surface all are equal horizontally and point toward the force, in agreement with claim 1. The points at \(|x| = 2{,}5\) cm, however, rise. This is not a property of the body but of the choice of the rigid displacement, for which the vertical displacement of the surface is zero at \(|x| = 1{,}96\) cm (03-check.py, C6). The right panel shows the surface after deformation: as \(x \to 0\) the sinking goes beyond every bound, like \(\ln(1/|x|)\). The solid line is \(w\) for the choice of the rigid displacement that gives \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = -(1 + \nu^*)F'/(\pi E^*)\) at \(|x| = 4\) cm, the dashed one at \(|x| = 40\) cm. They are the same curve, shifted by \(2\ln 10 = 4{,}605\) units of \(F'/(\pi E^*)\), which is \(0{,}68\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) at \(F' = 100\) N/mm.

The sinking is determined only up to a constant. The two curves of the sinking are the same up to a shift. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm, \(2F'/(\pi E^*) = 0{,}2956\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (num-03.py, N5). The difference of sinking between \(x_1 = 1\) mm and \(x_2 = 10\), \(100\), \(1000\) mm is \(0{,}681\), \(1{,}361\) and \(2{,}042\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) (N6): each tenfold distance adds the same. As \(x_2 \to \infty\) the difference goes beyond every bound, so the displacement \(w\) is never determined at a point but always only relative to a chosen reference point, and this choice is a decision of the model, not a result. The same cause lies behind the stress \(\propto 1/r\): a displacement is an integral of the strain, and \(\int\frac{1}{r}\,\mathrm{d}r = \ln r\) does not converge at infinity (by SADD PDF p. 203 this follows from the radial stress being \(O(1/r)\) and is a feature of the plane model, the three-dimensional solution of section 25.4 has no logarithm). Some authors remove the logarithm with the condition that the point on the load line at a chosen depth \(r_0\) does not move, in our notation \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(r_0, 0) = 0\) (SADD PDF p. 204 writes \(u_{\mathrm{r}}(r_0, \pi/2) = 0\), since it measures the angle from the surface). Then \(\ln(r/r_0)\) stands everywhere in (25.10) in place of \(\ln r\), which is exactly this choice.

Consequence for contact: we do not know the approach. When in section 25.5 two cylinders are pressed together, we would like to know by how much their centres approach. Each cylinder at a small contact is a half-plane, and its sinking at the contact is by this section determined up to a constant that depends on the size of the body. The approach (approach (pogrezanje)) \(\delta\) of cylinders therefore does not follow from the plane model. No choice repairs it: this is why for rollers the law \(Q \propto \delta^{10/9}\) of section 25.7 is fitted empirically, not derived (HK, PDF p. 156). For a three-dimensional contact the stiffness is well defined, for a two-dimensional one it is not (BOWER, PDF p. 330).

The line is not infinitely long. For a cylinder of length \(\ell\) the line of contact is not infinite, so the plane model holds only if the depth is small against \(\ell\). We can compute the quantity once we know the field of a point force, that is in section 25.4 (theorem 25.15). We state the result in advance. If we spread the force \(F'\ell = F\) over a line of length \(\ell\) and add the fields of the point forces, the stress under the centre at depth \(y\) equals the Flamant stress times \(\dfrac{1 + 6t^2}{(1 + 4t^2)^{3/2}}\), \(t = y/\ell\) (num-03.py, M2, the integral checked by differentiation and numerically). The expansion is \(1 - 6t^4\), so the difference is below \(1\,\%\) for \(t \leq 0{,}2\), and at \(t = 1\) the stress is only \(0{,}626\) of the Flamant one, at \(t = 2\) only \(0{,}357\) (figure 25.32).

Let us draw the strip of length \(\ell\) on the surface, over which the force \(F\) is spread. Under its centre we take the depth \(y\). The blue region reaches to \(0{,}2\,\ell\), and in it the plane solution holds to \(1\,\%\). On the right is the curve of the ratio: at \(y/\ell = 0{,}2\) it is \(0{,}993\) and at \(1{,}0\) it is \(0{,}626\). For a cylinder with \(\ell = 10\) mm the plane model is thus good to a depth of \(2\) mm. HK calls this edge loading (HK PDF p. 145-148): at the ends of the cylinder the pressure is larger than in the middle, which is why the cylinders are crowned, a matter we do not treat here (HK, PDF p. 147-148).

The plane solution is thus accurate only in the band of depths smaller than the length of the line. In it the stress and the displacement are fully determined by \(F'\), \(E^*\) and \(\nu^*\).

25.4 A point force on a half-space: the Boussinesq solution

The foundation of section 25.1 treated every point on its own: under the beam, a displacement \(v\) produced a force \(k\,v\) per unit length, and neighbouring points did not know each other. A real foundation, the ground under a footing or the steel of the ring on which a ball rests, does not act like that. If we press on one point only, its surroundings sink as well, as a mattress sinks around a single fist. The question of this section is therefore: by how much does the surface of an elastic body sink at a distance \(r\) from the point where a force \(F\) presses, and what stresses does the force cause inside? We need the answer for the contact of two bodies, where we must know how an elastic body gives way under a pressure on a small part of its surface.

The body we take is a half-space (polprostor): all the points with \(z \geq 0\), with the plane \(z = 0\) as its surface. The name says that we cut space in two by a plane and kept one half. The half-space is a model of a body that is much larger than the region where we press: the distances at which we want the field are much smaller than the dimensions of the body, so the far edge of the body has no influence (for a force of \(1000\) N the normal stress at a depth of \(10\) mm below the force is only \(4{,}8\) MPa, as we shall compute below). The material is homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic, with modulus \(E\) and Poisson's ratio \(\nu\) (theorem 3.19), the strains are small and the surface is smooth and frictionless. Let us take the steel of the book, \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\), and a force \(F = 1000\) N.

Let us draw figure 25.33, the left panel first. The surface is the horizontal line, the body is below it, and we measure the distance from the axis of the force with \(r\) along the surface. The force \(F\) presses downward at the point \(O\), so the arrow ends at \(O\), like any push. The axis \(z\) goes from \(O\) into the body, and \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\) is the distance of a point from \(O\). The letter \(R\) has another role later in the chapter, the radius of curvature, but in this section it is only a distance. We write the force \(F\), not \(P\), because we kept \(P\) for the load of the beam (section 25.1).

We shall first state and check the solution, not derive it, because the derivation with potentials (BARBER §23.2.1, PDF p. 372-374) goes beyond what the book has. Checking is an honest proof: we look for a displacement field that meets all the requirements, and verifying them is a calculation. We shall not prove uniqueness, see below the theorem.

The proof will use one more figure, 25.34. On the left is a section of the body and in it a small element, acted on by the stresses of the surrounding parts. The Navier-Lamé equations say that these stresses balance on the element. On the right is the hemisphere of radius \(R = 1\) around \(O\). On it lies the point \(\vek x/R\), which we reach from any point \(\vek x\) by returning along the ray from \(O\) to the hemisphere. In this way we shall estimate the displacements and stresses far away.

Theorem 25.15 Boussinesq solution (Boussinesqova rešitev)

Let a half-space \(z \geq 0\) be made of a homogeneous, isotropic, linearly elastic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) (theorem 3.64, shear modulus \(G = E/(2(1 + \nu))\), definition 3.17), let \(F > 0\) and \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\). The displacement field

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{F}{4\pi G}\Big(\frac{x z}{R^3} - \frac{(1 - 2\nu)\,x}{R\,(R + z)}\Big) , \quad u_{\mathrm{y}} = \frac{F}{4\pi G}\Big(\frac{y z}{R^3} - \frac{(1 - 2\nu)\,y}{R\,(R + z)}\Big) , \quad u_{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{F}{4\pi G}\Big(\frac{2(1 - \nu)}{R} + \frac{z^2}{R^3}\Big) \tag{25.11}\]

has continuous second derivatives at every point with \(R > 0\) and \(z \geq 0\), and:

  1. it satisfies the Navier-Lamé equations (11.3), that is, the element is in equilibrium, without body force,
  2. it has the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z^2}{2\pi R^5}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,y z^2}{2\pi R^5}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,z^3}{2\pi R^5}\), so on every plane \(z = c > 0\) the vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}})\) points along a line through \(O\) and has the length \(3F c^2/(2\pi R^4)\),
  3. the surface \(z = 0\) outside \(O\) is free of load, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\),
  4. on every plane \(z = c > 0\) the resultant of the stresses on the disc of radius \(\rho\) centred on the \(z\) axis has the components \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = \int \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = 0\), and its component \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\mathrm{d}A\) tends to \(-F\) as \(\rho \to \infty\),
  5. the displacements of the surface are \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = \dfrac{F\,(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E\,r}\) and in the radial direction \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)(1 + \nu)\,F}{2\pi E\,r}\) (towards \(O\)), \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\),
  6. the displacements go to zero like \(1/R\) and the stresses like \(1/R^2\) as \(R \to \infty\) (estimated on the hemisphere).
Proof

We must show six claims. We compute the derivatives with the chain rule with \(\partial R/\partial x = x/R\), \(\partial R/\partial y = y/R\), \(\partial R/\partial z = z/R\) and simplify the expressions with \(R^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\), which is a calculation in SymPy (outlines/ch-kontakt-lezaji/num-04.py). One more relation is important, \((R + z)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + 2z^2 + 2Rz\).

  1. The fields (25.11) are made of powers of \(R\) and quotients with \(R + z\), which is positive on \(z \geq 0\) at \(R > 0\). So they have continuous second derivatives. The divergence is \(\operatorname{div}\vek u = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)\,F\,z}{2\pi G R^3}\) and its derivatives are \(\dfrac{\partial\operatorname{div}\vek u}{\partial x} = \dfrac{3(1 - 2\nu)F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5}\), the same for \(y\), and \(\dfrac{\partial\operatorname{div}\vek u}{\partial z} = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi G R^5}\).
  2. The Laplace operators (definition 11.5) of the components are \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{x}} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5}\), the same for \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(y\), and \(\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{z}} = \dfrac{F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi G R^5}\).
  3. By theorem 11.6 we must show that the element is in equilibrium, that is, \(\mu\,\nabla^2 u_{\mathrm{i}} + (\lambda + \mu)\,\partial(\operatorname{div}\vek u)/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) with \(\mu = G\) and \(\lambda + \mu = G/(1 - 2\nu)\) (definition 3.18, \(\lambda = 2G\nu/(1 - 2\nu)\)). Component \(x\): \(G\cdot\Big(-\dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5}\Big) + \dfrac{G}{1 - 2\nu}\cdot\dfrac{3(1 - 2\nu)F\,x z}{2\pi G R^5} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi R^5} + \dfrac{3F\,x z}{2\pi R^5} = 0\), the same for \(y\). Component \(z\): \(\dfrac{F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi R^5} - \dfrac{F\,(x^2 + y^2 - 2z^2)}{2\pi R^5} = 0\). This is claim 1. We repeated the calculation exactly, with rational numbers, at the points \((1, 2, 2)\), \((2, 3, 6)\), \((4, 4, 7)\) and \((2, 6, 9)\), where \(R\) is the integer \(3\), \(7\), \(9\), \(11\), and got zero everywhere.
  4. We get the stresses from (11.4): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \lambda\operatorname{div}\vek u + 2G\,\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = G\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z + \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x)\). After differentiating and simplifying, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,z^3\,(R + z)^2}{2\pi R^5 (R + z)^2}\), because the numerator is \(2Rz + x^2 + y^2 + 2z^2 = (R + z)^2\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}} = -\dfrac{3F\,x z^2}{2\pi R^5}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) the same. The vector \((\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}, \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}) = -\dfrac{3F z^2}{2\pi R^5}\,(x, y, z)\) is proportional to \((x, y, z)\), so it points along a line through \(O\), and on the plane \(z = c\) its length is \(\dfrac{3F c^2}{2\pi R^5}\,R = \dfrac{3F c^2}{2\pi R^4}\). This is claim 2.
  5. At \(z = 0\), that is, on the surface, all three stresses have the factor \(z^2\) and \(R = r > 0\), so they are zero. This is claim 3.
  6. For the plane \(z = c\) we use cylindrical coordinates (lemma 11.15, \(J = r\)) and theorem 4.59. On a disc of radius \(\rho\), \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -\dfrac{3F c^3}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\rho} \dfrac{r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta}{(r^2 + c^2)^{5/2}} = -3F c^3\Big[-\dfrac{1}{3(r^2 + c^2)^{3/2}}\Big]_0^{\rho} = -F\Big(1 - \dfrac{c^3}{(\rho^2 + c^2)^{3/2}}\Big)\), which tends to \(-F\) as \(\rho \to \infty\) (definition 9.21). For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xz}}\) we have \(x = r\cos\theta\) and \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 0\), the same for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yz}}\) with \(\sin\theta\). This is claim 4.
  7. At \(z = 0\) we have \(R = r\) and the deflection of the surface \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = \dfrac{F}{4\pi G}\cdot\dfrac{2(1 - \nu)}{r} = \dfrac{F(1 - \nu)}{2\pi G r}\). Since \(1/G = 2(1 + \nu)/E\), this is \(\dfrac{F(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E r}\). The radial component: \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -\dfrac{F(1 - 2\nu)\,x}{4\pi G\,r^2}\), the same for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with \(y\), so \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = -\dfrac{F(1 - 2\nu)}{4\pi G\,r} = -\dfrac{(1 - 2\nu)(1 + \nu)F}{2\pi E r}\). This is claim 5.
  8. Every term of (25.11) is divided by \(t\) when we replace \((x, y, z)\) by \((t x, t y, t z)\) with \(t > 0\), so \(\vek u(t\vek x) = \vek u(\vek x)/t\) (SymPy). Differentiating this equation with respect to \(x\) gives \(t\,\dfrac{\partial\vek u}{\partial x}(t\vek x) = \dfrac{1}{t}\,\dfrac{\partial\vek u}{\partial x}(\vek x)\), so the derivatives are divided by \(t^2\), likewise with respect to \(y\) and \(z\), and the stresses with them. For \(t = 1/R\) we get \(\vek u(\vek x) = \vek u(\vek x/R)/R\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x) = \sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}(\vek x/R)/R^2\). The point \(\vek x/R\) lies on the hemisphere \(R = 1\), \(z \geq 0\), which is a closed and bounded set, and there \(R + z \geq 1\). So the displacements and stresses are continuous on it and by theorem 1.79 bounded by some constant \(M\). Hence \(|u_{\mathrm{i}}| \leq M/R\) and \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}}| \leq M/R^2\). This is claim 6.

Source: BARBER §23.2.1, (23.14), (23.17), (23.18) (PDF p. 373-374): \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) in the form \(3z^3/R^5\) with a potential of another normalisation, the surface displacements with proportionality \(1/r\) and the same factors \((1 - 2\nu)\) and \((1 - \nu)\). TIMO (PDF p. 268-269): the direction of the stress resultant towards the point of loading, the dependence \(1/R^2\) and \(w = P(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E r)\). We checked the field (25.11) in SymPy, the proof is a verification, it is not from the source. We do not prove uniqueness of the solution (see the text).

The proof showed that the field (25.11) solves the equations in the interior, that the surface is free of load everywhere except at the point \(O\), and that every plane below the surface carries the whole force \(F\). The last is what we expect of a point load: we cut off the part of the body above the plane \(z = c\) and the force \(F\) acts downward on it, so by the equilibrium of a part of a body (corollary 4.41, used here without proof on an unbounded part containing the point \(O\), so only as an expectation, the proof is step 6) the lower part must act with \(F\) upward, which with the normal \(+\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\vek t = \ten\sigma\,\vek n\) is exactly \(\int \sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\,\mathrm{d}A = -F\).

We do not prove uniqueness. Theorem 11.4 holds for bounded bodies and smooth data, while the half-space is unbounded and a force at a point is not a smooth load (we do not prove uniqueness of the contact problem of an interference fit either, section 11.7.6, there because the contact pressure is not given). For the chosen solution it helps that the displacements and stresses decay (claim 6), and that the displacements depend on \(1/r\), which also follows from a dimensional argument (BARBER PDF p. 374), but this is not a proof of uniqueness.

From history

Joseph Valentin Boussinesq (1842-1929) was the most distinguished pupil of Saint-Venant (TIMO, PDF p. 267). In 1867 he took his doctorate and at about the same time wrote a treatise on the theory of elasticity, which Saint-Venant reviewed and at once recognised the young author as exceptional (TIMO, PDF p. 267). In 1873 he became a professor in Lille (TIMO, PDF p. 268). His most important works are collected in a book on the application of potentials to the equilibrium and motion of elastic bodies, published in Paris in 1885 (TIMO, PDF p. 268). Timoshenko writes that among his solutions the most important for practice are those of the stresses and deformations in a semi-infinite body due to known forces on the boundary plane (TIMO, PDF p. 268). In the simplest case the force acts perpendicular to the plane. Boussinesq found that the resultant of the stress on a horizontal plane points along the line through the loaded point and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from it (TIMO, PDF p. 268-269). For the vertical displacement of the boundary plane he obtained \(w = P(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E r)\), so the product \(w r\) is constant (rectangles of the same area) and the lines from the origin on the boundary turn into hyperbolas with the asymptotes \(Or\) and \(Oz\) after deformation (TIMO, PDF p. 269).

Let us return to the field (25.11): the historical result is claim 5 of the theorem, and the corollary is its special case.

Corollary 25.16 Deflection of the surface of a half-space (poves površja polprostora)

Under the conditions of theorem 25.15, for every \(r > 0\) the deflection of the surface is \(w(r) = u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) = \dfrac{F\,(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E\,r}\), so the product \(w\,r = \dfrac{F\,(1 - \nu^2)}{\pi E}\) is constant, the graph of \(w\) over \(r\) is a hyperbola with the asymptotes the \(r\)-axis and the \(z\)-axis, and \(w \to \infty\) as \(r \to 0\).

Proof

By claim 5 of theorem 25.15, \(u_{\mathrm{z}}(r, 0) = F(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E r)\). If \(w(r_1) = C/r_1\) and \(w(r_2) = C/r_2\), then \(w(r_1)\,r_1 = C = w(r_2)\,r_2\) for any two distances, so the rectangles \(r_1 \times w_1\) and \(r_2 \times w_2\) with the common vertex \(O\) and sides on the axes are not similar, but they have the same area \(C\). As \(r \to 0\) the denominator has the limit zero and the numerator is constant, so \(w\) grows beyond every bound.

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 269), BARBER (23.18) (PDF p. 374). The proof is a corollary of the theorem.

Let us look at this on the graph of the deflection in the left panel of figure 25.33: the blue curve is \(w = C/r\) and its value is read by the scale downward. Two rectangular areas are the same number \(C\): at \(r_1 = 1\) the deflection \(w_1\) is four times larger than the deflection \(w_2\) at \(r_2 = 4\), because \(r_2 = 4r_1\) and \(w r\) is constant. For our steel and the force \(1000\) N, \(C = F(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E) = 1{,}478 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m\(^2\), so \(w = 1{,}478\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(r = 1\) mm, \(0{,}148\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(10\) mm and \(14{,}78\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(0{,}1\) mm (SymPy, num-04.py). The radial displacement is towards \(O\) and is \(0{,}422\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(r = 1\) mm, so smaller than the deflection by the factor \((1 - 2\nu)/(2(1 - \nu)) = 0{,}286\).

It is also worth seeing how such a deflection arises. For the foundation of section 25.1 the displacement of a point of the foundation is the force per unit length with which the beam presses on the foundation at that point, divided by \(k\), so it depends only on that force. Here the deflection at the distance \(r\) depends on the force acting at the distance \(r\) away, and it decays only like \(1/r\), more slowly than for any foundation with only local stiffness. Why exactly \(1/r\)? The reason is in the units: the force \(F\) is in N, the modulus \(E\) in N/m\(^2\), so \(F/E\) is in m\(^2\), while the deflection is a length in m. Since the theory is linear, the deflection is proportional to \(F\), so \(w = (F/E)\,f\), where \(f\) has the unit 1/m. The only length left is \(r\), so \(f = g(\nu)/r\) and \(w = g(\nu)\,F/(E\,r)\), and the number \((1 - \nu^2)/\pi\) only sets the size. This is not a proof, but it says why the deflection decays slowly and not faster. So for the half-space we shall have to add up the influence of the pressure from the whole region of contact.

Let us look at what the force does in the interior. The middle panel of figure 25.33 is a section of the body in true proportions. It shows the same surface and the same force \(F\) at the point \(O\) as on the left. The plane \(z = c\) is at the depth \(c\) below \(O\). We draw the dashed rays from \(O\) to chosen points of the plane, because by claim 2 of theorem 25.15 the stress resultant points along such lines. The orange arrows are the stresses that the part of the body above the plane transmits to the lower part. Each ends on the plane, on its own line, because they push the lower part downward, and their length falls with \((c/R)^4\), so quickly as we move away from the axis: at \(r = c\) the length is \(0{,}25\) of the length on the axis, and at \(r = 2c\) it is \(0{,}04\) (by \(3F c^2/(2\pi R^4)\), SymPy). The right panel shows only the vertical component: horizontally \(r/c\), vertically \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}|\) divided by its value on the axis. The bell is \((1 + (r/c)^2)^{-5/2}\), the stress \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}| = \dfrac{3F}{2\pi c^2}\big(1 + (r/c)^2\big)^{-5/2}\) divided by its value on the axis. When we rotate the area under the bell for the undivided stress about the axis, the solid obtained has by claim 4 the volume \(F\). At \(c = 5\) mm and \(F = 1000\) N, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) on the axis is \(-19{,}10\) MPa, at \(r = 5\) mm \(-3{,}376\) MPa, at \(10\) mm \(-0{,}342\) MPa and at \(15\) mm \(-0{,}060\) MPa. So at the depth \(c\) the load spreads over a disc of radius a few times \(c\). We trust the field of a point force as a stand-in for a pressure on a small region only at a distance much larger than the size of the region (at a distance of two radii of a loaded disc the difference is \(3{,}5\ \%\), at six radii \(0{,}35\ \%\), as we shall see below).

How close to \(O\) we may trust linear theory itself is told by the size of the derivatives of the displacements. On the surface the largest are \(|\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial r| = |\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial z| = C/r^2\), the first is the slope of the deflection curve, the others are smaller or zero (SymPy). Inside the body, at the same distance \(R\) from \(O\), the largest derivative is on the axis below \(O\), \(|\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z| = \dfrac{3 - 2\nu}{2(1 - \nu)}\,\dfrac{C}{R^2} = 1{,}71\,C/R^2\). At \(r = 1\) mm this is \(1{,}5\cdot 10^{-3}\), at \(r = 0{,}3\) mm it is \(1{,}6\cdot 10^{-2}\) and at \(r = 0{,}1\) mm it is \(0{,}148\). Linear theory assumes that all derivatives of the displacements are below about \(0{,}001\) in size (section 3.2.1, assumption 4), so for our force it holds for \(R \gtrsim 1{,}6\) mm, \(R = \sqrt{1{,}71\,C/0{,}001}\).

Near the point of loading. As \(r \to 0\) the deflection goes beyond every bound (corollary 25.16), and the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) on the axis goes as \(1/z^2\) as \(z \to 0\). This is not a mistake of the solution but a measure of the model: a force at one point means infinite pressure, because pressure is force over area and the area is zero. No steel bears such a pressure, so the model stops being used long before infinity is put into the calculation, at the yield limit. Timoshenko writes that we can help ourselves by cutting out the material near the point with a hemispherical surface of small radius and replacing the force by statically equivalent forces distributed over this surface (TIMO, PDF p. 269). The second way out, which we shall use, means the same: the force acts on a finite region of the surface, as a pressure.

25.4.1 Pressure on a finite region

Let the force act not at a point but as a pressure \(p\) on a region \(A\) of the surface. Pressure (tlak) is a function of a point of the surface: at the point \(s \in A\) the number \(p(s)\) is the force per unit area in N/m\(^2\) (in MPa), and the force on a part \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the region is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\) over a set with an area (definition 4.30). The sum over the parts is the whole force \(F = \int_{\mathrm{A}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\). We know how the surface sinks only for a point force, so we cut the region into finitely many parts, replace the force of each part by a point force and add the fields by the principle of superposition. Does the sum settle as the parts become ever smaller? Figure 25.37 (left) shows what we draw for the proof.

First the disc of radius \(a\) and centre \(O\): the region on which the pressure acts. In it is the point \(x\), at which we look for the deflection. If \(x\) lies outside the region, the function \(1/|x - s|\) is continuous on it, which we shall use in step 2. If it lies inside, the function is unbounded as \(s \to x\). So from \(x\) we draw a sector between two rays, where the distance \(\rho = |x - s|\) varies from zero to the edge, and write the integral in polar coordinates around \(x\), where the factor \(\rho\) from the Jacobian determinant just cancels \(1/\rho\). The length of this ray up to the edge is the chord \(\ell(\varphi)\) at the angle \(\varphi\).

The second figure, 25.38, shows what we do for a point outside and inside. On the left the region is cut into parts, the point \(x\) lies outside at the distance \(d\) from it, one part \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\) has diameter \(h\) and in it the point \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\), where we place its force. On the right the point lies inside the region and we cut out of it a small disc of radius \(\varepsilon\).

Lemma 25.17 Deflection under a pressure (poves pod tlakom)

The material and model as in theorem 25.15. Let \(A\) be a closed convex set with an area on the surface \(z = 0\) (a disc, an ellipse, a rectangle) of diameter \(D\) (the diameter of a set is the largest distance between two of its points), and \(p \geq 0\) a continuous pressure function on \(A\), \(p \leq p_{\max}\), \(F = \int_{\mathrm{A}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\). For a point \(x\) of the surface we denote

\[w(x) = \frac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\int_{\mathrm{A}} \frac{p(s)}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}A(s) . \tag{25.12}\]
  1. If \(x\) has the distance \(d > 0\) from \(A\) and we cut \(A\) into parts \(A_1, \dots, A_{\mathrm{n}}\) of diameter at most \(h\), with points \(s_{\mathrm{j}} \in A_{\mathrm{j}}\) and forces \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\), the deflection of the surface at \(x\) due to the point forces \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) at \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x) = \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} \dfrac{F_{\mathrm{j}}}{|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|}\) and \(\big|w_{\mathrm{n}}(x) - w(x)\big| \leq \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\cdot\dfrac{F\,h}{d^2}\).
  2. If \(x\) lies in \(A\), the integrand is unbounded at \(s = x\), so there the integral (25.12) means the limit of the integrals over \(A\) without the disc of radius \(\varepsilon\) around \(x\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). This limit exists and in polar coordinates around \(x\) it is \(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\ell(\varphi)} p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), where \(\ell(\varphi) \leq D\) is the length of the ray to the edge, and hence \(w(x) \leq \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\,2\pi D\,p_{\max}\).
Proof

We must show an estimate for a point outside and finiteness for a point inside the region.

  1. The field of the point force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\) at \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the field (25.11), shifted to \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\). By theorem 25.15 it satisfies the equations, and by corollary 11.3 (its proof uses only the linearity of derivatives and of Hooke's law, so it holds for the half-space as well) the sum of the fields is a field with displacements and stresses that are the same sums. On the surface, by corollary 25.16, the displacement is \(F_{\mathrm{j}}(1 - \nu^2)/(\pi E\,|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|)\), which gives \(w_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  2. For every \(j\) the difference \(\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A - F_{\mathrm{j}}/|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|\) equals \(\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p(s)\big(\dfrac{1}{|x - s|} - \dfrac{1}{|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|}\big)\mathrm{d}A\), because \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p\,\mathrm{d}A\). Since \(|x - s|\) and \(|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|\) are both at least \(d\) and differ by at most \(|s - s_{\mathrm{j}}| \leq h\), \(\Big|\dfrac{1}{|x - s|} - \dfrac{1}{|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|}\Big| = \dfrac{\big||x - s_{\mathrm{j}}| - |x - s|\big|}{|x - s|\,|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|} \leq \dfrac{h}{d^2}\). So the difference is \(|\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{j}} p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A - F_{\mathrm{j}}/|x - s_{\mathrm{j}}|| \leq F_{\mathrm{j}}\,h/d^2\). We add over \(j\) and use \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{j}} = F\) (additivity of the integral over a set). This is the estimate of claim 1. As \(h \to 0\) the right side tends to zero, so \(w_{\mathrm{n}}(x)\) tends to \(w(x)\).
  3. For \(x \in A\) we take \(A\) without the disc of radius \(\varepsilon\) around \(x\). Since \(A\) is convex, the set of points of \(A\) on the ray at the angle \(\varphi\) from \(x\) is a segment \(0 \leq \rho \leq \ell(\varphi)\) with \(\ell \leq D\). In polar coordinates around \(x\), \(J = \rho\) (theorem 4.59, \(\Phi(\rho, \varphi) = x + \rho\,(\cos\varphi, \sin\varphi)\)), so \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_\varepsilon^{\ell(\varphi)} (p/\rho)\,\rho\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), where \(\rho\) cancels \(1/\rho\) (where \(\ell(\varphi) < \varepsilon\), the inner integral is zero).
  4. The integrand \(p\) is continuous and bounded by \(p_{\max}\), and \(\ell(\varphi) \leq D\), so the integral \(\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\ell(\varphi)} p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\) exists and is at most \(2\pi D\,p_{\max}\). It differs from the integral of step 3 by the integral over \(0 \leq \rho \leq \varepsilon\), which is at most \(2\pi\varepsilon\,p_{\max}\) and tends to zero as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). So the limit exists and equals this integral. This is claim 2.

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 269): Boussinesq solves a load distributed over a part of the boundary plane by the principle of superposition. The proof is not from the source. For a point inside the region we do not prove that the value of the integral is the value of the true solution for a pressure, but take it as a definition and check it against TIMO on the example of a disc below (cited, not proved).

The proof showed two things: for points outside the region the sum of point forces does settle at the integral, with an error estimate proportional to \(h\), and for points inside the integral is finite although the integrand has a singularity. This is exactly what the point force lacks.

Uniform pressure on a disc. Let \(p = q\) be constant on a disc of radius \(a\). For \(x\) at the centre, \(\ell(\varphi) = a\) for every \(\varphi\) and by claim 2, \(\int_0^{2\pi} a\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = 2\pi a\), so \(w(0) = \dfrac{1 - \nu^2}{\pi E}\,q\,2\pi a = \dfrac{2(1 - \nu^2)\,q\,a}{E}\). For \(x\) on the edge, with \(\varphi\) measured from the direction towards the centre, \(\ell(\varphi) = 2a\cos\varphi\) for \(|\varphi| < \pi/2\) and zero elsewhere, so \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} 2a\cos\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = 4a\) and \(w(a) = \dfrac{4(1 - \nu^2)\,q\,a}{\pi E} = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\,w(0)\). TIMO (PDF p. 269) gives the same two numbers: \(w_0 = 2(1 - \nu^2)\,q\,a/E\) at the centre and \(2w_0/\pi\) at the edge. Our calculation gives them without quoting, so this is a verification of that claim (SymPy and NumPy, num-04.py). Let us take \(F = 1000\) N on a disc of radius \(a = 1\) mm, \(q = F/(\pi a^2) = 318{,}3\) MPa: \(w(0) = 2{,}956\ \mu\text{m}\), \(w(a) = 1{,}882\ \mu\text{m}\), and the point force would give \(1{,}478\ \mu\text{m}\) at the distance \(a\). The right panel of figure 25.37 shows the course of the deflection divided by the deflection at the centre, over \(r/a\): the blue curve is the deflection of the disc, at the edge it is \(2/\pi = 0{,}637\) of the deflection at the centre, and the orange curve is the deflection of the point force at the centre. At \(r = 2a\) the disc is \(3{,}5\ \%\) above the point force (\(0{,}7645\) against \(0{,}7389\ \mu\text{m}\)), and at \(r = 6a\) only \(0{,}35\ \%\), as we expect: from far away we cannot see whether the force acts at a point or on a small disc.

Sum and integral. Let us check the estimate of claim 1 at \(x\) at the distance \(2a\) from the centre, where \(d = a\), with \(a = 1\) mm and \(F = 1000\) N. We divide the plane into small squares of side \(2a/n\). The part \(A_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the intersection of a square with the disc, its force is \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = q\) times the area of the part, the point \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the centroid of the part, and the forces add up to \(F\). The exact value is \(w(2a) = 0{,}7645\ \mu\text{m}\) and the deviation of the sum \(w_{\mathrm{n}}\) at \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\) is \(-1{,}49\ \%\), \(-0{,}33\ \%\), \(-0{,}081\ \%\), \(-0{,}021\ \%\), \(-0{,}0049\ \%\), \(-0{,}0013\ \%\) (NumPy, areas and centroids approximately from \(200 \times 200\) points in each square). The estimate of claim 1 gives at most \(8{,}5\ \%\) at \(n = 64\) (the diameter of a part is at most \(h = \sqrt{2}\cdot 2a/64\)), while the actual deviation \(0{,}0013\ \%\) is much smaller: it falls by about a factor of four at each halving of the side, the estimate only by a factor of two. The estimate is therefore reliable but coarse. It falls with \(h\), which is what we need.

The point force is not a limit. Let us take the same force \(F = 1000\) N on an ever smaller disc: \(a = 1\) mm gives \(w(0) = 2{,}956\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(q = 318\) MPa, \(a = 0{,}1\) mm gives \(29{,}56\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(q = 31\,830\) MPa, \(a = 0{,}01\) mm gives \(295{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(q = 3{,}18\cdot 10^6\) MPa. The product \(w(0)\,a = 2(1 - \nu^2)F/(\pi E) = 2C\) is constant, so \(w(0) = 2C/a \to \infty\) as \(a \to 0\), as for a point force. So the deflection at the centre has no finite limit as \(a \to 0\), while away from the centre it tends to that of the point force. So we must not regard the point force as the limiting case of contact. Contact requires a finite region, which we do not know in advance, since it depends on the deflection. This will be the task of the following sections.

25.5 Hertz contact of two cylinders: the contact conditions and line contact

At the end of section 25.4 we found that a point force cannot be a model of contact: the deflection under it is infinite, and the pressure is infinite for every finite force. A contact needs a region of finite size, which we do not know in advance, because the deflection itself determines it. In a roller bearing such a contact is met at every step: a roller, a steel cylinder with a radius of a few millimetres, lies on a raceway, and the raceway pushes it with a force that the bearing has to carry. The question of this section is therefore: how wide is the strip along which roller and raceway touch, how large is the pressure in it, and how does the load connect them? We start with two cylinders, because this is a plane problem, and for the plane we have Flamant's solution (theorem 25.13). The ball, which needs a three-dimensional solution after Boussinesq, is treated in section 25.6.

Let us draw figure 25.39, first the left half. We take the lower body, whose surface bulges upwards with radius \(R_2\). It stands for a piece of the raceway under the roller, and we need its flat lower face only to have something to rest it on. On it we place the upper cylinder with radius \(R_1\), whose axis is perpendicular to the plane of the drawing. It is drawn as a circle because we look at a cross-section, and both bodies have the same length along the axis, which is much larger than everything in the cross-section. Therefore nothing changes along the axis and the plane of the drawing tells everything (plane strain, definition 11.32). The bodies are pressed together by the forces \(F'\): the upper cylinder pushes down, the lower body pushes up, both along the line through the centres. The prime on \(F'\) is not a derivative, it says that this is the force per unit length of the axis (sila na enoto dolžine), in N/m, in numbers in N/mm. The bodies touch at the point of the cross-section on this line, which in space is a line along the whole length of the axis. For this reason we call it a line contact (črtni stik).

Before we compute, let us say when the model is good. For the roller we take a steel cylinder with radius \(R_1 = 5\) mm, for the raceway the radius \(R_2 = 25\) mm and for the force \(F' = 100\) N/mm. Below we will compute that under this force the point of touching widens into a strip \(0{,}14\) mm wide, which is \(2{,}8\ \%\) of the radius of the roller. At the scale of figure 25.39 it would measure \(0{,}22\) mm, less than the thickness of the drawn line, so figure 25.41 below draws it strongly exaggerated. This is what we need: the strip is small compared with the bodies, so in computing the stresses near the contact we can take each body to be a half-plane, as if the surface were infinite. The assumption holds as long as the strip is small against both radii. It fails for a conformal contact, where the contact surface is comparable with the body, and for a body that is not much larger than the strip in every direction, for example a thin layer on a base. What it costs in the shape of the surfaces is told by lemma 25.20: for our numbers the error is of the order \((b/R_1)^2 = 2\cdot 10^{-4}\), where \(b\) is half the width of the strip. We do not estimate the error due to the finite thickness of the bodies.

Definition 25.18 Nonconformal contact (nekonformni stik)

A contact of two bodies is nonconformal if it has three properties:

  1. Before loading the bodies touch at a point or along a line.
  2. Both bodies are smooth near the contact, so that their local shape can be described by convex surfaces (here a cylinder or a sphere).
  3. The contact patch is much smaller than both bodies.

Source: BOWER §5.4.11 (PDF p. 333): "(1) the two contacting solids initially touch at a point or along a line, (2) both contacting solids are smooth in the neighborhood of the contact, so that their local geometry can be approximated as ellipsoids, and (3) the size of the contact patch between the two solids is much smaller than either solid." Frictionless contact is assumed there too (same place). For surface shear see HK §6.5 (PDF pp. 139-142), which we do not treat here.

The name says the opposite, as figure 25.40 shows. On the left is a ball in a groove of almost the same radius: in a conformal contact (konformni stik) the bodies fit each other and the contact patch is already large at a small load. On the right is a roller on a raceway, where before loading the bodies touch at a point or a line and the contact patch is small. This section treats the roller on the raceway, section 25.6 the ball. In addition we take the bodies to be linearly elastic, isotropic and homogeneous, the strains to be small, and the contact to be frictionless, so that only normal forces act on the contact surface (BOWER, section 5.4.11, PDF p. 333).

Why may we leave out friction? Friction acts only where the surfaces would slide on each other. By lemma 25.14 (claim 1) under the force \(F'\) every point of the surface moves sideways toward the force, by \((1 - 2\nu)(1 + \nu)F'/(2E)\), which depends only on the material and not on the distance to the force. The same pressure acts on both surfaces (Newton's third law), so for a roller and a raceway of the same steel the points of both surfaces at the same place move sideways by the same distance and in the same direction. The surfaces therefore do not slide on each other, friction does not act, and for us the assumption costs nothing. For different materials, for example steel on bronze, the sideways displacements differ, friction adds shear stresses and these change the pressure. BARBER (§12.7, PDF p. 200) shows that this effect vanishes for equal materials and may be neglected when Dundurs' parameter \(\beta\) of his (12.72) is much smaller than \(1\). We do not compute this correction.

Property 3 is an inequality that we must check, and we will: for our numbers \(b/R_1 = 0{,}014\), and at four times the load \(0{,}028\). Property 1 tells where we start: as the load grows, the point of touching, a line in space, widens into a strip.

The contact strip (stična ožina) is the set of points where the surfaces touch, and we do not know which points these are. So we describe it with two functions, which we draw in figure 25.41. Let \(x\) be the coordinate along the common tangent at the point of touching, measured in the plane of the cross-section. The orange lines are the surfaces of bodies 1 and 2 after loading. In the middle they touch along the strip of width \(2b\), outside it they part. The gap (zazor) \(g(x)\) is the distance between the surfaces at the coordinate \(x\), measured in the direction of the force. The pressure (tlak) \(p(x)\) is the normal force per area of the contact surface that the bodies exert on each other, in N/m\(^2\), in numbers in MPa. By Newton's third law body 1 acts on body 2 with the same force as body 2 on body 1, so on both surfaces we have the same \(p\). The force per unit length of the axis is then \(\int p\,\mathrm{d}x\) over the contact strip, in the figure the area under the pressure curve.

Definition 25.19 Contact conditions (stični pogoji)

Let two bodies that are in contact before loading be loaded by a force \(F' > 0\) per unit length. The unknowns are the functions of gap \(g\) and pressure \(p\) on the line of contact, both with values in \(\mathbb{R}\). The gap is the one the pressure produces: \(g = g_0 - \delta + w\), where \(g_0\) is the gap of the undeformed bodies, \(w\) the sum of the surface displacements under the pressure \(p\) and \(\delta\) an unknown number (explained below). The contact problem (stični problem) requires that conditions 1 to 3 hold for every \(x\) and that condition 4 holds:

  1. \(g(x) \geq 0\): the bodies do not penetrate each other.
  2. \(p(x) \geq 0\): the contact does not pull, the surfaces only push each other.
  3. \(g(x)\,p(x) = 0\): there is pressure only where the gap is zero, and the gap is larger than zero only where there is no pressure.
  4. \(\int p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = F'\): the pressure carries the whole force.

The set \(\Omega = \{x : g(x) = 0\}\) is the contact set (stična množica). Besides \(p\) and \(g\) we must determine it, and for this very reason the contact problem is not linear: the solutions for the forces \(F'_1\) and \(F'_2\) have different \(\Omega\), so their sum is not the solution for \(F'_1 + F'_2\).

Source: BARBER §12.5.3 (PDF p. 195), inequalities (12.48) "contact traction should not be tensile" and (12.49) "no interference between the bodies outside the contact area". The complete form with requirement (3) is my formulation of both. Uniqueness of the solution is not proved (see the remark below theorem 25.24).

Let us read the conditions in figure 25.41. Condition 1 says that the orange lines must not pass through each other, because the bodies are solid and cannot be in the same place at once. Condition 2 says that the pressure is everywhere above the axis: the surfaces are not glued, so they can push each other but cannot pull, like a palm laid on a table. Condition 3 connects the two: where there is a gap between the surfaces, they do not touch and there is no force between them, and where they touch, in the strip, there is no gap.
