At every point at least one of the numbers \(g\) and \(p\) is therefore zero. Condition 4 is the equilibrium of the cylinder: the area under the pressure is the force with which the raceway holds the cylinder, and it must equal the force \(F'\) that presses it.

Let us compare this with the previous example of a contact. In the shrink fit of tubes (section 11.7.6) the contact was on the whole cylindrical surface, so \(\Omega\) was known and only the pressure \(p_{\mathrm{c}}\) was unknown. Uniqueness of the contact problem itself, where \(p_{\mathrm{c}}\) is not given, was not proved there, and it is not proved here either. For the cylinders we do not know in advance how wide the strip is: the deformation itself decides it.

The gap after loading consists of three parts, which we show in figure 25.41. The first is the gap of the undeformed bodies \(g_0\), the distance between the surfaces before we press them. The second is the movement of the bodies towards each other: if the bodies could pass through each other, their distant parts would come closer by \(\delta\) and the undeformed surfaces would overlap, as the grey dashed lines show. In the middle the overlap is largest, exactly \(\delta\), and the gap would be \(g_0 - \delta\), negative in the middle. The third part are the elastic displacements of the surfaces: the pressure pushes each surface back into its body, from the grey dashed to the orange line, and we denote the sum of the two displacements by \(w\). Together the gap is \(g = g_0 - \delta + w\) (in theorem 25.24 equation (25.19)). In the middle of the strip \(g_0 = 0\) and \(g = 0\), so there the two displacements together make up exactly \(\delta\). First the first part, \(g_0\).

Let us draw the cylinders before loading in figure 25.42. Through the point of touching \(O\) we draw the common tangent, which is the \(x\) axis, and perpendicular to it the normal, on which the centres of both circles lie. The upper circle with radius \(R_1\) rises from the tangent, the lower one with radius \(R_2\) falls away from it. We choose a distance \(x\) from the normal. The point of the upper circle is there \(d_1\) above the tangent, the point of the lower one \(d_2\) below it. The distance between them is the gap \(g_0(x) = d_1 + d_2\), which by symmetry is the same on both sides of the normal, so it is drawn on the left. We get the offset \(d_1\) from the right triangle: its hypotenuse is the radius \(R_1\) from the centre to the point on the circle, the horizontal leg is \(x\), and the vertical leg is \(\sqrt{R_1^2 - x^2}\) and reaches from the centre to the height of the point. The centre is \(R_1\) above the tangent, so \(d_1 = R_1 - \sqrt{R_1^2 - x^2}\). The dashed parabolas \(x^2/(2R_1)\) and \(x^2/(2R_2)\) fit the circles near \(O\), and further from \(O\) they stay between the tangent and the circle. The lemma tells by how much.

Lemma 25.20 Gap of two cylinders (zazor dveh valjev)

Let two cylinders with radii \(R_1, R_2 > 0\) be convex, touching at the point \(O\) of the cross-section where \(x = 0\). The gap of the undeformed cylinders at the distance \(x\) from \(O\), \(|x| \leq \min(R_1, R_2)\), is

\[g_0(x) = \big(R_1 - \sqrt{R_1^2 - x^2}\big) + \big(R_2 - \sqrt{R_2^2 - x^2}\big) , \tag{25.13}\]

and it satisfies

\[\frac{x^2}{2R} \leq g_0(x) \leq \frac{x^2}{2R}\Big(1 + \frac{x^2}{R_{\min}^2}\Big) , \qquad \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} , \tag{25.14}\]

where \(R_{\min} = \min(R_1, R_2)\).

Proof

We must show that \(g_0\) is the sum of the offsets of two circles from the common tangent, and estimate each.

  1. A circle with radius \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) that touches the tangent at \(O\) has its centre on the normal at \(O\) at the distance \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\). Its point at the distance \(x\) from the normal is at the distance \(d_{\mathrm{i}} = R_{\mathrm{i}} - \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2}\) from the tangent by Pythagoras' theorem in the triangle. The bodies lie on the two sides of the tangent, so the gap is the sum of the two offsets, which is (25.13).
  2. For each offset we extend the fraction: \(R_{\mathrm{i}} - \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2} = x^2/(R_{\mathrm{i}} + \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2})\).
  3. Lower bound. Since \(\sqrt{R_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - x^2} \leq R_{\mathrm{i}}\), the denominator is at most \(2R_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the offset is at least \(x^2/(2R_{\mathrm{i}})\): the parabola nowhere reaches beyond the circle.
  1. Upper bound: the offset does not exceed the parabola multiplied by \(1 + q^2\), where \(q = |x|/R_{\mathrm{i}} \leq 1\). We need two inequalities, drawn in figure 25.43. On the left, above the axis \(q\) from \(0\) to \(1\), is the quarter circle \(\sqrt{1 - q^2}\) and below it the parabola \(1 - q^2\), at \(q = 0{,}6\) the lengths \(0{,}8\) and \(0{,}64\). That the circle is above everywhere follows from \(1 - q^2 \geq (1 - q^2)^2 = 1 - 2q^2 + q^4\), which holds exactly when \(q^2 \geq q^4\), so for every \(q^2 \leq 1\). So the denominator is at least \(R_{\mathrm{i}}(2 - q^2)\) and the offset at most \(\dfrac{x^2}{R_{\mathrm{i}}(2 - q^2)} = \dfrac{x^2}{2R_{\mathrm{i}}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1 - q^2/2}\). On the right, above the axis \(u\) from \(0\) to \(\tfrac12\), is the curve \(1/(1 - u)\) and above it the line \(1 + 2u\), at \(u = 0{,}25\) the lengths \(1{,}333\) and \(1{,}5\). The line is above, because \((1 + 2u)(1 - u) - 1 = u(1 - 2u) \geq 0\) for \(0 \leq u \leq \tfrac12\), so \(1/(1 - u) \leq 1 + 2u\). With \(u = q^2/2 \leq \tfrac12\) the offset is at most \(\dfrac{x^2}{2R_{\mathrm{i}}}(1 + q^2)\).
  2. We add the two offsets to the gap: the lower bound is \(\tfrac{x^2}{2}(1/R_1 + 1/R_2) = x^2/(2R)\), the upper bound is \(\tfrac{x^2}{2R}(1 + q_{\max}^2)\) with \(q_{\max} = |x|/R_{\min}\), because \(q_{\mathrm{i}} \leq q_{\max}\).

Source: The computation is mine. BARBER §12.6 (PDF p. 197) takes the radii to be large compared with the contact width, \(R_1, R_2 \gg a\), and describes the gap by a known function \(h(x)\). Our estimate tells how large the correction is.

For our roller and raceway at \(x = b = 70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\) the largest relative error is \(\big(b/R_1\big)^2 = 2{,}0\cdot 10^{-4}\), and the actual error of a single circular offset, for example for \(R_1\), at \(x = b\) is only \(4{,}9\cdot 10^{-5}\) (SymPy, num-05.py). In the contact strip we may therefore write the gap of the undeformed bodies as \(g_0 = x^2/(2R)\), a parabola, and this is the gap of one cylinder with radius \(R\) against a plane. The replacement holds only near the point of touching: in figure 25.42, where \(x = 0{,}77\,R_1\) is drawn, the parabola is \(18\ \%\) too low, while in the strip \(x \leq 0{,}014\,R_1\). For what follows we need one more number: both bodies deform under load, and their elasticity must enter in a single number.

Definition 25.21 Effective modulus and effective radius of contact (efektivni modul in polmer stika)

For two bodies in contact with moduli \(E_1, E_2\), Poisson ratios \(\nu_1, \nu_2\) and radii \(R_1, R_2\) we define the numbers \(E^*\) (half-plane) and \(R\) (rigid cylinder) by

\[\frac{1}{E^*} = \frac{1 - \nu_1^2}{E_1} + \frac{1 - \nu_2^2}{E_2} , \qquad \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} . \tag{25.15}\]

Both are numbers with the units Pa and m. If the surface of a body is convex, its radius is positive, if it is concave, negative (BOWER, PDF p. 333, and the treatment in section 25.6).

Source: BOWER §5.4.11 (PDF p. 333): "effective modulus" is our \(E^*\). Our \(R\) is in Bower the first principal relative contact radius (glavni relativni polmer stika), in his notation \(1/R_1 = (A + B)/2\) (his \(R_1\) is not our roller radius), which for parallel cylinders (angle \(\alpha = 0\), second radii of curvature infinite) gives our sum \(1/R_1 + 1/R_2\). His "effective contact radius" \(R_{\mathrm{e}} = \sqrt{R_1 R_2}\) is infinite for parallel cylinders, because there his \(1/R_2 = (A - B)/2 = 0\). HK (6.51) (PDF p. 132): \(b = \big[\tfrac{4Q}{\pi l\,\Sigma\rho}\big(\tfrac{1 - \xi_{\mathrm{I}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{I}}} + \tfrac{1 - \xi_{\mathrm{II}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{II}}}\big)\big]^{1/2}\) contains the same sum \((1 - \xi^2)/E\) and \(\Sigma\rho = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2\).

Three warnings about notation. The letter \(E^*\) is here an italic number, while in the chapter on deformation the bold \(\mat E^*\) is the Euler-Almansi tensor, a different object. In section 25.3, \(E^* = E/(1 - \nu^2)\) was the modulus of one body in plane strain (corollary 11.38). The effective modulus extends it to two bodies: if the second body is rigid (\(E_2 \to \infty\)), then \(E^* = E_1/(1 - \nu_1^2)\), the same number. For two equal bodies, however, it is half as large, because (25.15) has two equal terms \((1 - \nu^2)/E\) instead of one. The letter \(R\) is the radius of the contact, not to be confused with the distance \(R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\) of section 25.4. For two steel bodies of the book (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)) we have \(E^* = E/(2(1 - \nu^2)) = 107{,}692\) GPa, because both terms are equal and each is \((1 - \nu^2)/E\). For the roller and the raceway \(R = 4{,}1667\) mm.

Now we can look at the right half of figure 25.39. The equivalent problem is drawn: a half-plane with modulus \(E^*\) replaces both elastic bodies, and a rigid cylinder with radius \(R\) and the same force \(F'\) replaces the gap \(g_0 = x^2/(2R)\). The horizontal and the vertical coordinate are drawn with the axes, as in sections 25.3 and 25.4. Whether the problem is really equivalent is shown by the computation of displacements below: the displacements of the surfaces of the two bodies add up in the gap, and their sum has the same form as for a half-plane with modulus \(E^*\).

Why such a sum appears we see when we compute the deflection that a pressure causes on the half-plane.

Let us draw the left half of figure 25.44. On the surface of the half-plane the pressure \(p(s)\) acts between \(-b\) and \(b\). We cut out of it a narrow slice \([s, s + h]\) of width \(h\), which carries the force \(\int_{\mathrm{s}}^{s+h} p\,\mathrm{d}s\) per unit length. So narrow a slice acts as a single force, and for that we have Flamant's solution (lemma 25.14): a force \(F\) per unit length at the point \(s\) of the surface of the half-plane gives the deflection into the body \(-\dfrac{2(1 - \nu^2)\,F}{\pi E}\ln|x - s| + \text{const.}\), where the constant does not depend on \(x\). This is the orange dimple, deepest at the slice and ever shallower with the distance \(|x - s|\). At the point \(x\) the slice contributes the deflection that the blue distance shows. We cut the pressure \(p\) on the interval \([-b, b]\) into such pieces \([s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}} + h]\) with forces \(F_{\mathrm{j}} = \int p\,\mathrm{d}s\) over the piece and add the contributions by the principle of superposition (corollary 11.3). The limit of the Riemann sums is an integral (as in lemma 25.17, where here the kernel \(\ln|x - s|\) is integrable even at \(s \to x\)). We state it in a lemma.

Lemma 25.22 Surface deflection under a line pressure (poves površja pod črtnim tlakom)

Let each body of definition 25.18 be replaced by a half-plane in plane strain with constant \(E_{\mathrm{i}}, \nu_{\mathrm{i}}\) (the assumption from the start of the section), and let \(p \geq 0\) be a continuously differentiable function on \((-b, b)\) that is zero outside, for which \(p(s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\) is continuous on \([-b, b]\) (this allows a pressure that grows like \(1/\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\) at the edge), and that has the integral (improper if needed, definition 9.21) \(\int p\,\mathrm{d}s = F'\). The sum of the displacements \(w = w_1 + w_2\) of the surfaces of the bodies into each body, caused by pressure \(p\), is

\[w(x) = -\frac{2}{\pi E^*}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b} p(s)\,\ln|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}s + C_0 , \tag{25.16}\]

where \(C_0\) does not depend on \(x\) (and is undetermined, see lemma 25.25), and

  1. for \(|x| > b\) we have \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\displaystyle\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{p(s)}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s\), an ordinary integral,
  2. for \(|x| < b\) we have \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\,\mathrm{PV}\displaystyle\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{p(s)}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s\), the principal value (glavna vrednost) \(\mathrm{PV}\displaystyle\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b} f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0}\Big(\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{x - \varepsilon} + \int_{\mathrm{x} + \varepsilon}^{b}\Big) f(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
Proof

We must show the form (25.16) of the deflection of the surface and both expressions for the derivative.

  1. Each body is a half-plane by hypothesis. By lemma 25.14 the deflection of the surface under the force \(F\) of a slice at the point \(s\) is the dimple \(-\tfrac{2(1 - \nu_{\mathrm{i}}^2)F}{\pi E_{\mathrm{i}}}\ln|x - s| + \text{const.}\) (checked in SymPy, num-05.py, part A: it satisfies Hooke's law and the relation between strains and displacements, residual zero). Both bodies carry the same force \(F\) at the point \(s\) by Newton's third law.
  2. The sum of the deflections of the two bodies has the factor \(2\big((1 - \nu_1^2)/E_1 + (1 - \nu_2^2)/E_2\big)/\pi = 2/(\pi E^*)\) by definition 25.21. Superposition of the slices and the passage to the limit of the Riemann sums (lemma 25.17 for point forces, the argument is the same) give (25.16).
  3. For \(|x| > b\) we substitute \(s = b\sin\varphi\) (theorem 4.59 on \([-b + \eta, b - \eta]\), then \(\eta \to 0\)). The integral becomes \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} q(\varphi)\ln|x - b\sin\varphi|\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\) with \(q(\varphi) = p(b\sin\varphi)\,b\cos\varphi\), which is continuous on \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\) by hypothesis, because \(b\cos\varphi = \sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\). Since \(|x - b\sin\varphi| \geq |x| - b > 0\), the integrand and its derivative with respect to \(x\), \(q(\varphi)/(x - b\sin\varphi)\), are continuous on the rectangle \([-\pi/2, \pi/2] \times [x_0 - \eta', x_0 + \eta']\) around every point \(x_0\) with \(|x_0| - \eta' > b\), so we may differentiate under the integral (lemma 4.19). The same substitution back gives claim 1.
  4. For \(|x| < b\) the slice reaches the point \(x\), the distance \(|x - s|\) tends to zero and the integrand in claim 2 has a pole at \(s = x\), so the expression is an ordinary integral only as a principal value. That this is really the derivative is a result of BARBER (12.27), (12.28) (PDF p. 190), which we quote without proof. For the case we need, we check it in step 3 of the proof of theorem 25.24 by computing the displacement itself (NumPy, num-05.py, part G).

Source: BARBER §12.3.1 (PDF p. 188, (12.12) to (12.20)) and §12.4 (PDF pp. 189-190, (12.26) to (12.28)): the deflection under a distributed pressure as an integral of the Flamant kernel, logarithmically unbounded far from the contact, and therefore the formulation of contact problems with the derivative (12.27), in which, for a point inside the region, the integral is a Cauchy principal value. Claim 2 is therefore quoted and not proved.

The proof showed two things: the displacement depends on the logarithm of the distance, so it is determined only up to a constant (this will matter at the end of the section), while its derivative is determined and we need it. The first is shown by the right half of figure 25.44: the surface is lowest in the strip, and outside it rises along a straight line with the distance on the logarithmic axis and never levels off, so there is no level from which to measure the deflection. The derivative is an integral with a pole, which we must compute for the half-ellipse, and so let us first say what the pole does.

Let us draw figure 25.45. On the axis \(s\) there is the interval \([-b, b]\), bounded by the vertical lines at \(\pm b\), where the pressure vanishes. The point where we compute the slope we mark with \(x\), in the figure \(x = 0{,}4\,b\). There the integrand has a pole, because the denominator \(x - s\) becomes zero. The left branch lies to the left of the pole, where \(x - s > 0\), so the value grows beyond every bound as \(s\) approaches \(x\). The right branch lies to the right, where \(x - s < 0\), and goes to \(-\infty\). Each branch alone has an infinite area, but the sum need not be infinite. So we cut out the interval \((x - \varepsilon, x + \varepsilon)\) with the half-width \(\varepsilon\) on both sides and take the limit \(\varepsilon \to 0\). With such a symmetric cut-out the infinities cancel each other. With an asymmetric cut-out, for example \((x - \varepsilon, x + 2\varepsilon)\), the value would change by \(\sqrt{b^2 - x^2}\,\ln 2\), which at \(x = 0{,}4\,b\) equals \(0{,}635\,b\), and this is large compared with the true value \(\pi x = 1{,}257\,b\). Without an agreement on the cut-out the integral therefore has no value, and this agreement is the principal value.

Lemma 25.23 Integrals of the half-circle with a pole (integrali polkroga s polom)

Let \(b > 0\). If \(|x| < b\), then

\[\mathrm{PV}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\,\mathrm{d}s = 0 , \qquad \mathrm{PV}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s = \pi x . \tag{25.17}\]

If \(x > b\), both integrals are ordinary and

\[\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}} , \qquad \int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s = \pi\big(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}\big) . \tag{25.18}\]
Proof

We must show four values. The key is that \(1/((x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2})\) has elementary antiderivatives, different for \(x\) inside and outside the interval.

  1. Let \(|x| < b\) and \(c = \sqrt{b^2 - x^2} > 0\). We denote \(N(s) = b^2 - x s + c\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\) and \(H(s) = \dfrac{1}{c}\ln\dfrac{N(s)}{|x - s|}\). The derivative is \(H'(s) = \dfrac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\) on every interval where \(s \neq x\), that is on the left and on the right branch separately (checked in SymPy, num-05.py, part B, residual \(10^{-16}\) at three points).
  2. At the end points \(N(b) = b(b - x)\) and \(|x - b| = b - x\), so \(N(b)/|x - b| = b\). Similarly \(N(-b) = b(b + x)\) and \(|x + b| = b + x\), so \(N(-b)/|x + b| = b\). Hence \(H(b) = H(-b) = \tfrac1c\ln b\) (num-05.py, part B, values \(1{,}0\)).
  3. The integral over both branches without the cut-out is \(\big[H(x - \varepsilon) - H(-b)\big] + \big[H(b) - H(x + \varepsilon)\big]\) by steps 1 and 2 \(= H(x - \varepsilon) - H(x + \varepsilon) = \dfrac{1}{c}\ln\dfrac{N(x - \varepsilon)}{N(x + \varepsilon)}\), since \(|x - s| = \varepsilon\) cancels on both sides. The function \(N\) is continuous at \(s = x\) with the value \(N(x) = 2c^2 > 0\), so the ratio tends to \(1\) and the value to \(0\) as \(\varepsilon \to 0\). For \(b = 1\), \(x = 0{,}4\) the value is \(0{,}1047\), \(0{,}01039\), \(0{,}001039\), \(0{,}0001039\) at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-1}, \dots, 10^{-4}\), so proportional to \(\varepsilon\). This is the first value in (25.17).
  4. For the second value we write \(b^2 - s^2 = (b^2 - x^2) + (x - s)(x + s)\). Therefore the integrand \(\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s} = \dfrac{c^2}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}} + \dfrac{x + s}{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\).
  5. The principal value of the first term is \(0\) by step 3. The second term, with the substitution \(s = b\sin\varphi\) by theorem 4.59 (the Jacobian factor \(b\cos\varphi\), and \(\sqrt{b^2 - s^2} = b\cos\varphi\), which cancels), equals \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(x + b\sin\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = \pi x\), because \(\sin\) is odd. The second term has no pole at \(s = x\), so no cut-out is needed and the integral is ordinary (improper at \(\pm b\), definition 9.21). This is the second value in (25.17).
  6. Let \(x > b\), a point to the right of the vertical line at \(b\), where the integrand has no pole on \([-b, b]\), and \(c' = \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}\). We denote \(K(s) = \dfrac{1}{c'}\arctan\dfrac{b^2 - x s}{c'\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\). The derivative is \(K'(s) = -\dfrac{1}{(x - s)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}\) on \((-b, b)\) (num-05.py, part B). As \(s \to b\) the argument has the value \(b(b - x)/0 \to -\infty\) and as \(s \to -b\) the value \(b(b + x)/0 \to +\infty\), so \(K(b) = -\pi/(2c')\) and \(K(-b) = \pi/(2c')\). The integral is \(K(-b) - K(b) = \pi/c'\) (improper integral, definition 9.21). This is the first value in (25.18).
  7. With the split of step 4, for a point outside the interval the second integral is \(c^2\cdot\pi/c' + \pi x\) with \(c^2 = b^2 - x^2 = -c'^2\), so \(-\pi c' + \pi x\). This is the second value in (25.18).

Source: The computation is mine, the pattern with an antiderivative with a pole is a standard technique (BARBER, §12.5, PDF pp. 191-196, solves the same integral with Fourier series). We check the antiderivatives in SymPy, the numerical principal value agrees to \(10^{-8}\) (num-05.py, part C): \(\pi x\) at \(x/b = 0{,}3, 0{,}6, 0{,}9\) and \(\pi(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2})\) at \(x/b = 1{,}2, 2, 5\).

The proof showed that the pressure \(p_0\sqrt{1 - s^2/b^2}\) gives a straight line in \(x\) in the expression for the slope. The gap is constant in the contact if its derivative is zero, which the theorem achieves by choosing \(p_0\), and zero by choosing \(\delta\).

Let us draw what the theorem will do with the slopes, in figure 25.46. Horizontally is \(x\) in units of \(b\), vertically the slope in units of \(b/R\), and the contact strip is the band from \(-b\) to \(b\). The grey dashed line is the slope \(x/R\) of the gap of the undeformed bodies \(x^2/(2R)\): rigid cylinders would part ever faster with the distance from the middle. The orange curve is the slope \(w'\) of the elastic displacements under the pressure \(p_0\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2}\). In the strip, by lemmas 25.22 and 25.23, it is the line \(-2p_0 x/(E^* b)\), which at \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\) is exactly \(-x/R\), the mirror image of the grey one. Outside the strip, by (25.18), it equals \(-(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2})/R\) and dies away toward zero with the distance, at \(x = 2b\) it is only \(-0{,}27\,b/R\). The blue curve is the sum of both, the slope of the gap \(g'\). In the strip it is zero, because the two lines cancel, also at the edge, where they are \(b/R\) and \(-b/R\). Outside the strip it is \(\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}/R\), at \(x = 2b\) already \(1{,}73\,b/R\), so there the surfaces part. For our numbers \(b/R = 0{,}0168\).

Before the theorem derives this exactly, let us estimate the result roughly, with figure 25.47. This is a second view of the same thing: it does not give the exact factors, but it shows where the root in \(b \propto \sqrt{F'}\) comes from.

Let us draw figure 25.47. It is the equivalent problem from the right half of figure 25.39: the half-plane with modulus \(E^*\) has a flat surface before loading, grey dashed. On it we lay the rigid cylinder of radius \(R\) and press it with the force \(F'\). The surface yields under the cylinder and touches it along the strip of width \(2b\).

  1. Geometry. For the surfaces to touch along the whole strip with half-width \(b\), they must close the gap that at its edge was \(g_0(b) = b^2/(2R)\) (lemma 25.20). By that much they must yield together, from the grey dashed to the orange line.
  2. Strain and pressure. The only length near the strip is \(b\), so we take the displacement \(b^2/(2R)\) to be spread over a depth of the order \(b\). The strain is then of the order \(\dfrac{b^2/(2R)}{b} = \dfrac{b}{2R}\) and the pressure by Hooke's law of the order \(p \approx E^*\,\dfrac{b}{2R}\).
  3. Force. The pressure acts on the width \(2b\), so \(F'\) \(\approx p\cdot 2b = \dfrac{E^* b^2}{R}\) and \(b \approx \sqrt{F'R/E^*}\).

A wider strip therefore counts twice: the pressure acts on a larger width and is itself larger, so the force grows with the square of \(b\) and \(b\) with the root of the force. For our numbers the estimate gives \(b \approx 62\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(p \approx 804\) MPa, the theorem \(70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(907{,}0\) MPa. Both times the estimate misses by the factor \(\sqrt{4/\pi} = 1{,}13\). Step 2 is an assumption and not a proof, since we did not compute the depth over which the strain is spread. That is why we need the theorem, which fixes the factor and also gives the shape of the pressure.

Theorem 25.24 Hertz line contact of cylinders (Hertzov črtni stik valjev)

Let the bodies of definition 25.18 be two convex cylinders with radii \(R_1, R_2\) in plane strain with effective modulus \(E^*\) and radius \(R\) (definition 25.21), pressed together by a force \(F' > 0\) per unit length. Let the gap of the undeformed bodies be \(g_0(x) = x^2/(2R)\) (lemma 25.20) and the gap after loading

\[g(x) = \frac{x^2}{2R} + w(x) - \delta , \tag{25.19}\]

where \(w\) is from lemma 25.22 and \(\delta\) is a number still unknown (the approach, explained below lemma 25.25). Let

\[b = \sqrt{\frac{4F'R}{\pi E^*}} , \qquad p_0 = \frac{2F'}{\pi b} = \frac{E^*\,b}{2R} = \sqrt{\frac{F'E^*}{\pi R}} , \qquad p(x) = \begin{cases} p_0\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2} & |x| \leq b \\ 0 & |x| > b . \end{cases} \tag{25.20}\]

Then:

  1. The functions \(p\) and \(g\) satisfy the contact conditions of definition 25.19 with \(\Omega = [-b, b]\) for a suitable value of \(\delta\).
  2. Outside the contact \(g(x) = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\,G(|x|/b)\) with \(G(t) = \tfrac12\big(t\sqrt{t^2 - 1} - \ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\big)\), which is positive for \(t > 1\), and \(g\) is continuous at \(x = \pm b\).
  3. For \(\kappa \neq 0\) the family \(p_\kappa(x) = p_0\big(\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2} + \kappa/\sqrt{1 - x^2/b^2}\big)\) on \(|x| < b\) (with the same \(b\) and \(p_0\), zero outside, the force is then \((1 + 2\kappa)\) times larger) satisfies the slope equation \(g'(x) = 0\) on \((-b, b)\) but not the contact conditions: for \(\kappa > 0\) we have \(g(x) = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\big(G(t) - \kappa\ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\big) < 0\) for \(t > 1\) close to \(1\), for \(\kappa < 0\) we have \(p_\kappa(x) < 0\) for \(|x| < b\) with \(1 - x^2/b^2 < -\kappa\).
Idea

We show that the inserted pressure makes the gap constant in the contact strip, then we compute the gap outside with the same lemma. The width \(b\) is determined by equating the force and the slope. The edge separates the solution from the remaining ones through the requirement that the gap does not penetrate and the pressure does not pull.

Proof
  1. Slope. For \(|x| < b\) lemma 25.22 gives \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\,\mathrm{PV}\!\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{p(s)}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s = -\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\,\mathrm{PV}\!\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\dfrac{\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}}{x - s}\,\mathrm{d}s\), because \(p(s) = (p_0/b)\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\). By lemma 25.23 this is \(-\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\,\pi x = -\dfrac{2p_0\,x}{E^* b}\), the orange line in the strip.
  2. Gap in the strip. The derivative of (25.19) is \(g'(x) = x/R + w'(x) = x\big(1/R - 2p_0/(E^* b)\big)\). This is zero for every \(|x| < b\) exactly when \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\) (then the grey and the orange line cancel), which is the second equality in (25.20). The function \(g\) is constant on \([-b, b]\), because it is continuous and has zero derivative. With a suitable choice of \(\delta\) (the constant \(C_0\) in (25.16) and \(\delta\) appear only in the sum \(C_0 - \delta\)) this constant is zero, \(g = 0\) on \(\Omega = [-b, b]\).
  3. Check. We obtained the derivative \(w'\) in step 1 from claim 2 of lemma 25.22, which is stated without proof. So we check the integral of the displacement itself under the strip: \(J(x) = \int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\ln|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}s\) must by step 1 have the difference \(J(x) - J(0) = \pi x^2/2\). For \(b = 1\) we get (NumPy) \(0{,}14137\), \(0{,}56549\), \(1{,}27235\) at \(x = 0{,}3, 0{,}6, 0{,}9\), and \(\pi x^2/2\) is equal to five places (num-05.py, part G). By (25.16) we have therefore \(w(x) - w(0) = -\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\cdot\dfrac{\pi x^2}{2} = -\dfrac{p_0\,x^2}{E^* b}\), which is \(-x^2/(2R)\) for \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\).
  4. Force. The force is the area under the half-ellipse. With \(s = b t\) we have \(\int p\,\mathrm{d}s = p_0 b\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1 - t^2}\,\mathrm{d}t = p_0 b\,\pi/2\) (half the area of a circle, numerically also \(1{,}5707963\)). Equating with \(F'\) gives \(p_0 = 2F'/(\pi b)\). By step 2 \(p_0 = E^* b/(2R)\), so \(E^* b/(2R) = 2F'/(\pi b)\) and \(b^2 = 4F'R/(\pi E^*)\). The remaining expression \(p_0 = \sqrt{F'E^*/(\pi R)}\) follows by inserting \(b\) in \(E^*b/(2R)\).
  5. Outside the strip. For \(x > b\), by lemma 25.22, claim 1, and the second value in (25.18), \(w'(x) = -\dfrac{2p_0}{\pi E^* b}\,\pi\big(x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}\big) = -\dfrac{x - \sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}{R}\), with the same \(p_0 = E^*b/(2R)\). Therefore \(g'(x) = \dfrac{x}{R} + w'(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}{R}\), the blue curve outside the strip.
  6. Since \(w\) is continuous (an integral with an integrable kernel) and \(g(b) = 0\) from step 2, we have \(g(x) = \int_{\mathrm{b}}^x\dfrac{\sqrt{s^2 - b^2}}{R}\,\mathrm{d}s = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\int_1^t\sqrt{\tau^2 - 1}\,\mathrm{d}\tau\) with \(s = b\tau\). The derivative \(G'(t) = \tfrac12\big(\sqrt{t^2 - 1} + t^2/\sqrt{t^2 - 1} - 1/\sqrt{t^2 - 1}\big) = \sqrt{t^2 - 1}\), because \(\dfrac{1 + t/\sqrt{t^2 - 1}}{t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{t^2 - 1}}\), and \(G(1) = 0\). So \(g = (b^2/R)\,G(t)\). Since \(G' > 0\) for \(t > 1\), \(G > 0\) there. For \(x < -b\) the same by evenness. This is claim 2, the orange curve outside the strip.
  7. Contact conditions. Condition 1 (gap) is satisfied in the strip (\(g = 0\)) and outside (\(g > 0\)). Condition 2 (\(p \geq 0\)) holds because the root is nonnegative. Condition 3 is satisfied because \(p = 0\) where \(g > 0\), and \(g = 0\) where \(p > 0\). Condition 4 is step 4. This is claim 1.
  8. The family (figure 25.49, the orange and the grey curve). The term \(\kappa p_0/\sqrt{1 - s^2/b^2} = \kappa p_0 b/\sqrt{b^2 - s^2}\) gives zero in the slope by the first value in (25.17), so the same \(b, p_0\) keep \(g' = 0\) on \((-b, b)\). Outside, by the first value in (25.18), it adds \(-\dfrac{2\kappa p_0 b}{E^*}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}} = -\dfrac{\kappa b^2}{R\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}\) to \(w'\). Therefore \(g'(x) = \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}{R} - \dfrac{\kappa b^2}{R\sqrt{x^2 - b^2}}\), and with \(x = b t\) we get \(g = \dfrac{b^2}{R}\big(G(t) - \kappa\ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\big)\) by \(\int_1^t\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\tau^2 - 1}}\,\mathrm{d}\tau = \ln(t + \sqrt{t^2 - 1})\). As \(t \to 1^+\) we have \(G = O\big((t - 1)^{3/2}\big)\), while the logarithm is \(\sim\sqrt{2(t - 1)}\), so for \(\kappa > 0\) the value of \(g\) near the edge is negative. For \(\kappa < 0\) and \(|x| < b\) we write \(v = 1 - x^2/b^2 > 0\). Then \(p_\kappa(x) = p_0\big(\sqrt{v} + \kappa/\sqrt{v}\big) = p_0(v + \kappa)/\sqrt{v} < 0\) exactly when \(v < -\kappa\).

Source: BARBER §12.5.3 (PDF pp. 195-196): the same \(p(x) = -2F\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}/(\pi a^2)\) (12.60) with the edge from the requirement that the pressure is not singular at \(x = \pm a\) (12.56) (BARBER computes with a pressure of negative sign and a rigid cylinder, and calls the half-width \(a\)). HK (6.50), (6.51) (PDF p. 132): \(\sigma = \frac{2Q}{\pi l b}\big[1 - (y/b)^2\big]^{1/2}\) and \(b\) in the same form (after converting the symbols, \(4Q/(\pi l\,\Sigma\rho)\cdot 1/E^*\)). The proof of claim 3 and of the outside gap is mine. The fact that \(p_\kappa\) covers all solutions of the slope equation is classical (BARBER §12.5, PDF pp. 191-193, Fourier series, and Muskhelishvili, whom BARBER cites in a footnote on p. 192) and we do not prove it, so we do not claim uniqueness of the contact problem.

The meaning of the theorem is easiest to see in a figure.

Let us draw figure 25.48. At the top there is the axis \(x\) and an axis for the pressure. On the contact strip from \(-b\) to \(b\) the pressure is half an ellipse with the largest value \(p_0\) in the middle and zero at the edges. Below it is the second axis, on which we measure the gap downwards. The dashed parabola is the gap of the undeformed bodies \(x^2/(2R)\), which the cylinders would have if they were rigid. The orange curve is the gap under load: in the strip it is zero, outside it is positive, at the edge it grows with the power \(3/2\), as \(G(t) \sim (t - 1)^{3/2}\) shows, and it is everywhere smaller than the parabola. This is the difference between elastic and rigid bodies: under the pressure the bodies are compressed and the gap next to the strip closes.

Let us test the theorem on numbers. For a roller \(R_1 = 5\) mm on a raceway \(R_2 = 25\) mm of the book's steel, \(E^* = 107{,}692\) GPa and \(R = 4{,}1667\) mm. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm the theorem gives the half-width \(b = 70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\) and the largest pressure \(p_0 = 907{,}0\) MPa, at \(F' = 400\) N/mm \(b = 140{,}37\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(p_0 = 1814{,}1\) MPa (num-05.py, part D). Four times the force gives twice the width and twice the pressure, because \(b\) and \(p_0\) grow as \(\sqrt{F'}\). So the contact is not linear: twice the force does not give twice the pressure. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm we have \(b^2/R = 1{,}182\ \mu\text{m}\). The gap at \(t = 2\), that is \(140\ \mu\text{m}\) from the centre, is \(G(2)\,b^2/R = 1{,}0736\cdot 1{,}182 = 1{,}269\ \mu\text{m}\), while the undeformed gap is \(x^2/(2R) = 2{,}365\ \mu\text{m}\). The two elastic displacements therefore reduce the gap by a little less than half.

Does HK have the same result? His equation (6.51) has the same form \(b = [4Q/(\pi l\,\Sigma\rho)\cdot(\ldots)]^{1/2}\), and for steel his (6.52) gives \(b = 3{,}35\cdot 10^{-3}\sqrt{Q/(l\,\Sigma\rho)}\) (mm, N, 1/mm). For our numbers (\(Q/l = 100\) N/mm, \(\Sigma\rho = 0{,}24\) mm\(^{-1}\)) this is \(68{,}4\ \mu\text{m}\), while we got \(70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\). The difference of \(2{,}6\ \%\) is a difference of moduli: from (6.51) and (6.52) at \(\nu = 0{,}3\) it follows that the constant corresponds to \(E = 2{,}065\cdot 10^5\) MPa, while we took \(E = 196\) GPa. The ratio of the roots \(\sqrt{2{,}065/1{,}96} = 1{,}026\) gives \(68{,}4\cdot 1{,}026 = 70{,}2\ \mu\text{m}\), which agrees.

Our two numbers are a measure for the question whether the model still holds. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm we have \(p_0/E^* = 0{,}0084\), at \(400\) N/mm \(0{,}0168\), which is the order of magnitude of the strain under the strip. Section 25.4 took displacement gradients below \(10^{-3}\) for the linear theory, because the theory drops their squares. Here we are above that bound, but the dropped terms are of order \(p_0/E^*\) relative to those kept, so about \(0{,}8\ \%\) at \(100\) N/mm and \(1{,}7\ \%\) at \(400\) N/mm. This limits the model, it does not refute it. Whether the steel stays linearly elastic is a separate question, the yield limit. The steel of the book has the yield stress (definition 2.7) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa (chapter 3), while our \(p_0 = 907\) MPa is four times larger. For the ball, section 25.6 (lemma 25.29) shows that the steel of the book starts to yield already at \(p_0 = 1{,}613\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 355\) MPa. The stresses below the surface of a line contact we do not compute here (HK §6.4, PDF pp. 133-138), so we do not give the yield limit for the cylinders and do not claim that the steel of the book stays elastic at our forces. The numbers of this section hold for a steel with \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) that does not yet yield at such a pressure.

The theorem chose one shape of the pressure, the half-ellipse. Would another shape also give zero gap in the strip? Claim 3 says there is a whole family of them, but all except one violate the contact conditions at the edge. This is the near miss of the theorem: a solution of the slope equation is not yet a solution of the contact problem.

Let us draw figure 25.49. On the left is the pressure from \(t = 0{,}6\) to the edge, which is the vertical dashed line at \(b\). The blue curve is \(\kappa = 0\) and falls to zero at \(b\), as in the theorem. The orange one has \(\kappa = 0{,}3\): at the edge it does not fall to zero but grows beyond every bound, and at \(0{,}99\,b\) it is \(2{,}27\,p_0\), at \(0{,}999\,b\) it is \(6{,}75\,p_0\). The grey one has \(\kappa = -0{,}3\) and goes to \(-\infty\) at the edge: at \(0{,}99\,b\) it is \(-1{,}99\,p_0\) and at \(0{,}999\,b\) it is \(-6{,}67\,p_0\), so the contact pulls, which condition 2 forbids. On the right is the gap outside the strip, drawn above the second axis, which starts at the edge of the strip \(t = 1\). For \(\kappa = 0\) (blue) it is positive. For \(\kappa = 0{,}3\) (orange) the gap near the edge is negative, at least \(-0{,}1065\,b^2/R = -126\) nm at \(t = 1{,}14\), and positive only from \(t = 1{,}41\): the bodies would penetrate each other, which condition 1 forbids. For \(\kappa = -0{,}3\) (grey) the gap is positive, but this is reached with a pressure that pulls. Conditions 1 and 2 together therefore leave only \(\kappa = 0\), and this is what BARBER says in words, that the pressure at the edge is not singular: \(\kappa \neq 0\) has a singular pressure at the edge.

Uniqueness of the contact problem as a whole is not proved by this: we showed that among the family \(p_\kappa\) only the theorem satisfies the contact conditions. That the family covers all solutions of the slope equation is stated by BARBER (see the source of the theorem), we do not prove it. Uniqueness of the contact problem is unproved also in chapter 11 (section 11.7.6), and here too we state it as open.

The proof of the theorem gave the pressure, the width and the gap, but not the approach \(\delta\) of the bodies. This is not a defect of the proof, it is a property of the plane problem.

Lemma 25.25 The approach of a line contact is not defined (približevanje pri črtnem stiku ni določeno)

Let \(p\) be from theorem 25.24 and \(L > b\). Let \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(x)\) be the deflection from lemma 25.22 with the choice \(C_0 = \dfrac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\ln L\), that is \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(x) = \dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}p(s)\,\ln\dfrac{L}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}s\). This is the deflection relative to the point at the distance \(L\) from the middle of the contact, which for \(L \gg b\) approximately stays at rest, since there \(\ln\big(L/|L - s|\big) \approx s/L\) and \(\int p\,s\,\mathrm{d}s = 0\) by the evenness of \(p\). Then the deflection under the middle of the strip is

\[w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = \frac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\Big(\ln\frac{2L}{b} + \frac12\Big) , \tag{25.21}\]

and as \(L \to \infty\) it grows beyond every bound, like \(\ln L\). Therefore the distance between the bodies that the contact requires is not determined by \(F'\), \(E^*\) and \(R\) alone, but also by \(L\).

Proof

We must show the value of the integral \(\int p\,\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s\) over the slices of pressure and think about \(L\).

  1. By definition the deflection under the middle \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = \dfrac{2}{\pi E^*}\Big(F'\ln L - \int_{-\mathrm{b}}^{b}p(s)\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s\Big)\), because \(\int p = F'\).
  2. With \(s = b u\) on the strip and \(p = p_0\sqrt{1 - u^2}\) we have \(\int p\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s = p_0 b\Big(\ln b\int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1 - u^2}\,\mathrm{d}u + \int_{-1}^{1}\sqrt{1 - u^2}\ln|u|\,\mathrm{d}u\Big)\). The first integral is \(\pi/2\). The second is \(\tfrac{\pi}{2}\big(\ln\tfrac12 - \tfrac12\big)\) (numerically \(-1{,}8741912\) against \(-1{,}8741912\), num-05.py, part G). Since \(p_0 b\,\pi/2 = F'\), we get \(\int p\ln|s|\,\mathrm{d}s = F'\big(\ln\tfrac{b}{2} - \tfrac12\big)\).
  3. We insert into step 1, for the deflection under the middle we get \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = \dfrac{2F'}{\pi E^*}\big(\ln L - \ln\tfrac b2 + \tfrac12\big)\), which is (25.21).

Source: The computation is mine. BARBER §12.4 (PDF p. 190): the deflection is logarithmically unbounded, and the rigid-body displacement of the loaded region relative to distant parts of the body cannot be found without taking the finite size of the body into account.

Let us look at this on numbers and on the right half of figure 25.44. At \(F' = 100\) N/mm we have \(2F'/(\pi E^*) = 0{,}5911\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(b = 70{,}19\ \mu\text{m}\). For \(L_1 = 0{,}1\) m we get \(w_{\mathrm{L}}(0) = 4{,}998\ \mu\text{m}\), for \(L_2 = 1\) m \(6{,}359\ \mu\text{m}\). In the figure these are the blue distances from the bottom of the dimple to the level at which the surface lies at \(L_1\) and at \(L_2\). The same bodies therefore "approach" by \(5{,}0\) or by \(6{,}4\ \mu\text{m}\), depending on where on the bodies we measure the distance, and the difference of \(1{,}361\ \mu\text{m}\) is larger than \(b^2/R = 1{,}182\ \mu\text{m}\), which is the scale of everything that happens in the strip (figure 25.48). For the ball (section 25.6) this does not happen, because the deflection \(1/r\) of section 25.4 falls with distance and distant points stay at rest. A logarithm in the plane grows and does not allow anything to stay at rest. For a real cylinder the scale of the body is the length \(l\) of the cylinder, and indeed the Lundberg and Sjövall deflection of a line contact (HK (6.53), PDF pp. 132-133) has in front of the logarithm a factor proportional to \(Q/l\) and in the logarithm the length of the cylinder squared, \(\ln\big(\pi E l^2/(Q\cdots)\big)\). We do not copy the symbols that HK does not explain on this page, and we do not claim agreement with the lemma. The fact is that for roller bearings HK uses the force-approach law \(Q \propto \delta^{n}\) with \(n = 10/9\), not \(3/2\) as for balls (HK (7.3), PDF pp. 155-156). This law is empirical: it comes from the equation \(\delta \propto Q^{0{,}9}/l^{0{,}8}\) (HK (6.54), PDF p. 133), which Palmgren obtained from tests of rollers slightly convex along their length (crowned rollers) loaded against raceways, and \(1/0{,}9 = 10/9\). Whether this is because of what was described, HK does not say. We do not derive the law with \(10/9\) in the book, we quote it as HK.

For a line contact we therefore have the pressure, the width of the strip (\(b \propto \sqrt{F'}\)) and the gap, but the model does not give the approach. Section 25.6 does the same for a sphere, and there the approach exists, because the deflection falls with distance.

Notation and what is left out. Notation of the section: \(b\) is the half-width of the contact, not the radius of a tube from chapter 11. The letter \(\delta\) is the approach of the bodies, not a virtual increment. The letter \(p\) is the pressure in N/m\(^2\), and the force per unit length of the axis is \(F'\) in N/m. Outside the chapter: the ends of cylinders and the crowning of rollers that prevents edge loading (HK, PDF pp. 145-148) are not part of this section, and neither is friction in the contact (HK §6.5, PDF pp. 139-142).

25.6 Hertz contact of a sphere: point contact and elliptical contact

A ball of diameter \(12{,}7\) mm lies on a steel plate and the shaft presses it with a force of \(1000\) N. In section 25.4 we saw that a point force on a half-space gives an infinite deflection and an infinite pressure, so contact at a single point is a model that fails. A real ball and a real plate squeeze together over a small circle. How large is this circle, by how much do the ball and plate approach each other, and what is the pressure in it? We need all three numbers, because in the next sections we build the stiffness of a bearing from them. Since all contacts in a ball bearing are point contacts, we treat them first: a sphere against a plane or another sphere, then a sphere in the groove of a raceway, which is elliptical.

Let us draw figure 25.50, first the left panel. The flat body is the support: its surface is a horizontal line and the steel is below it. On it stands the sphere of radius \(R\) and centre \(C\), which touches the support at the point \(O\). At a distance \(r\) from \(O\) we measure horizontally, which the dimension \(r\) shows. The sphere moves away from the support with distance, the gap \(g_0(r)\) between them is shaded in the figure. We compute it from the right triangle with sides \(R - g_0\) and \(r\) and hypotenuse \(R\): \((R - g_0)^2 + r^2 = R^2\), hence \(g_0 = R - \sqrt{R^2 - r^2}\). Since \(r\) in the contact is much smaller than \(R\), \(\sqrt{R^2 - r^2} \approx R - r^2/(2R)\) and

\[g_0(r) \approx \frac{r^2}{2R} . \tag{25.22}\]

This parabola is accurate enough for the contact. At a force of \(1000\) N, when \(a = 353{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\) (result below), the true gap at the edge of the contact is \(9{,}8545\ \mu\text{m}\) and the parabola gives \(9{,}8468\ \mu\text{m}\), which is \(0{,}078\ \%\) less (NumPy, num-06.py). Why we need this number at all: the contact condition requires the gap to be exactly zero, and we must therefore know it precisely, not only roughly.

What happens when we press? The right panel shows the support after loading: under the pressure it yields and in the circle it increases its distance from the far plane. The sphere is also flattened at the bottom. In the contact circle of radius \(a\) the two surfaces are the same curve, outside it the gap opens again. The force \(F\) acts along the axis and ends at the sphere, because it pushes it. The centre of the sphere has moved from its initial position by the approach \(h\) (približevanje), which the dimension \(h\) shows. We measure it against points far from the contact, because the deflection of a half-space decays as \(1/r\) (corollary 25.16), so for \(r \gg a\) there is no displacement left.

The model has several simplifications. We state each at the part of figure 25.50 where it enters: why we may take it, when it fails and what it does to the result.

  1. The bodies are homogeneous, isotropic and linearly elastic (theorem 3.19). We need this so that the flat body may yield by the half-space solution and the deflections add. It holds while the strains are small and the steel does not yield. What it costs we compute below: at \(1000\) N the strains under the contact are of the order \(0{,}019\), and mild steel would yield already at \(0{,}80\) N.
  2. Near the contact we replace each body by the half-space of section 25.4. We may, because the contact circle is much smaller than the sphere: in our example \(a/R = 0{,}056\) (the figure is exaggerated), and the error of the gap is therefore only \(0{,}078\ \%\). It fails for a thin plate and for a contact that reaches the edge of a body. Hertz required the same, that the contact circle is small against the radii of curvature (HK, PDF p. 125). This is one of the three properties of a nonconformal contact (nekonformni stik) from definition 25.18, the other two (contact at a point, smooth surfaces) hold for a sphere.
  3. The force \(F\) is perpendicular to the surface and there is no friction on the contact surface, so the surfaces act on each other by pressure only. Why may we leave friction out? Two bodies of the same material are, as half-spaces under the same pressure, mirror images of each other, so two points that touch also move equally along the surface. They do not slide on each other and friction has nothing to hold back, the result is the same as with friction. With different materials the surfaces move differently along the surface, friction then changes the pressure and the Hertz solution is an approximation (our sources do not give the size of this error). It also fails when the force has a component along the surface.
  4. The contact conditions are those of definition 25.19: the gap is nonnegative, the pressure is nonnegative, and at every point at least one of them is zero.

With two bodies we have two ingredients, shown in figure 25.51. The first is the gap: if the bodies have radii \(R_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\), the gap is the sum of the gaps, \(g_0 = r^2/(2R_{\mathrm{A}}) + r^2/(2R_{\mathrm{B}}) = r^2/(2R)\) with the radius \(R\) given by

\[\frac1R = \frac1{R_{\mathrm{A}}} + \frac1{R_{\mathrm{B}}} . \tag{25.23}\]

A plane is \(R_{\mathrm{B}} \to \infty\). The second is the modulus. Both bodies receive the same pressure \(p\) (by Newton's third law the forces of opposite directions are equal), each yields as a half-space, and by lemma 25.17 the deflections \(w_{\mathrm{A}}\) and \(w_{\mathrm{B}}\) add. For each body \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \dfrac{1 - \nu_{\mathrm{i}}^2}{\pi E_{\mathrm{i}}}\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A\), so the total indentation is

\[u(x) = w_{\mathrm{A}} + w_{\mathrm{B}} = \frac{1}{\pi E^*}\int_{\mathrm{A}} \frac{p(s)}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}A(s) , \qquad \frac1{E^*} = \frac{1 - \nu_{\mathrm{A}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{A}}} + \frac{1 - \nu_{\mathrm{B}}^2}{E_{\mathrm{B}}} . \tag{25.24}\]

This is the effective modulus (učinkoviti modul) \(E^*\) as BOWER writes it (PDF p. 331) and as section 25.5 has it for cylinders, here expressed with two fractions (its form \(E_{\mathrm{A}} E_{\mathrm{B}}/((1 - \nu_{\mathrm{A}}^2)E_{\mathrm{B}} + (1 - \nu_{\mathrm{B}}^2)E_{\mathrm{A}})\) is the same). For two equal steel bodies (\(E = 196\) GPa, \(\nu = 0{,}3\)) \(E^* = E/(2(1 - \nu^2)) = 107{,}692\) GPa, and for a sphere \(D = 12{,}7\) mm on a plane \(R = 6{,}35\) mm, for two such spheres \(R = 3{,}175\) mm. We write the approach \(h\) (BOWER), in the following sections \(\delta\), which is the same quantity. The word Hertz comes from Heinrich Hertz, of whom the history a little below tells.

Before we write the solution, we ask what kind of pressure we expect at all. The gap \(g_0\) is a parabola, so in the contact the indentation \(u\) must have the form \(h - r^2/(2R)\) for the gap to be zero. With the uniform pressure that we computed in section 25.4.1 this does not happen: the deflection is largest at the centre and at the edge it is \(2/\pi\) of the central one. We therefore look for a pressure that gives a parabolic deflection. Hertz took a pressure of the shape of a semi-ellipsoid. Why does exactly a semi-ellipsoid give a parabola? The reason is the Pythagorean theorem, and we see it on a chord.

In panel (a) of figure 25.52 we look at the contact from above. The circle of radius \(a\) with centre \(O\) is the region on which the pressure acts. We choose the point \(x\) at which we want the deflection, at distance \(r\) from the centre. The deflection at \(x\) is the sum of the contributions of all points of the circle, each the pressure divided by the distance to \(x\) (equation (25.24)). We sum them direction by direction: through \(x\) we draw a chord at angle \(\varphi\) and first sum along it. In polar coordinates around \(x\) the distance in the denominator cancels against the Jacobian \(\rho\), so a chord contributes simply the area under the pressure along it. From the centre we drop a perpendicular of length \(d = r\sin\varphi\) onto the chord, with foot \(M\). A point of the chord at distance \(t\) from \(M\) is, by the Pythagorean theorem, at distance \(\sqrt{d^2 + t^2}\) from the centre, so the pressure there is

\[p = p_0\sqrt{1 - \frac{d^2 + t^2}{a^2}} = \frac{p_0}{a}\sqrt{c^2 - t^2} , \qquad c = \sqrt{a^2 - d^2} .\]

The length \(c\) is half the chord, which the same theorem says in the triangle with sides \(d\), \(c\) and \(a\). The graph of \(\sqrt{c^2 - t^2}\) is a half-circle of radius \(c\), so the pressure along the chord is the half-ellipse of panel (c): over the chord with half length \(c\) it is \(p_0c/a\) high. Its area is half the area of an ellipse,

\[\frac{\pi}{2}\,c\cdot\frac{p_0c}{a} = \frac{\pi p_0}{2a}\,\big(a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi\big) .\]

This is the whole reason. The area under the pressure on a chord is proportional to the square of half the chord, and by the Pythagorean theorem that square is \(a^2\) minus the square of the distance \(d\). Panel (a) of figure 25.53 has the angle \(\varphi\) horizontally and the square \(c^2\) vertically. The blue curve is \(c^2 = a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi\) for \(\varphi\) from \(0\) to \(\pi\), which is half a revolution, since at \(\varphi + \pi\) the chord lies on itself again. The curve lies below the rectangle of height \(a^2\) by the hump \(r^2\sin^2\varphi\). The hump lies in the strip of height \(r^2\) and fills exactly half of it: the rest of the strip below the curve has height \(r^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi = r^2\cos^2\varphi\), which is the same hump shifted by \(\pi/2\). So \(\sin^2\varphi\) averages to \(\tfrac12\) and the area under the curve is \(\pi(a^2 - r^2/2)\). Panel (c) draws this area, divided by \(\pi\), against \(r\): it is the parabola \(a^2 - r^2/2\), and its point at \(r = 0{,}65\,a\) is the area from panel (a). Under a uniform pressure a chord would contribute its length \(2c\), not the square, and there would be no parabola. The lemma says this exactly.

Lemma 25.26 Deflection under a semi-ellipsoidal pressure (poves pod polelipsoidnim tlakom)

Let \(A_{\mathrm{a}}\) be a disc of radius \(a\) centred at \(O\) on the surface of a half-space, let \(p_0 > 0\) and let the pressure be \(p(s) = p_0\sqrt{1 - |s|^2/a^2}\) for \(|s| \leq a\) and zero outside. Let \(u(x) = \dfrac{1}{\pi E^*}\int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{a}} \dfrac{p(s)}{|x - s|}\,\mathrm{d}A(s)\) (equation (25.24)) and \(r = |x|\). Then:

  1. on the disc, \(F = \int_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{a}} p\,\mathrm{d}A = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\,p_0\,a^2\),
  2. at the centre, \(u(0) = \dfrac{\pi\,p_0\,a}{2E^*}\),
  3. for \(r \leq a\), \(u(r) = \dfrac{\pi\,p_0}{4E^*a}\,(2a^2 - r^2)\) (proved chord by chord, checked numerically),
  4. for \(r > a\), \(u(r) = \dfrac{p_0}{2E^*a}\Big((2a^2 - r^2)\arcsin\dfrac ar + a\sqrt{r^2 - a^2}\Big)\).
Proof

We prove all four claims. We use polar coordinates (theorem 4.59, \(J = \rho\)), in steps 1 and 2 around the centre, in step 3 around a point \(x\) in the disc (panel (a) of figure 25.52), in steps 4 and 5 around a point \(x\) outside the disc (panel (b)).

  1. By the change of variables theorem \(F = p_0\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a \sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\;s\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}\theta\). With \(t = 1 - s^2/a^2\), \(\int_0^a s\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,\mathrm{d}s = \dfrac{a^2}{2}\int_0^1\sqrt t\,\mathrm{d}t = \dfrac{a^2}{3}\). So \(F = 2\pi p_0 a^2/3\). This is the volume under the semi-ellipsoid of pressure, claim 1.
  2. At the centre (\(r = 0\), every chord is a diameter) \(|x - s| = s\) and the factor \(s\) from the Jacobian cancels \(1/s\). Hence \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = p_0\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}\theta = 2\pi p_0\cdot\dfrac{\pi a}{4}\), because \(\int_0^a\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,\mathrm{d}s\) is the area of a quarter of a circle of radius \(a\) divided by \(a\), which is \(\pi a/4\) (multiplied by \(p_0\) it is half of the half-ellipse over a diameter, where \(c = a\)). Dividing by \(\pi E^*\) gives claim 2.
  3. Claim 3: the point \(x\) is in the disc, \(r \leq a\). In polar coordinates around \(x\), \(J = \rho\) and \(\rho\) cancels \(1/|x - s| = 1/\rho\), so \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\). The rays in the directions \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi + \pi\) together make a chord, so this is an integral over chords for \(\varphi\) from \(0\) to \(\pi\). On a chord \(p = (p_0/a)\sqrt{c^2 - t^2}\) with \(c^2 = a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi\) (the Pythagorean theorem with \(d\) and \(c\)), and the integral over \(t\) from \(-c\) to \(c\) is the area of the half-ellipse, \(\dfrac{\pi p_0}{2a}(a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi)\). Since \(\int_0^\pi\sin^2\varphi\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = \pi/2\) (the hump fills half of the strip), \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = \dfrac{\pi p_0}{2a}\Big(\pi a^2 - \dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}\Big) = \dfrac{\pi^2p_0}{4a}(2a^2 - r^2)\). Dividing by \(\pi E^*\) gives claim 3, which is a parabola in \(r\). At \(r = 0\) it is claim 2.
  4. Claim 4: the point \(x\) is outside the disc at distance \(r > a\) from the centre. A ray from \(x\) at angle \(\varphi\) from the axis through the centre meets the disc only when the perpendicular \(d = r\sin\varphi\) is shorter than \(a\), that is for \(|\sin\varphi| \leq a/r\) (between the tangents), at distances \(\rho_{1,2} = r\cos\varphi \mp \sqrt{a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi}\). A point \(s = x + \rho\,\vek e\) on the ray (with \(\vek e\) the unit vector of the ray) has \(|s|^2 - a^2 = (\rho - \rho_1)(\rho - \rho_2)\), so \(p = (p_0/a)\sqrt{(\rho_2 - \rho)(\rho - \rho_1)}\). In polar coordinates around \(x\), \(J = \rho\) and \(\rho\) cancels \(1/|x - s|\), so \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = \int\!\int p\,\mathrm{d}\rho\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\). The inner integral \(\int_{\rho_1}^{\rho_2}(p_0/a)\sqrt{(\rho_2 - \rho)(\rho - \rho_1)}\,\mathrm{d}\rho\) is the area of a half-disc of radius \((\rho_2 - \rho_1)/2\) multiplied by \(p_0/a\), that is \(\dfrac{p_0}{a}\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{8}(\rho_2 - \rho_1)^2 = \dfrac{\pi p_0}{2a}(a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi)\), because \(\rho_2 - \rho_1 = 2\sqrt{a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi}\).
  5. Continuation of claim 4. We integrate over \(\varphi\) between the tangents, from \(-\varphi_0\) to \(\varphi_0\) with \(\sin\varphi_0 = a/r\). In panel (b) of figure 25.53 the integrand is the curve, which drops to zero at \(\pm\varphi_0\), where the ray only touches the disc, and the integral is the rectangle \(2a^2\varphi_0\) less the hump \(r^2\sin^2\varphi\): \(\int_{-\varphi_0}^{\varphi_0}(a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}\varphi = (2a^2 - r^2)\,\varphi_0 + r^2\sin\varphi_0\cos\varphi_0 = (2a^2 - r^2)\,\varphi_0 + a\sqrt{r^2 - a^2}\), because \(\sin^2\varphi = \tfrac12(1 - \cos 2\varphi)\). Multiplying by \(\pi p_0/(2a)\) and dividing by \(\pi E^*\) is claim 4. At \(r = a\) the formula gives \(\pi p_0 a/(4E^*)\), which is half the value at the centre and equals what claim 3 gives at \(r = a\).

Source: Claims 1 and 2 are a calculation in SymPy (num-06.py B). Claim 4 is our calculation (num-06.py G). Claim 3 agrees with BOWER (PDF p. 331, the equations for \(a\), \(h\), \(p_0\) that follow from it and that we check below) and HK (PDF pp. 125-129), a proof for points inside the circle is not given there. The proof chord by chord (step 3) is our calculation, checked in SymPy (chk-06-teach.py) and numerically with the one-dimensional integral over \(\varphi\): the ratio \(u(r)\big/\big(\tfrac{\pi p_0}{4E^*a}(2a^2 - r^2)\big)\) equals \(1\) to ten digits at \(r/a = 0\), \(0{,}3\), \(0{,}6\), \(0{,}9\), \(0{,}99\) (num-06.py F).

The proof has four parts, which we read on the figure. The right panel of figure 25.54 has \(r/a\) on the horizontal axis and the indentation and the gap, divided by \(h = u(0)\), on the vertical one. The blue curve is the deflection \(u/h\). Inside the contact it is a parabola from \(1\) to \(\tfrac12\) by claim 3, outside it decays as by claim 4. At \(r = a\) the two branches meet at the same point \(\tfrac12\), which is a check of both claims. For large \(r\) claim 4 goes to \(\dfrac{u}{h} \to \dfrac{4a}{3\pi r}\), so \(u \to \dfrac{F}{\pi E^* r}\) with \(F\) from claim 1: the same \(1/r\) as in corollary 25.16. So a pressure on a circle acts from afar as a point force, which we also saw for uniform pressure in section 25.4.1 with another number.

Uniform pressure would not do. We check that the semi-ellipsoid is not just one of the possibilities. For uniform pressure \(q\) on the same circle, in polar coordinates around a point \(x\) inside the circle, \(\int p/|x - s|\,\mathrm{d}A = q\int_0^{2\pi}\ell(\varphi)\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\), where \(\ell(\varphi) = \sqrt{a^2 - r^2\sin^2\varphi} - r\cos\varphi\) is the distance from \(x\) to the edge of the circle in the direction \(\varphi\). The term \(-r\cos\varphi\) gives zero over a full turn, so the integral equals \(4q\,a\,E(r/a)\) with the complete elliptic integral of the second kind \(E(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - k^2\sin^2\varphi)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}\varphi\) (this \(E\) is not a modulus). So \(u(a)/u(0) = 2/\pi = 0{,}6366\) (this is the ratio of section 25.4.1, the blackwhite dot in the right panel of figure 25.54), while for the semi-ellipsoid it is \(\tfrac12\) (the blue dot). Let the radius \(R\) be chosen so that the gap at the edge matches (\(a^2/(2R) = u(0) - u(a)\)). At half the radius the deflection of uniform pressure is \(u(a/2)/u(0) = 0{,}9342\) and a parabola through both ends would give \(0{,}9092\), so the gap there is \(+0{,}0251\,u(0)\), larger than zero, and in the contact the surfaces would not touch (num-06.py J). For the semi-ellipsoid the fit is exact: \(u(a/2)/u(0) = 0{,}875 = 1 - \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac14\).

The contact condition also requires that the pressure is nonnegative everywhere and that the gap outside the contact is larger than zero. The first is satisfied, since the root is nonnegative. For the second we open the left panel of figure 25.54. The surface is a line, the pressure is the semi-ellipse, drawn as arrows that push the body down, and the cylinder of height \(p_0\) on the same circle of diameter \(2a\) is for comparison. The volume of a semi-ellipsoid is two thirds of the cylinder, \(\tfrac23\,p_0\pi a^2\), which is claim 1. The gap in the right panel is the orange curve: outside the contact \(g = \dfrac{r^2}{2R} - h + u(r)\), and with \(h = a^2/R\) (we derive this equality in the proof of the theorem below) and claim 4 at \(r/a = 1{,}1\), \(1{,}3\), \(2\), \(3\) we get \(g/h = 0{,}0378\), \(0{,}196\), \(1{,}218\), \(3{,}643\), so everywhere more than zero.

What the solution must do we draw in true dimensions for our ball at \(1000\) N (the numbers are computed after the theorem).

We start in the bottom panel of figure 25.55. Before loading the ball touches the plate at one point, and we draw both surfaces grey and dashed. Now we lower the centre of the ball by \(h\), as if the bodies were rigid. The ball would dig into the plate: the dotted line is its surface and the overlap is shaded. On the axis it is \(h\) deep, and at distance \(r\) it is \(h - r^2/(2R)\) deep, because the ball moves away from the plate by the gap \(r^2/(2R)\) (equation (25.22)). The bodies cannot overlap, so they yield: after loading the surfaces are orange and in the contact they lie on each other. Being of the same steel, each yields by half. The total indentation of the two must take up exactly the overlap in the contact,

\[u(r) = h - \frac{r^2}{2R} \qquad \text{for } r \leq a .\]

This is a parabola, and lemma 25.26 says that the semi-ellipsoidal pressure of the top panel gives it. The contact reaches to the edge \(a\), outside it the surfaces part.

So we can write the theorem. Its proof is supplemented by a statement of what remains outside the book.

Theorem 25.27 Hertz contact of two spheres (Hertzov stik dveh krogel)

Let two bodies touch at a point, let them have radii \(R_{\mathrm{A}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{B}}\) and effective modulus \(E^*\) (equation (25.24)), \(R\) by equation (25.23), let the gap be \(g_0 = r^2/(2R)\) (equation (25.22)) and the force \(F > 0\). Then the radius of the contact circle \(a\), the approach \(h\) and the maximum pressure \(p_0\) have the values

\[a = \Big(\frac{3FR}{4E^*}\Big)^{1/3} , \qquad h = \frac{a^2}{R} = \Big(\frac{9F^2}{16\,R\,E^{*2}}\Big)^{1/3} , \qquad p_0 = \frac{3F}{2\pi a^2} = \Big(\frac{6F\,E^{*2}}{\pi^3R^2}\Big)^{1/3} , \tag{25.25}\]

the pressure \(p(r) = p_0\sqrt{1 - r^2/a^2}\) for \(r \leq a\) satisfies all contact conditions (definition 25.19) and \(F = \dfrac43\,E^*\sqrt R\;h^{3/2}\).

Proof

We must show that the triple \((a, h, p)\) satisfies all three contact conditions, and express \(a\), \(h\), \(p_0\) from them.

  1. In the contact the gap must be zero, the indentation takes up the overlap: \(g_0(r) + u(r) - h = 0\) for \(r \leq a\). By claim 3 of lemma 25.26 this is \(\dfrac{r^2}{2R} + \dfrac{\pi p_0}{4E^*a}(2a^2 - r^2) - h = 0\).
  2. The equality holds for every \(r\) in the contact, so the coefficient of \(r^2\) must be zero, the parabola of the indentation and the parabola of the overlap have the same curvature: \(\dfrac1{2R} - \dfrac{\pi p_0}{4E^*a} = 0\), so \(p_0 = \dfrac{2E^*a}{\pi R}\). The constant term must be zero too, the two parabolas have the same height \(h\) on the axis: \(h = \dfrac{\pi p_0 a}{2E^*} = \dfrac{a^2}{R}\) (with \(p_0\) from the previous step). This is the second equality.
  3. By claim 1 of the lemma the force is the volume under the pressure, \(F = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}p_0a^2\). Inserting \(p_0\): \(F = \dfrac{4E^*a^3}{3R}\) and \(a^3 = \dfrac{3FR}{4E^*}\), which is the first equality. The equality \(p_0 = 3F/(2\pi a^2)\) is claim 1 of the lemma, the second expression for \(p_0\) follows from \(p_0^3 = \dfrac{8E^{*3}a^3}{\pi^3R^3} = \dfrac{6FE^{*2}}{\pi^3R^2}\).
  4. Outside the circle the pressure is zero (so nonnegative), and the gap is \(g = \dfrac{r^2}{2R} - h + u(r)\) with \(u\) from claim 4 of the lemma. With \(\rho = r/a > 1\), \(h = a^2/R\) from step 2 and \(\arcsin(1/\rho) = \pi/2 - \arccos(1/\rho)\) we get \(\dfrac gh = \dfrac1\pi\Big((\rho^2 - 2)\arccos\dfrac1\rho + \sqrt{\rho^2 - 1}\Big)\) (SymPy, chk-06.py), which is the blue curve in panel (a) of figure 25.56. For \(\rho \geq \sqrt2\) the first term is nonnegative and the second positive, so \(g > 0\). For \(1 < \rho < \sqrt2\) the first term is negative. There we write \(\rho = 1/\cos\vartheta\) with \(\vartheta \in (0, \pi/4)\), which is the angle in the right triangle with hypotenuse \(r\) and leg \(a\) in panel (b). Then \(\sqrt{\rho^2 - 1} = \tan\vartheta\) (the other leg divided by \(a\)) and \(\rho^2 - 2 = -\cos 2\vartheta/\cos^2\vartheta\), so \(\pi\cos^2\vartheta\cdot\dfrac gh = \sin\vartheta\cos\vartheta - \vartheta\cos 2\vartheta = \tfrac12\cos 2\vartheta\,(\tan 2\vartheta - 2\vartheta)\). Since \(2\vartheta \in (0, \pi/2)\), \(\cos 2\vartheta > 0\). Also \(\tan x > x\) for \(x \in (0, \pi/2)\) (panel (c)), because by theorem 1.85 \(\tan x - x = x\,(1/\cos^2\xi - 1) = x\tan^2\xi > 0\) for some \(\xi \in (0, x)\). Hence \(g > 0\) for every \(r > a\). In numbers: at \(r/a = 1{,}1\), \(1{,}3\), \(2\), \(3\), \(g/h = 0{,}0378\), \(0{,}196\), \(1{,}218\), \(3{,}643\). In the circle \(p \cdot g = 0\) (\(g = 0\)), outside (\(p = 0\)), which is the third condition.
  5. From \(h = a^2/R\) and \(a = (3FR/(4E^*))^{1/3}\), \(h^{3/2} = a^3/R^{3/2} = \dfrac{3F}{4E^*\sqrt R}\), so \(F = \dfrac43E^*\sqrt R\,h^{3/2}\).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.10 (PDF p. 331): the equations for \(a\), \(h\), \(p_0\), checked on the crop (p331-b2, p331-b3). HK (PDF p. 129) the same with general \(a^*\), \(b^*\), \(\delta^*\) (\(a^* = b^* = \delta^* = 1\) for spheres). The proof by steps is a derivation from the lemma, not from a book. We do not prove that the solution is unique (the same reason as for theorem 11.4: the book does not prove it for the contact problem, see the remark in chapter 11), only that the triple satisfies the conditions. Step 4 for \(r > a\) is our proof, not from a book. HK gives numerical constants for steel, (6.41) \(b = 0{,}0236\,b^*\,(Q/\Sigma\rho)^{1/3}\) mm and (6.43) \(\delta = 2{,}79\cdot10^{-4}\,\delta^*(Q^2\Sigma\rho)^{1/3}\) mm (PDF p. 129, \(Q\) in N, \(\rho\) in mm\(^{-1}\)). For a sphere on a plane (\(\Sigma\rho = 2/R\)) at \(Q = 1000\) N they give \(346{,}9\ \mu\text{m}\) and \(18{,}98\ \mu\text{m}\) against our \(353{,}6\) and \(19{,}69\ \mu\text{m}\), because the constant \(0{,}0236\) corresponds to \(E = 207{,}7\) GPa at \(\nu = 0{,}3\), which is \(6{,}0\ \%\) more than our \(196\) GPa (num-06.py I).

Step 4 of the proof can be read off figure 25.56. Panel (a) has \(\rho = r/a\) horizontally and the gap in units of \(h\) vertically. The blue curve is \(g/h\), the sum of the orange first term and the grey second term. In the right band, \(\rho \geq \sqrt2\), both terms are nonnegative, so the sum is positive without any computation. In the left band the first term goes below zero, down to \(-0{,}112\) at \(\rho = 1{,}14\), while the grey term there is larger than its absolute value, and this is exactly what the proof shows. Panel (b) tells where the angle \(\vartheta\) comes from: from the point \(x\) at distance \(r\) we draw the tangent to the contact circle. The radius at the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent, so \(\cos\vartheta = a/r = 1/\rho\) and the tangent has length \(a\tan\vartheta = a\sqrt{\rho^2 - 1}\). At \(\rho = 1{,}25\) this is a triangle with sides in the ratio \(3 : 4 : 5\) and \(\vartheta = 36{,}9^\circ\). Panel (c) draws the inequality \(\tan x > x\) as two heights over the same \(x\): the curve \(\tan x\) starts at the origin with the same slope \(1\) as the line \(y = x\), after that its slope \(1/\cos^2 x\) is larger than \(1\), so it stays above the line. At \(\rho = 1{,}25\), \(2\vartheta = 1{,}287\) and the difference \(\tan 2\vartheta - 2\vartheta\) is \(2{,}142\). The points on the blue curve are the numbers at the end of step 4.

The same solution by hand. Where the cube root comes from is told already by an estimate without integrals, in the bottom panel of figure 25.55 (the sign \(\sim\) means the same order of magnitude). The only length of the contact is \(a\), so the deformation reaches about \(a\) deep. The indentation is of the order \(h\), and since the edge of the contact is where the gap \(a^2/(2R)\) reaches the size of \(h\), \(h \sim a^2/R\). The strain is the indentation divided by the depth, \(h/a \sim a/R\). The pressure is, by Hooke's law, \(p \sim E^*a/R\), and the force is pressure times area, \(F \sim p\,a^2 \sim E^*a^3/R\). So \(a^3 \sim FR/E^*\), and the exact calculation only adds the factor \(\tfrac34\) (the estimate gives \(389\ \mu\text{m}\) at \(1000\) N instead of \(353{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\)). The estimate also tells why the contact is not a linear spring: a larger force enlarges the contact area, not only the pressure.

We test the Hertz solution on numbers that we read from figure 25.55. A ball \(D = 12{,}7\) mm lies on a flat steel plate (\(E^* = 107{,}692\) GPa, \(R = 6{,}35\) mm), and in the last row on another such ball (\(R = 3{,}175\) mm):

contact \(F\) \(a\) \(h\) \(p_0\)
ball on a plate \(100\) N \(164{,}1\ \mu\text{m}\) \(4{,}24\ \mu\text{m}\) \(1772\) MPa
ball on a plate \(1000\) N \(353{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\) \(19{,}69\ \mu\text{m}\) \(3818\) MPa
two balls \(1000\) N \(280{,}7\ \mu\text{m}\) \(24{,}81\ \mu\text{m}\) \(6061\) MPa

In the top panel, over the axis \(r\), the half-ellipse of pressure at \(100\) N is dashed, with the radius \(164{,}1\ \mu\text{m}\), and the half-ellipse at \(1000\) N is solid, with the radius \(353{,}6\ \mu\text{m}\). A ten times larger force gives a \(10^{1/3} = 2{,}154\) times larger \(a\) and \(p_0\), not ten times: the solid half-ellipse is wider and higher than the dashed one by this factor. The approach \(19{,}69\ \mu\text{m}\) in the bottom panel is \(10^{2/3} = 4{,}64\) times larger than at \(100\) N. Two balls have a larger pressure than a ball on a plate, because the curvature is larger and the contact smaller (num-06.py A).

We check the sense of the model with the stated bounds. At \(F = 1000\) N, \(a\) is only \(0{,}056\) of the radius of the ball, \(a/R = 0{,}056\), so the error of the parabola for the gap is \(a^2/(4R^2) = 7{,}8\cdot 10^{-4}\), which is \(0{,}078\ \%\), and a half-space is a good picture of the bodies. Linearity is different: the strains under the contact are of the order \(p_0/E = 3818/196\,000 = 0{,}019\), which is more than the \(10^{-3}\) that linear theory assumes (section 25.4), and at \(100\) N \(0{,}009\). This error is therefore more than an order of magnitude larger than the error of the gap, and with the warning that follows we add that we take the elastic calculation as an approximation.

Corollary 25.28 Contact stiffness (togost stika)

Under the conditions of theorem 25.27 the contact stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}h}\) equals \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = 2E^*a = \dfrac{3F}{2h}\). It grows as \(F^{1/3}\) and goes to zero as \(F \to 0\).

Proof

From theorem 25.27 \(F = K h^{3/2}\) with \(K = \tfrac43E^*\sqrt R\), so by the rule of differentiation \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}h} = \tfrac32 K h^{1/2} = \dfrac{3F}{2h}\), which is the slope of the tangent to the curve. With \(h = a^2/R\), \(K h^{1/2} = \tfrac43E^*\sqrt R\cdot a/\sqrt R = \tfrac43E^*a\), so \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}F}{\mathrm{d}h} = 2E^*a\). Because \(a \propto F^{1/3}\) (equation (25.25)), \(k_{\mathrm{c}} \propto F^{1/3}\) and \(a \to 0\) as \(F \to 0\).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.10 (PDF pp. 331-332): \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = 2E^*a\), for every axisymmetric contact with radius \(a\). The proof for a sphere is the differentiation of the theorem.

Let us draw this on figure 25.57. Horizontally is the approach \(h\) in \(\mu\)m, vertically the force \(F\) in N. The blue curve is \(F = K h^{3/2}\). The orange tangent at \(100\) N has the slope \(k_{\mathrm{c}} = 35{,}35\) N/\(\mu\)m, the tangent at \(1000\) N \(76{,}17\) N/\(\mu\)m, which is \(2{,}154\) times more. If the contact were a linear spring, the curve would be the dashed straight line through the origin and \(1000\) N with the stiffness \(F/h = 50{,}8\) N/\(\mu\)m. The curve is below it, because the contact area grows with load and the contact stiffens (hardening, otrdi), which is the reason the Hertz contact is a nonlinear spring. At zero force the tangent is horizontal: an unloaded contact has zero stiffness, which we will need in section 25.8 as a critical point.

Under the ball. Until now we looked at the surface. For a bearing we are also interested in what happens in the interior, because that is where the steel begins to yield. We have the answer from the point force: we cut the pressure into rings and add the stresses of the Boussinesq solution over the rings.

Let us draw how we add them, in figure 25.58. The pressure \(p_0\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\) acts on a disc of diameter \(2a\) and pushes the surface down. The axis runs vertically through the centre of the contact, and on it lies the point \(P\) where we want the stress. We cut the pressure into thin rings of radius \(s\), because every point of a ring is at the same distance from \(P\). The distance \(R\) from a ring to \(P\) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs \(s\) and \(z\), so \(R = \sqrt{s^2 + z^2}\).

Lemma 25.29 Stresses on the axis of the contact (napetosti na osi stika)

Under the conditions of theorem 25.27 and for \(z \geq 0\) the stresses on the axis under the centre of the contact are principal and:

  1. the vertical stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}(z) = -\dfrac{p_0}{1 + z^2/a^2}\) (proved),
  2. the radial and hoop stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}(z) = \sigma_\theta(z) = -p_0\Big((1 + \nu)\Big(1 - \dfrac za\arctan\dfrac az\Big) - \dfrac{1}{2(1 + z^2/a^2)}\Big)\) (cited, checked numerically),
  3. the largest shear stress on the axis is \(\tau_{\max} = 0{,}310\,p_0\) at \(z = 0{,}481\,a\) for \(\nu = 0{,}3\), and the von Mises stress there is \(0{,}620\,p_0\).
Proof
  1. We cut the pressure into rings: a point on the axis at depth \(z\) is at distance \(R = \sqrt{s^2 + z^2}\) from a point of a ring of radius \(s\). By theorem 25.15 the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of a point force is \(-3Fz^3/(2\pi R^5)\), so by superposition (lemma 25.17, Riemann sums of rings, which theorem 4.59 sends to an integral) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}(z) = -\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^a\dfrac{3z^3}{2\pi R^5}\,p_0\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\;s\,\mathrm{d}s\,\mathrm{d}\theta = -3z^3p_0\int_0^a\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - s^2/a^2}\,s}{(s^2 + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. With \(t = s^2/a^2\) and \(a = 1\) (units),
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} = -\tfrac32\,p_0z^3\int_0^1\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\mathrm{d}t .\]
    The function \(G(t) = (1 - t)^{3/2}(t + z^2)^{-3/2}\) has the derivative (SymPy, checked at three points)
    \[G'(t) = -\tfrac32\,\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\big((t + z^2) + (1 - t)\big) = -\tfrac32(1 + z^2)\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}} .\]
    The derivative is thus proportional to the integrand.
  3. Hence
    \[\int_0^1\dfrac{\sqrt{1 - t}}{(t + z^2)^{5/2}}\,\mathrm{d}t = -\dfrac{2}{3(1 + z^2)}\big(G(1) - G(0)\big) = \dfrac{2}{3(1 + z^2)\,z^3} ,\]
    because \(G(1) = 0\) and \(G(0) = z^{-3}\). Inserting:
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} = -\dfrac{p_0}{1 + z^2} .\]
    This is claim 1.
  4. Claim 2: we get the radial stress by the same summation from the Boussinesq \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). We quote the formula for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\) from BOWER (PDF p. 332) and check it: the sum over rings with \(4000\) terms gives at \(z/a = 0{,}1\), \(0{,}48\), \(1\), \(2\) the values \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}/p_0\) \(= -0{,}99010\), \(-0{,}81274\), \(-0{,}50000\), \(-0{,}20000\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}/p_0\) \(= -0{,}61370\), \(-0{,}19270\), \(-0{,}02898\), \(+0{,}00548\), which equals the two formulas to five digits (num-06.py D).
  5. On the axis, by axial symmetry, \(\sigma_\theta = \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{zr}} = 0\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\sigma_\theta\) are principal stresses (definition 2.82). By theorem 2.93 \(\tau_{\max} = |\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}|/2\) and the von Mises stress (definition 2.107) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}} = \sigma_\theta\) equals \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}| = 2\tau_{\max}\). We compute the difference \(|\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}}|/2\) by claims 1 and 2 (\(\nu = 0{,}3\)) at \(30\,000\) points (the blue curve is half the distance between the orange and the grey one) and get the largest value \(0{,}3100\,p_0\) at \(z = 0{,}481\,a\). There \(\sigma_{\mathrm{z}} = -0{,}8122\,p_0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}} = -0{,}1922\,p_0\).

Source: BOWER, §5.4.10 (PDF pp. 332-333): \(\sigma_{33}\) and \(\sigma_{11} = \sigma_{22}\) on the axis (crop p332-b3), the largest von Mises \(0{,}6200\) at \(0{,}481\,a\). HK (PDF p. 136) reads from a graph \(0{,}467\) at the largest shear, which is \(3\ \%\) less, and we do not know which Poisson ratio it took. Claim 1 is a proof and is not in the sources in this form, claim 2 is cited and checked.

Let us look at this on figure 25.59. On the left is the depth \(z/a\) vertically and the stress in units of \(p_0\) horizontally. The orange curve is \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{z}}\) and at the surface it is \(1\): there the pressure equals \(p_0\), and at depth \(a\) only \(\tfrac12\). The grey curve is \(-\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\) and at the surface it is \(0{,}8\,p_0\), because \((1 + 2\nu)/2 = 0{,}8\). For the shear stress we take the difference, the blue curve has only \(0{,}1\,p_0\) at the surface and reaches its maximum \(0{,}310\,p_0\) deep below the surface. What does this mean? The largest load is under the contact, not in it. On the right this is drawn in true proportions: the contact is the wide line of width \(2a\), the point is on the axis \(z\) at depth \(0{,}481\,a\), which at \(F = 1000\) N is \(0{,}481\cdot 353{,}6 = 170\ \mu\text{m}\).

Outside the elastic range. Steel begins to yield at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{vM}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (definition 2.7) and the book takes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa for steel (chapter 11, BOWER Table 3.9, PDF p. 156). By claim 3 of lemma 25.29 this happens at \(0{,}620\,p_0 = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), so at \(p_0 = 1{,}613\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 354{,}8\) MPa. With \(p_0 \propto F^{1/3}\) (equation (25.25), the straight line) this means \(F_{\mathrm{Y}} = 0{,}80\) N for a ball \(D = 12{,}7\) mm, at a contact radius of \(32{,}9\ \mu\text{m}\) and a depth of \(15{,}8\ \mu\text{m}\).

Let us compare with the earlier values. At \(100\) N and \(1000\) N (the blue points) \(p_0/\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 8{,}05\) and \(17{,}35\), so the Hertz result in these contacts is not usable for the book's mild steel: the steel yields long before.

Let us read the remaining parts of figure 25.60. Both axes have a logarithmic scale, the horizontal one for the force \(F\) in N, the vertical one for the pressure \(p_0\) in MPa. The blue straight line is \(p_0 \propto F^{1/3}\) (slope \(\tfrac13\)). The orange line is the limit \(1{,}613\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) and the straight line crosses it at \(F_{\mathrm{Y}} = 0{,}80\) N, in the orange point with the vertical. The points for \(100\) N and \(1000\) N are the blue points, far above the limit. What does a bearing do?
