Numerical check: the difference between equation (25.41) and finite differences of \(\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}\) is at most \(1{,}6\cdot 10^{-10}\) at \(Z = 9\) (relative to \(Q_{\max}\), NumPy).

What does the theorem say? The matrix is a sum of contributions of the compressed balls, each with stiffness \(nK_{\mathrm{n}}\delta_{\mathrm{j}}^{n-1}\) along its line \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) and zero perpendicular to it. Balls at the edge of the zone, where \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}}\) is small, are soft, and the ball under the shaft is the stiffest. The third claim also says how small the displacement must be. For \(n = 3/2\) the error of one ball is about \(|\xi|/(4\delta_{\mathrm{j}})\) of the stiffness term (numerically at \(x/\delta = 0{,}05\): \(1{,}24\,\%\), at \(0{,}1\): \(2{,}46\,\%\), at \(0{,}2\): \(4{,}85\,\%\)). For a vibration of amplitude \(1\) µm about \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 11{,}54\) µm the error of the linear model is therefore about \(2{,}2\,\%\). This is a sensible measure, and at larger amplitudes the linear model does not suffice. An estimate for the whole bearing must also count the balls that start or stop touching during the vibration. At zero clearance and vibration along \(v\) no ball starts or stops carrying (the balls at \(\pm 80^\circ\) have \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} = 2{,}00\) µm and \(\xi = \pm 0{,}17\) µm), and \(F_{\mathrm{v}}(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} + x) = F_{\mathrm{v}}(\delta_{\mathrm{r}})(1 + x/\delta_{\mathrm{r}})^{3/2}\) holds exactly, so the linearization error of the whole bearing at \(x = \pm 1\) µm is \(2{,}1\) to \(2{,}2\,\%\). A ball with \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} \le 0\) adds at most \(K_{\mathrm{n}}|\xi|^n\) to the remainder.

Example 25.41 Stiffness of the nine-ball bearing at 1000 N (togost ležaja z devetimi kroglicami)

The bearing of the introduction has zero clearance, \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 1000\) N and a ball on the direction of the force. Five balls are compressed (\(0^\circ\), \(\pm 40^\circ\), \(\pm 80^\circ\)). The sum over these five balls in equation (25.41) with \(K_{\mathrm{n}}\) from equation (25.37) gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 11{,}57\) µm, \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = 129{,}63\) N/µm, \(k_{\mathrm{vh}} = 0\) and \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}/k_{\mathrm{vv}} = 0{,}746\). The integral model with \(J_{\mathrm{r}}\) from the introduction gives \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 11{,}54\) µm and \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = 1{,}5\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 129{,}93\) N/µm (next corollary), a difference of \(0{,}2\,\%\). The first direction is stiffer than the second because the balls under the shaft lie in the direction \(v\) and support it more than in the direction \(h\). For \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 284\) N, \(1000\) N and \(5000\) N the stiffnesses by the integral model are \(85{,}40\), \(129{,}93\) and \(222{,}18\) N/µm (NumPy), at the approaches \(4{,}99\), \(11{,}54\) and \(33{,}76\) µm.

At zero clearance the matrix has one more special property, called homogeneity. Since \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}}\) is then proportional to \(\vek u\), we have \(\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}(\lambda\vek u) = \lambda^n\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek u)\) for \(\lambda > 0\). This is the same relation between \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) as in the previous section.

Corollary 25.42 Stiffness along the load (togost v smeri sile)

For a bearing with zero clearance (\(P_{\mathrm{d}} = 0\)) and the displacement \(\vek u = (\delta_{\mathrm{r}}, 0)\) in the direction \(v\),

\[k_{\mathrm{vv}} = \frac{n\,F_{\mathrm{v}}}{\delta_{\mathrm{r}}} , \qquad k_{\mathrm{vh}} = \frac{n\,F_{\mathrm{h}}}{\delta_{\mathrm{r}}} , \tag{25.42}\]

where \(F_{\mathrm{v}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{h}}\) are the components of \(\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek u)\). For a position of the cage that is symmetric about the direction \(v\), \(F_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{v}} = F_{\mathrm{r}}\), so \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = \tfrac32 F_{\mathrm{r}}/\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) at \(n = 3/2\). The ratio \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}/k_{\mathrm{vv}}\) does not depend on the size of the load.

Proof

We must show equation (25.42) and the independence of the ratio.

  1. At \(P_{\mathrm{d}} = 0\) we have \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}}(\lambda\vek u)\) = \lambda,\delta_j(\vek u)\( and \)\max(\lambda\delta_j, 0)^n = \lambda^n\max(\delta_j, 0)^n\( for \)\lambda > 0\(. So \)\vek F_b(\lambda\vek u) = \lambda^n\vek F_b(\vek u)$.
  2. We differentiate with respect to \(\lambda\), that is along the displacement, at \(\lambda = 1\). The left side gives \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek u)\,\vek u\) (chain rule, theorem 25.40), the right side \(n\,\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek u)\). So \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\vek u = n\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}\).
  3. At \(\vek u = (\delta_{\mathrm{r}}, 0)\) we have \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\vek u = \delta_{\mathrm{r}}(k_{\mathrm{vv}}, k_{\mathrm{vh}})\), which gives equation (25.42). For a symmetric position of the cage the mirror image of the balls about the axis \(v\) is the same, so \(F_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\), and \(F_{\mathrm{v}} = F_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the equilibrium of the ring.
  4. From equation (25.41), \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}(\lambda\vek u) = \lambda^{n-1}\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek u)\), since every term is proportional to \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}}^{n-1}\). All entries of the matrix are multiplied by the same factor, so the ratio \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}/k_{\mathrm{vv}}\) stays.

Source: The independence of the ratio from the load follows FPGL (PDF p. 203): "this ratio is independent of the static load". Equation (25.42) is not from the source. Numerically: at \(\vek u = (0{,}7, 0{,}2)\) we have \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\vek u = 1{,}5\,\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}\) (NumPy, \(Z = 9\), cage position \(0{,}3\) rad), and at the cage position \(0{,}3\) rad \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = 3{,}0977 = 1{,}5 F_{\mathrm{v}}\).

At \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 1000\) N, therefore, \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = 1{,}5 \cdot 1000/11{,}54 = 129{,}9\) N/µm, which figure 25.74 shows as the slope of the tangent. Since \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} \propto F_{\mathrm{r}}^{2/3}\), we have \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = \tfrac32 F_{\mathrm{r}}/\delta_{\mathrm{r}} \propto F_{\mathrm{r}}^{1/3}\): the stiffness grows with the load, but more slowly than the force (the bearing is a hardening spring). At five times the force, at the point at \(5000\) N and \(33{,}76\) µm, the tangent is steeper: the stiffness is \(222{,}18/129{,}93 = 1{,}71\) times larger, not five times.

FPGL (5.90) writes the same in the form \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = \kappa\,Z^{2/3}d^{1/3}F_{\mathrm{s}}^{1/3}\cos^{5/3}\alpha\) with the constant \(\kappa = 13\cdot 10^6\) N\(^{2/3}\) m\(^{-4/3}\) (PDF p. 202, equation read from the crop). From \(k_{\mathrm{vv}} = \tfrac32 F_{\mathrm{r}}/\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) and equation (25.37) our model gives the form \(\kappa = \tfrac32 J_{\mathrm{r}}^{2/3}/(4{,}36\cdot 10^{-8}) = 12{,}87\cdot 10^6\), so the two forms agree to \(1{,}0\,\%\) (at \(1000\) N: \(131{,}23\) against \(129{,}93\) N/µm). We do not know the cause of the difference, since FPGL does not state how \(\kappa\) was determined.

FPGL quotes the ratio \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}/k_{\mathrm{vv}}\) after Kramer (PDF p. 203) for \(8\), \(12\) and \(16\) balls: \(0{,}46\), \(0{,}64\), \(0{,}73\). Our model with a ball on the direction of the force gives \(0{,}457\), \(0{,}555\) and \(0{,}595\), and with the direction between two balls \(0{,}734\), \(0{,}701\) and \(0{,}688\). For \(8\) balls the first position agrees with Kramer, for \(12\) and \(16\) neither does. Kramer's load, clearance and definition of the ratio are not on the page, so we do not claim that the results agree or disagree, only that they cannot be compared on this basis.

25.8.2 A preloaded pair of bearings

At zero load every \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} \le 0\) in the model of theorem 25.40, so \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}} = \mat 0\): the bearing has zero stiffness at \(\vek u = \vek 0\) and \(P_{\mathrm{d}} = 0\). Why would this be a problem? The theorem holds here and correctly gives \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}} = \mat 0\). But the force \(\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek x)\) grows like \(|\vek x|^{3/2}\), so the zero line is a correct first-order approximation, yet a useless one: the linear model has no restoring force, and without load the shaft would have no natural frequency, although the bearing under a small force still holds the shaft. What fails is the bound of point 3 of the theorem, which needs \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\) and \(|\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\vek x| \le \delta_{\mathrm{j}}/2\). At \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) this allows only \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\cdot\vek x = 0\), so the linear model has no range where its error is bounded. This is the near miss of point 3: without load no ball has \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\). A bearing avoids this by preload (predobremenitev).

We draw the walls left and right, between them two bearings as springs, bearing \(2\) on the left and bearing \(1\) on the right, and the shaft block between them, grey dashed before loading. The springs are compressed against each other, each with force \(F_{\mathrm{p}}\) and approach \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) (the preload). An external force \(F_{\mathrm{e}}\) acts on the block towards the right and the block moves by \(s\) towards bearing \(1\), and we draw the new position orange. Bearing \(1\) is compressed to \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s\), bearing \(2\) is relieved to \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} - s\). Each follows the law \(F = c\,\delta^{3/2}\) (a simplification: the contact angle does not change, HK (8.13) to (8.16), PDF pp. 181-183, also treats the change of angle in angular-contact bearings, which the book does not). In the example below the bearings are the radial bearing of the introduction, pressing on the shaft block from opposite sides in the radial direction, as in the figure, so \(c = 25{,}49\) N/µm\(^{3/2}\). HK in section 8.3.1 (PDF pp. 180-181) preloads a pair of angular-contact bearings in the axial direction. There the law relates the axial force to the axial displacement and has another constant, and the lemma holds for every law of this form.

Lemma 25.43 Stiffness of a preloaded pair (togost predobremenjenega para)

Let two identical bearings follow the law \(F = c\,\delta^{3/2}\) for \(\delta > 0\) and \(F = 0\) for \(\delta \le 0\), with preload \(F_{\mathrm{p}} = c\,\delta_{\mathrm{p}}^{3/2}\). For a displacement \(s\) of the block with \(0 \le s \le \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) the external force is \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = c\big[(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s)^{3/2} - (\delta_{\mathrm{p}} - s)^{3/2}\big]\) and the stiffness of the pair is \(k = dF_{\mathrm{e}}/ds = \tfrac32c\big[(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s)^{1/2} + (\delta_{\mathrm{p}} - s)^{1/2}\big]\). Then:

  1. At \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\), \(k = 2k_{\mathrm{p}}\) with \(k_{\mathrm{p}} = \tfrac32c\,\delta_{\mathrm{p}}^{1/2}\) the stiffness of one bearing at the preload.
  2. \(k\) decreases with \(s\) and at \(s = \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) we have \(k = \sqrt2\,k_{\mathrm{p}}\) at \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = 2^{3/2}F_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  3. At \(F_{\mathrm{e}} \ge 2^{3/2}F_{\mathrm{p}}\) bearing \(2\) is free, the pair behaves as one bearing with \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = c(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s)^{3/2}\), and the stiffness is the continuous continuation.
Proof

We must show three claims.

  1. For \(s \le \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) the approaches \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} \pm s \ge 0\). Equilibrium of the block: the force of bearing \(1\) on the block points towards \(-\), that of bearing \(2\) towards \(+\), so \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = F_1 - F_2\). This gives the stated equation, and its derivative with respect to \(s\) gives \(k\).
  2. At \(s = 0\), \(k = \tfrac32c\cdot 2\delta_{\mathrm{p}}^{1/2} = 2k_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  3. The function \(\sqrt t\) is concave, so \(\sqrt{\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s} + \sqrt{\delta_{\mathrm{p}} - s} \le 2\sqrt{\delta_{\mathrm{p}}}\), and the sum decreases for \(s > 0\) (derivative \(\tfrac12(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s)^{-1/2} - \tfrac12(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} - s)^{-1/2} < 0\)). At \(s = \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\): \(k = \tfrac32c\sqrt{2\delta_{\mathrm{p}}} = \sqrt2k_{\mathrm{p}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = c(2\delta_{\mathrm{p}})^{3/2} = 2^{3/2}F_{\mathrm{p}}\).
  4. For \(s > \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) we have \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} - s < 0\), bearing \(2\) has no force, \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = c(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} + s)^{3/2}\), and at \(s = \delta_{\mathrm{p}}\) the value and the stiffness are the same as in step 3.

Source: The phenomenon follows HK section 8.3.1 (PDF pp. 180-183): "the unit acts as a single bearing under thrust load" after the preload is lost. The lemma and equations are not from the source, HK writes them for angular-contact bearings with \(\alpha\) (8.13)-(8.16).

On the right of the figure are the axes: horizontally the external force \(F_{\mathrm{e}}\) in newtons, vertically the stiffness \(k\) of the pair in N/µm. The example with the bearing of the introduction (\(F_{\mathrm{p}} = 1000\) N, \(\delta_{\mathrm{p}} = 11{,}54\) µm, \(k_{\mathrm{p}} = 129{,}93\) N/µm, NumPy): at \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) the stiffness of the pair is \(259{,}86\) N/µm, twice that of one bearing. It is double because a displacement \(s\) of the block raises the force of bearing \(1\) and lowers the force of bearing \(2\), and both changes push the block back. At \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = 1000\) N the stiffness of the pair is \(256{,}08\) N/µm and at \(2000\) N \(241{,}83\) N/µm, and at \(2828\) N (\(= 2^{3/2}\cdot 1000\) N) \(183{,}75\) N/µm, which is \(\sqrt2 \cdot 129{,}93\). The displacement of the pair at \(1000\) N is \(3{,}87\) µm against \(11{,}54\) µm for one bearing. For one bearing without preload the stiffness at \(F_{\mathrm{e}} = 0\) is zero (the grey curve starts at the origin), at \(1000\) N it is \(129{,}93\) and at \(2000\) N \(163{,}70\) N/µm. Above \(2828\) N the two graphs meet: the pair becomes one bearing, so at \(5000\) N the stiffness is \(222{,}18\) N/µm as for one bearing. The blue curve is therefore higher than the grey one up to this point, but the preload comes at a full price: each bearing carries a constant \(1000\) N. At a force above \(2{,}83\) kN the gain is lost.

25.8.3 Stiffness fluctuation during rotation

So far the position of the cage was fixed. In reality the cage rotates and the balls travel past the direction of the force, so the two positions of figure 25.75, a ball on the direction of the force and the direction of the force between two balls, follow one another. If the cage turns the position \(\psi_0\) forward, the set \(\{\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\}\) maps onto itself when \(\psi_0\) increases by a multiple of \(2\pi/Z\).

Lemma 25.44 Stiffness fluctuation due to ball passage (nihanje togosti zaradi prehajanja kroglic)

For a bearing of definition 25.39 let the displacement \(\vek u\) be constant and the cage position \(\psi_0 = \omega_{\mathrm{c}} t\). Then \(\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) are periodic in time with period \(2\pi/(Z\omega_{\mathrm{c}})\). At \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{v}}, 0)\), \(F_{\mathrm{v}}\), \(k_{\mathrm{vv}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}\) are even functions of \(\psi_0\) and \(F_{\mathrm{h}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{vh}}\) odd ones, about \(0\) and about \(\pi/Z\).

Proof
  1. At \(\psi_0 \to \psi_0 + 2\pi/Z\) the angle \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) changes to \(\psi_{\mathrm{j}+1}\) (index modulo \(Z\)), so the set of angles is the same. The sums (25.39) and (25.41) are sums over the set and do not change. The period in \(\psi_0\) is \(2\pi/Z\), in time \(2\pi/(Z\omega_{\mathrm{c}})\).
  2. At the position \(-\psi_0\) the balls are at the angles \(-\psi_0 + 2\pi j/Z = -\big(\psi_0 + 2\pi(Z - j)/Z\big) + 2\pi\), so they are the mirror images about the direction \(v\) of the balls at the position \(\psi_0\). At \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{v}}, 0)\) we have \(\delta_{\mathrm{j}} = u_{\mathrm{v}}\cos\psi_{\mathrm{j}} - P_{\mathrm{d}}/2\), which is the same for the mirrored ball, since \(\cos\) is even. In the sum (25.39) \(\cos\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) is therefore kept and \(\sin\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) changes sign: \(F_{\mathrm{v}}\) is an even and \(F_{\mathrm{h}}\) an odd function of \(\psi_0\). In the sum (25.41) \(\cos^2\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\sin^2\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) are kept and \(\cos\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\sin\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\) changes sign: \(k_{\mathrm{vv}}\) and \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}\) are even, \(k_{\mathrm{vh}}\) is odd.
  3. About \(\pi/Z\): for an even function \(f\) with period \(2\pi/Z\) we have \(f(\pi/Z + t) = f(-\pi/Z + t) = f(\pi/Z - t)\), for an odd one \(f(\pi/Z + t) = f(-\pi/Z + t) = -f(\pi/Z - t)\).

Source: The frequency of the fluctuation follows HK section 14.3.3 (PDF p. 352): equal to the cage rotation frequency times the number of balls, "the frequency of balls passing the outer raceway". The proof is not from the source.

The lemma does not give the size of the fluctuation, so we compute it. At the displacement \(\vek u = (1, 0)\) and the same \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\), the ratio of the force at the position between two balls to the force at the position with a ball on the direction of the force is: \(Z = 8\): \(0{,}9898\) (\(-1{,}02\,\%\)), \(Z = 9\): \(1{,}0064\), \(Z = 12\): \(0{,}9977\), \(Z = 16\): \(0{,}9992\). For \(Z = 9\) and \(12\) balls the deviations are therefore \(0{,}64\,\%\) and \(0{,}23\,\%\). FPGL (PDF p. 203) states: "the fluctuation in the stiffness is typically less than 1 percent", which agrees for all four ball counts at constant force, the case FPGL describes: the displacement (secant stiffness \(F/\delta\)) changes by \(0{,}68\,\%\), \(0{,}43\,\%\), \(0{,}16\,\%\) and \(0{,}06\,\%\). Only at equal displacement does the force difference for \(8\) balls reach \(1{,}02\,\%\). At equal force the displacement at the position between balls is \(0{,}69\,\%\) larger than with a ball on the direction (\(Z = 8\)), and the stiffness is \(0{,}68\,\%\) smaller. At \(Z = 16\) the deviation of the force at equal \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is \(0{,}08\,\%\), that of the displacement at equal force \(0{,}06\,\%\).

HK (PDF p. 352) gives an example of bearing 204 with \(D = 7{,}938\) mm, \(Z = 8\) and \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 4450\) N: displacement \(0{,}001702\) in with a ball on the direction of the force and \(0{,}001714\) in at the position between two. In millimetres the page prints \(0{,}04232\) mm and \(0{,}04353\) mm. The second pair agrees (\(0{,}001714\) in \(= 0{,}04354\) mm), the first does not: \(0{,}001702\) in is \(0{,}04323\) mm, so two digits are swapped in \(0{,}04232\). With the correct values the difference is \(0{,}71\,\%\). Our model gives \(0{,}03937\) and \(0{,}03964\) mm with the same data, a difference of \(0{,}69\,\%\). The direction and size of the fluctuation therefore agree (the bearing is stiffer with a ball on the direction of the force). The displacements, however, are \(8{,}9\,\%\) smaller than HK's at both positions. HK does not say on the page how the displacement was computed (for example the clearance or the constant), so we cannot determine the cause of this difference. The fluctuation of stiffness is also a source of excitation, since the shaft moves at \(Z\omega_{\mathrm{c}}\) although the force is constant.

Notation of this section. The letter \(k\) with indices (\(k_{\mathrm{vv}}\), \(k_{\mathrm{hh}}\), \(k_{\mathrm{vh}}\)) is the stiffness of the bearing, not the foundation modulus of section 25.1 and not the conductivity of the chapter on heat. The letter \(v\) here is the index of the direction of the force, not the deflection of a beam. The matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the stiffness matrix of the bearing, and \(K_{\mathrm{n}}\) is a number, the contact constant of equation (25.29). The letter \(\kappa\) is the constant from FPGL and not a curvature. The letter \(x\) is a small displacement about the working point and not a beam coordinate, the letter \(s\) the displacement of the block between the bearings and not an arc length. The letter \(\alpha\) is the contact angle.

We have computed how the force of a bearing changes under a small displacement. The next section (25.9) builds this stiffness into a finite element model of the shaft. Since \(\vek F_{\mathrm{b}}\) is nonlinear, the equilibrium must first be found by iteration, and only then the vibration about the resulting position with the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) of this section.

25.9 The bearing in the finite element model

So far we have described the bearing by a law between force and approach (section 25.7) and by its stiffness (section 25.8). Now we put it into the finite element model of a shaft from chapter 12. The difficulty is that the force of the bearing is a power of the approach, \(F = \kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,\delta^{3/2}\), so the equations of equilibrium are no longer linear and the matrix equation \(\mat K\,\vek d = \vek F\) cannot simply be inverted. The section takes two steps. The first is statics: where the shaft comes to rest in the bearings. There we use Newton's method (Newtonov postopek), which replaces a nonlinear equation by a sequence of linear ones. The second is small vibration about this state: we replace the bearing by a tangent spring (tangentna vzmet) and obtain the natural frequencies. We test both steps on a rotor whose outcome we know.

25.9.1 The rotor as a model

Take a steel shaft of diameter \(40\) mm and length \(L = 0{,}8\) m, with a disk of mass \(m_{\mathrm{d}} = 50\) kg at its middle and a bearing with nine balls from section 25.8 at each end (\(D = 12{,}7\) mm, zero clearance). The steel is the book's, \(E = 196\) GPa and density \(7800\) kg/m³. The cross section gives \(EI = 24\,630{,}1\) N m² and the mass per length \(\rho A = 9{,}802\) kg/m, so the mass of the shaft is \(7{,}84\) kg. The total weight of shaft and disk is \(W = (50 + 7{,}84)\cdot 9{,}81 = 567{,}42\) N.

We name the idealizations before we use them. The shaft is an Euler-Bernoulli beam in a vertical plane, divided into four equal elements of length \(h = 0{,}2\) m (definition 12.3). The disk is a point mass at the middle node, without rotary inertia. In the first mode of vibration this costs nothing, because the middle of the shaft does not turn there and the disk only moves up and down. In the second mode the middle turns and the simplification costs a lot: a steel disk of diameter \(0{,}3\) m (thickness \(91\) mm, moment of inertia about a diameter \(0{,}316\) kg m²) would lower the second frequency from \(472\) Hz to \(164\) Hz (NumPy). The second mode below is therefore the mode of a shaft with a point mass, not of a rotor with a wide disk. The shaft does not spin, so there are no gyroscopic terms, which chapter 24 treats. The bearing acts only on the vertical displacement of the end node and carries no moment. This holds when the inner ring can tilt without the balls resisting noticeably. The other extreme, a bearing that fully prevents the rotation of the end of the shaft, would raise the first frequency from \(32{,}7\) to \(64{,}7\) Hz (NumPy), and a real bearing lies between the two. The bearing supports are rigid and the bearing has no internal degrees of freedom. FPGL (PDF p. 214 to 215) also names such a model of a shaft with rigid foundations a shaft-line model. A real bearing does carry some moment, and FPGL (PDF p. 203) gives extended stiffness matrices of the bearing (Lim and Singh), which we do not use here.

We draw the shaft as a thick horizontal line of length \(0{,}8\) m, since the beam lies along it. On it we place the nodes \(1\) to \(5\) at a spacing of \(0{,}2\) m, because the finite element method of chapter 12 needs them. The distance between two neighbouring nodes is the length of an element \(h = 200\) mm. At the middle, in node \(3\), we fix the disk of mass \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\), because the disk sits at the middle of the shaft. Under each end we draw a bearing as a nonlinear spring: the zigzag line means a spring and the arrow across it means that its force is not proportional to the displacement. The bearing is under the shaft, because the shaft presses on it downward.

The lower picture shows what happens under the weight. The deflection curve is an orange curve below the grey straight line of the undeformed shaft. We have enlarged it vertically \(300\) times relative to the horizontal scale \(1:10\), because the deflection at the middle is only \(0{,}238\) mm, which is \(0{,}71\) cm in the drawing. Forces act on the shaft: the weight \(W = 567\) N at the middle downward and the forces \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = 284\) N of the two bearings at the ends upward. Each arrow lies on the line along which the force acts, and the upward ones end at the point of action, because the bearing pushes the shaft up. The vertical displacement \(w_{\max} = 238\) µm is the blue measure from the straight line to the lowest point. The ends of the shaft move down by \(\delta^* = 4{,}98\) µm. This is not visible at this enlargement, so the circle shows the left end enlarged: the grey dashed line is the end of the shaft before loading, the orange one after it, and the blue measure between them is \(\delta^*\). The number is small: \(4{,}98\) µm is \(2{,}09\,\%\) of the deflection at the middle, in the drawing \(0{,}015\) cm. Why this small number nevertheless counts is shown by the section on vibration.

The unknowns are the nodal displacements and rotations \(\vek d = (v_1, \theta_1, \dots, v_5, \theta_5)^\T\), in all \(N = 10\). We measure the displacement \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) downward, because we are interested in how the shaft presses on the bearing. By theorem 12.9 the stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) is the sum of the element matrices of lemma 12.4. Since the shaft is not clamped, \(\mat K\) is singular, because moving the whole shaft does not deform it. The middle picture of the figure shows the shaft before the move (grey dashed) and after it (orange): all nodes go down by the same length (blue arrows), the shaft stays straight, and a straight shaft bends nowhere, so there are no forces in it. The right-hand side \(\vek F\) consists of the nodal forces of the weight, namely by theorem 12.9 for the uniform load \(q = \rho A\,g\) on an element the force \(q h/2\) and the moment \(\pm q h^2/12\) at its two nodes, and the weight of the disk \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\,g\) at node \(3\). The bearing forces we write for each bearing separately. For the bearing of section 25.8 with zero clearance and \(n = 3/2\) we have by theorem 25.35 \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = Z\,J_{\mathrm{r}}(\tfrac12)\,K_{\mathrm{n}}\,\delta_{\mathrm{r}}^{3/2}\), which we write as

\[F_{\mathrm{r}}(\delta) = \kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,\delta^{3/2} , \qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{b}} = Z\,J_{\mathrm{r}}\big(\tfrac12\big)\,K_{\mathrm{n}} = 2{,}549\cdot 10^{10}\ \text{N/m}^{3/2} . \tag{25.43}\]

The constant \(\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the constant \(c = Z\,J_{\mathrm{r}}\,K_{\mathrm{n}}\) of section 25.8, there in units N and µm (\(c = 25{,}49\) N/µm\(^{3/2}\)), computed with Palmgren's formula (25.37) (HK (8.1), PDF p. 179). Here we write \(\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\), because we need the letter \(c\) for other quantities. Check: at \(\delta = 11{,}54\) µm equation (25.43) gives \(999{,}4\) N, which is the \(1000\) N of example 25.41. The law holds only for \(\delta > 0\), since the bearing does not pull (definition 25.19). So the vector of bearing forces \(\vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d)\) is zero everywhere except in two components, \(v_1\) and \(v_5\), where it is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\max(v_{\mathrm{i}}, 0)^{3/2}\). The equilibrium of the rotor is then

\[\mat K\,\vek d + \vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d) = \vek F . \tag{25.44}\]

The law \(F_{\mathrm{r}} = \kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,\delta^{3/2}\) is the model with a continuous angle (theorem 25.35). At \(Z = 9\) the largest ball load differs by about \(10\,\%\) with the position of the cage (\(4{,}385\) and \(3{,}969\,F_{\mathrm{r}}/Z\), section 25.7), so the law (25.43) has that much uncertainty too. The rotor is a test of the method, not an exact computation of a bearing.

The equilibrium (25.44) has one property that does not depend on the law of the bearing, and we prove it before we solve the nonlinear part.

Lemma 25.45 The bearing forces add up to the weight (vsota sil ležajev je teža)

Let \(\vek d\) be a solution of equation (25.44). Then the sum of the forces of the two bearings equals the total weight of the rotor, \(\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\max(v_1, 0)^{3/2} + \kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\max(v_5, 0)^{3/2} = W\).

Proof

We must show that we move the whole shaft without deforming it, and that this turns the equation of equilibrium into a sum of forces. Let \(\vek t\) be the column with ones at the places \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) and zeros at the places \(\theta_{\mathrm{i}}\), that is, the displacement of the whole shaft by \(1\) downward.

  1. For every element \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\,(1, 0, 1, 0)^\T = \vek 0\): by lemma 12.4 each row of the matrix \(\mat k_{\mathrm{e}}\) gives the sum \(12 - 12 = 0\), \(6h - 6h = 0\), \(-12 + 12 = 0\), \(6h - 6h = 0\). This is the computation of what the middle picture shows: the moved shaft is straight, so it has no curvature, and without curvature there is no bending moment and there are no nodal forces. By theorem 12.9 therefore \(\mat K\,\vek t = \vek 0\), and since \(\mat K\) is symmetric, also \(\vek t^\T\mat K = \vek 0^\T\).
  2. We multiply equation (25.44) by the row \(\vek t^\T\): \(\vek t^\T\mat K\,\vek d + \vek t^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{b}} = \vek t^\T\vek F\). The first term is zero by step 1.
  3. The sum \(\vek t^\T\vek F\) is the sum of the nodal forces. Each element contributes \(q h/2 + q h/2 = q h\) (moments do not count, since they stand at the places with a zero in \(\vek t\)), four elements \(q L\), the disk \(m_{\mathrm{d}}\,g\), so \(\vek t^\T\vek F = \rho A\,g\,L + m_{\mathrm{d}}\,g = W\), which is the arrow of the weight \(W = 567\) N in the lower picture.
  4. The vector \(\vek f_{\mathrm{b}}\) has nonzero components only at \(v_1\) and \(v_5\), so \(\vek t^\T\vek f_{\mathrm{b}} = f_{\mathrm{b},1} + f_{\mathrm{b},5}\), the two arrows \(F_{\mathrm{r}}\) at the ends of the shaft. The claim follows from step 2.

Source: The proof is ours, with the help of theorem 12.9. FPGL (PDF p. 214, equation 5.109) writes the assembled equations of motion of the shaft-line model, whose static part with linear bearings has the form of equation (25.44).

The lemma says that the two bearings together carry the weight whatever their stiffness. In our case the load and the supports are symmetric, so each bearing carries \(W/2 = 283{,}71\) N (section 25.8 gives the approach \(4{,}99\) µm at \(284\) N). From equation (25.43) follows \(\delta^* = (W/(2\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}))^{2/3} = 4{,}9847\) µm and the tangent stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = \tfrac32\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\sqrt{\delta^*} = 8{,}5375\cdot 10^7\) N/m. So we have obtained the solution in closed form. This is a consequence of the shaft on two bearings being statically determinate and is not general. On two bearings the balance of forces and the balance of moments already fix both forces, also when the bearings are not equal. With a third bearing there are three unknown forces and only two equations of equilibrium, so we do not know the force of each bearing until we know the bending of the shaft and the displacements of the bearings. The method that can do this we now develop on the example with a known outcome.

25.9.2 Newton's method

We solve a nonlinear equation \(g(x) = 0\) like someone walking along a slope: at the current point he replaces the curve by its tangent and looks where the tangent cuts the axis. In a rotor with two equal bearings the displacements of both bearings are equal, so there is one unknown, the displacement \(x\). The bearings together carry the weight \(W\) (lemma 25.45), so \(x\) is the solution of the equation

\[g(x) = 2\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,x^{3/2} - W = 0 , \qquad x > 0 . \tag{25.45}\]

The function \(g(x)\) is the difference between the force that the two bearings give at the displacement \(x\) and the weight. The zero \(x^* = \delta^*\) we know from the previous section, so we shall see the error of the method. As at a board we draw first the axes: horizontally \(x\) in µm, vertically \(g\) in N. On them we lay the curve \(g\), which equals \(-W\) at \(x = 0\) and grows with \(x\) as the power \(3/2\). Its zero is the root \(x^*\).

Definition 25.46 Newton's method (Newtonov postopek)

Let \(\vek r\colon \mathbb R^N \to \mathbb R^N\) be a differentiable vector function whose solution \(\vek r(\vek u) = \vek 0\) we seek. We call the function \(\vek r(\vek u)\) the residual (ostanek), because it is what remains of the equation when we insert the approximation \(\vek u\). The Jacobian matrix (matrika odvodov) \(\mat J(\vek u)\) is the square matrix of order \(N\) with entries \(J_{\mathrm{ij}} = \partial r_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial u_{\mathrm{j}}\). Newton's method with the start \(\vek u_0\) is the sequence

\[\vek u_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek u_{\mathrm{k}} - \mat J(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}})^{-1}\,\vek r(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}}) , \tag{25.46}\]

that is, \(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek u_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek\Delta_{\mathrm{k}}\), where \(\vek\Delta_{\mathrm{k}}\) is the solution of the linear system \(\mat J(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}})\,\vek\Delta_{\mathrm{k}} = -\vek r(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}})\), if \(\mat J(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}})\) is invertible. For \(N = 1\) we have \(r = g\), \(\mat J = g'\) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - g(x_{\mathrm{k}})/g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})\).

Source: KREYSZIG (PDF p. 827 to 828, algorithm Newton and table 19.1) for one unknown, COOK (PDF p. 611 to 612) for a system. KREYSZIG (PDF p. 827) also says that the method is called Newton-Raphson as well, after Raphson, who published a similar method.

The geometric meaning is the tangent: \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is the intersection of the tangent to the curve at the point \((x_{\mathrm{k}}, g(x_{\mathrm{k}}))\) with the axis \(x\). The tangent has the equation \(y = g(x_{\mathrm{k}}) + g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})(x - x_{\mathrm{k}})\) and its zero we get from \(0 = g(x_{\mathrm{k}}) + g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} - x_{\mathrm{k}})\), which is the definition for \(N = 1\). The same notation holds for a system, because the linear approximation of a vector function is \(\vek r(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}}) + \mat J(\vek u_{\mathrm{k}})(\vek u - \vek u_{\mathrm{k}})\). In the rotor \(\vek r(\vek d) = \mat K\vek d + \vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d) - \vek F\) and, since each bearing has only one component, \(\mat J = \mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d)\), where \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the diagonal matrix with the tangent stiffness of the bearing \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = \tfrac32\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\max(v_{\mathrm{i}}, 0)^{1/2}\) at the places \(v_1\) and \(v_5\) (the tangent stiffness matrix of the bearing from definition 25.39 and theorem 25.40). The function \(\max(v, 0)^{3/2}\) has the derivative \(\tfrac32\max(v, 0)^{1/2}\) everywhere, also at \(v = 0\), where it is zero.

Let us take the steps on figure 25.78. We start at a very small displacement \(x_0 = 0{,}1\) µm, where the two bearings together carry only \(1{,}6\) N. At \(x_0\) the residual is \(g(x_0) = -565{,}8\) N, so the first tangent meets the curve below the axis and is very shallow, because \(g'(x_0) = 3\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\sqrt{x_0} = 2{,}42\cdot 10^7\) N/m is small. A shallow tangent cuts the axis far away, at \(x_1 = 23{,}50\) µm, which is \(4{,}7\) times farther from the origin than the root. There the second tangent is much steeper and cuts the axis at \(x_2 = 9{,}36\) µm, the third at \(x_3 = 5{,}546\) µm. Then \(x_4 = 4{,}9991\) µm (\(0{,}3\,\%\) above the root), \(x_5 = 4{,}9847\) and \(x_6 = 4{,}9847\) µm. The start at \(20\) µm gives \(8{,}3257\), \(5{,}3465\), \(4{,}9909\), \(4{,}9847\) µm, the start at \(2\) µm gives \(5{,}9129\), \(5{,}0221\), \(4{,}9847\) µm (NumPy, num-09.py). Everywhere the iterates fall from the first one on, from the right toward the root. This is no accident.

Theorem 25.47 Newton's method for a convex increasing function (Newtonov postopek za konveksno naraščajočo funkcijo)

Let \(g\) be a twice continuously differentiable function on the interval \((0, \infty)\) with \(g'(x) > 0\) and \(g''(x) > 0\) for every \(x > 0\), and let it have a zero \(x^* > 0\). Let \(x_0 > 0\) be arbitrary and \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - g(x_{\mathrm{k}})/g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})\). Let \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - x^*\). Then:

  1. The zero \(x^*\) is the only one.
  2. For every \(k \ge 0\) we have \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} > 0\) and \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} \ge 0\), equality only at \(e_{\mathrm{k}} = 0\).
  3. For \(k \ge 1\) we have \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le x_{\mathrm{k}}\), the sequence \((x_{\mathrm{k}})\) converges and its limit is \(x^*\).
  4. Let \(m = g'(x^*)\) and \(M\) the largest value of \(g''\) on \([x^*, x_1]\). For \(k \ge 1\) we have \(0 \le e_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le \dfrac{M}{2m}\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\).
Idea

The tangent of a convex curve lies below the curve, so its intersection with the axis cannot be to the left of the zero. Why does it lie below? The slope of the curve grows (\(g'' > 0\)): to the right of the point of contact the curve is steeper than the tangent and escapes upward, to the left of it the curve is flatter and falls more slowly than the tangent. In figure 25.78 all three blue tangents (the first, the second, the third) lie below the blackwhite curve. From there on the residual is nonnegative, and so every step only decreases \(x\). The square in the error estimate comes from the second derivative in Taylor's theorem.

Proof
  1. Since \(g' > 0\), by theorem 1.85 for \(a < b\) the value \(g(b) - g(a) = g'(\xi)(b - a) > 0\), so \(g\) is strictly increasing and has at most one zero.
  2. Let \(x_{\mathrm{k}} > 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}} \ne x^*\). By theorem 8.68 for \(g\) about \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) there is \(\xi\) between \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(x^*\) such that \(0 = g(x^*) = g(x_{\mathrm{k}}) + g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})(x^* - x_{\mathrm{k}}) + \tfrac12 g''(\xi)(x^* - x_{\mathrm{k}})^2\). So \(g(x_{\mathrm{k}}) + g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})(x^* - x_{\mathrm{k}}) = -\tfrac12 g''(\xi)\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\). We divide by \(g'(x_{\mathrm{k}}) > 0\) and use \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - g(x_{\mathrm{k}})/g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})\): \(x^* - x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = -\dfrac{g''(\xi)}{2\,g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})}\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2 < 0\), so \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \dfrac{g''(\xi)}{2\,g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})}\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2 > 0\). Hence \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} > x^* > 0\). In figure 25.78 this is the first tangent, which starts to the left of the root and crosses the axis to the right of it, at \(x_1\). At \(x_{\mathrm{k}} = x^*\) we have \(g(x_{\mathrm{k}}) = 0\) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. For \(k \ge 1\) step 2 gives \(x_{\mathrm{k}} \ge x^*\), so \(g(x_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge g(x^*) = 0\) (step 1) and \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - g(x_{\mathrm{k}})/g'(x_{\mathrm{k}}) \le x_{\mathrm{k}}\). The sequence is therefore decreasing from \(k = 1\) on and bounded below by \(x^*\) (in figure 25.78 \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) follow one another from the right toward the root), and by theorem 1.52 it converges to a limit \(L \ge x^* > 0\). The functions \(g\) and \(g'\) are continuous at \(L\) and \(g'(L) > 0\), so from \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - g(x_{\mathrm{k}})/g'(x_{\mathrm{k}})\) in the limit follows \(L = L - g(L)/g'(L)\), so \(g(L) = 0\) and by step 1 \(L = x^*\).
  4. For \(k \ge 1\) we have \(\xi \in (x^*, x_{\mathrm{k}}) \subset [x^*, x_1]\), so \(g''(\xi) \le M\). Since \(g'' > 0\), by theorem 1.85 \(g'\) is increasing, so \(g'(x_{\mathrm{k}}) \ge g'(x^*) = m\). Step 2 gives \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1} \le M\,e_{\mathrm{k}}^2/(2m)\).

Source: The theorem and the proof are ours. The convergence of Newton's method is proved in KREYSZIG (PDF p. 829 to 830, theorem 2) as quadratic convergence near the zero by a different route.

What did the theorem show? If the curve is convex and increasing, Newton's method lands to the right of the zero after one step whatever the start \(x_0\), then falls monotonically, and the error is squared at every step. This is the reason for the sequence of figure 25.78: \(x_1 = 23{,}50\) is to the right of the root and falls from there without turning back. In the rotor \(g'' = \tfrac32\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,x^{-1/2}\) is decreasing, so \(M = g''(x^*)\) and the constant is \(M/(2m) = g''(x^*)/(2g'(x^*)) = 1/(4x^*) = 0{,}0502\) per µm. The measured ratios \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}/e_{\mathrm{k}}^2\) from the start \(0{,}1\) µm are, at \(k = 1, 2, 3, 4\), \(0{,}0128\), \(0{,}0293\), \(0{,}0459\), \(0{,}0500\) per µm, all below the bound \(0{,}0502\), and approach \(0{,}0502\) with each step: the errors \(e_1, \dots, e_5\) in µm are \(18{,}511\), \(4{,}378\), \(0{,}561\), \(0{,}01443\), \(0{,}00001\) (the error \(e_2\) is the blue measure from the root to \(x_2\) in the figure, the initial error \(e_0 = -4{,}885\) µm is to the left of the root). So each step is not merely a few times smaller, the number of correct digits roughly doubles, as the estimate predicts. The estimate holds for the one-dimensional case. For a system of equations we do not prove it: COOK (PDF p. 612) writes that the method is not guaranteed to converge for all nonlinear problems, but in practice the residuals decrease.

The theorem requires \(x_0 > 0\) and \(g'' > 0\). Each requirement has a case where we remove it. Let us look first at a start that is not in \((0, \infty)\).

Example 25.48 A start at zero (začetek v ničli)

Let \(x_0 = 0\), which the theorem does not allow. At \(x = 0\) the tangent stiffness of the bearing is \(g'(0) = 3\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\sqrt 0 = 0\), the tangent is horizontal and never cuts the axis, and the step \(x_1 = x_0 - g(x_0)/g'(x_0)\) divides by zero. KREYSZIG says the same (PDF p. 828): if it happens that the derivative is zero at some \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) (line 2 of the algorithm), we try another start. In the system the matrix \(\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek 0)\) equals \(\mat K\) and is singular, since the displacement of the whole shaft is not a deformation (lemma 25.45, step 1), so the system \(\mat J\,\vek\Delta = -\vek r\) cannot be solved. Physically: a bearing without load and without preload has no stiffness, and the shaft in such a model is supported nowhere.

So we start with a linear guess. In the rotor we take bearings of linear stiffness \(k_0 = 1{,}0\cdot 10^8\) N/m, solve \((\mat K + \mat K_0)\,\vek d_0 = \vek F\) (\(\mat K_0\) has \(k_0\) at \(v_1\) and \(v_5\)) and obtain the end of the shaft at \(2{,}8371\) µm. This is the start \(\vek d_0\).

Example 25.49 Newton's method on the rotor (Newtonov postopek na rotorju)

The rotor of section 25.9.1, \(N = 10\), residual \(\vek r = \mat K\vek d + \vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d) - \vek F\) and \(\mat J = \mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d)\). The start: linear bearings with \(k_0 = 1{,}0\cdot 10^8\) N/m. The displacement of the end of the shaft \(v_1\) and the norm of the residual \(\|\vek r\|\) by steps (NumPy, num-09.py):

\(k\) \(v_1\) (µm) \(\|\vek r\|\) (N)
0 \(2{,}83712\) \(228{,}9\)
1 \(5{,}35049\) \(44{,}97\)
2 \(4{,}99099\) \(0{,}7640\)
3 \(4{,}98467\) \(2{,}421\cdot 10^{-4}\)
4 \(4{,}98467\) \(2{,}44\cdot 10^{-11}\)

The quotient \(\|\vek r_{\mathrm{k}+1}\|/\|\vek r_{\mathrm{k}}\|^2\) is from the second step on \(3{,}8\cdot 10^{-4}\), \(4{,}1\cdot 10^{-4}\) and \(4{,}2\cdot 10^{-4}\) per N, which is nearly constant and shows quadratic convergence also for a system with ten unknowns. The first step overshoots the solution (\(5{,}35\) against \(4{,}98\) µm), as theorem 25.47 predicts for one unknown, and then it approaches from the right. The displacement of the end of the shaft \(4{,}98467\) µm agrees with the closed solution \(\delta^* = 4{,}9847\) µm of lemma 25.45, which is a check that the system solves the right equation. The deflection at the middle is \(0{,}2382\) mm. Independently we get it as the sum of the deflections of a simply supported beam: the force of the disk \(490{,}5\) N gives \(F L^3/(48 EI) = 0{,}2124\) mm (equation (5.60)), the weight of the shaft \(q L = 76{,}93\) N gives \(5qL^4/(384 EI) = 0{,}0208\) mm (equation (5.41)), and the bearings lower the whole shaft by another \(0{,}0050\) mm. The sum \(0{,}2382\) mm agrees. The Jacobian matrix \(\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) agrees with numerical differences: the largest relative difference is \(1{,}2\cdot 10^{-9}\).

The theorem requires \(g'' > 0\). If we remove it, convergence stops, as the next example shows.

Example 25.50 A concave function: the cube root (konkavna funkcija: kubični koren)

On the axes we draw the curve \(g(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}\) with the zero \(x^* = 0\). It is increasing (\(g' = \tfrac13 x^{-2/3} > 0\)) but concave, \(g'' = -\tfrac29 x^{-5/3} < 0\) for \(x > 0\). The step is \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - \sqrt[3]{x_{\mathrm{k}}}\big/\big(\tfrac13\,x_{\mathrm{k}}^{-2/3}\big) = x_{\mathrm{k}} - 3\,x_{\mathrm{k}} = -2\,x_{\mathrm{k}}\). From \(x_0 = 0{,}1\) we come to \(x_1 = -0{,}2\) along the first tangent, to \(x_2 = 0{,}4\) along the second and to \(x_3 = -0{,}8\) along the third: each step doubles the distance from the zero and changes side (NumPy, num-09.py: \(0{,}1,\ -0{,}2,\ 0{,}4,\ -0{,}8,\ 1{,}6\)). In theorem 25.47 step 2 fails, because \(g''(\xi) < 0\) and so \(e_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is not nonnegative: the tangent of a concave curve lies above the curve and cuts the axis on the other side of the zero. The example also removes the condition \(x^* > 0\), since the zero of the cube root is at \(0\). That concavity alone already causes the failure is shown by \(g(x) = \ln x\) on \((0, \infty)\), which fulfils every condition of the theorem except \(g'' > 0\): \(g' = 1/x > 0\), \(g'' = -1/x^2 < 0\), zero \(x^* = 1\). The step is \(x_{\mathrm{k}+1} = x_{\mathrm{k}} - \ln x_{\mathrm{k}}/(1/x_{\mathrm{k}}) = x_{\mathrm{k}}(1 - \ln x_{\mathrm{k}})\), and with the start \(x_0 = 3\) it gives \(x_1 = 3(1 - \ln 3) = -0{,}296\), which is no longer in \((0, \infty)\), where \(\ln\) is defined. Point 2 of the theorem fails and the method stops (NumPy). Without the condition \(g'' > 0\) convergence does not follow from \(g' > 0\) and a zero. Our bearing fulfils this condition, since \(g''(x) = \tfrac32\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,x^{-1/2} > 0\).

For the bearing we therefore use Newton's method with a start that is not zero. For a system we have no proof, so we check each step with the residual.

25.9.3 Small vibration about equilibrium

Once we know the static state \(\vek d_0\), we are interested in the natural frequencies of the rotor about it. The equations of motion are Lagrange's equations of a system with a potential: the kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek d}\) with the mass of the shaft (the consistent mass matrix by lemma 12.43) and with the mass of the disk at the place \(v_3\). The potential is

\[V(\vek d) = \tfrac12\,\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d + \sum_{\mathrm{b}}\tfrac25\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\max(v_{\mathrm{b}}, 0)^{5/2} - \vek F^\T\vek d , \tag{25.47}\]

the sum runs over the components of the bearings \(v_1\) and \(v_5\). The first term is the strain energy of the shaft (theorem 12.9), the second the energy of the two bearings, since its derivative with respect to \(v_{\mathrm{b}}\) is exactly \(\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\max(v_{\mathrm{b}}, 0)^{3/2}\), the third the work of the weight. The derivative \(\partial V/\partial\vek d = \mat K\vek d + \vek f_{\mathrm{b}} - \vek F\) is the left side of equation (25.44) without its right side, so the equilibrium is a stationary point of the energy.

Let us ask what this means for small departures. The bearing is not linear, so it does not behave like one spring. In statics the secant (sekanta), \(F/\delta\), applies, in small vibration the tangent (tangenta), as in figure 25.74 of section 25.8. The next theorem says exactly when and how much.

Let us draw this for our bearing. On the axes we put the bearing displacement \(v_{\mathrm{b}}\) horizontally and its force \(f_{\mathrm{b}}\) vertically. The curve is the bearing law \(f_{\mathrm{b}} = \kappa_{\mathrm{b}} v_{\mathrm{b}}^{3/2}\). To the left of the origin the force is zero, because the bearing does not pull. The static state is the point on the curve at \(v_{\mathrm{b},0} = 4{,}98\) µm and \(284\) N, where the shaft settles under the weight. Through it we draw the tangent with slope \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\): this is the spring that replaces the bearing. When the shaft in vibration departs by \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\), in the figure by half the static displacement, the true force is on the curve (the orange point) and the force of the spring on the tangent. The difference between them is the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{b}}\), here \(25\) N at a change of force of \(237{,}5\) N. Closer to the static state the tangent and the curve nearly coincide.

Theorem 25.51 Linearization of the bearing and the natural frequencies of the rotor (linearizacija ležaja in lastne frekvence rotorja)

Let the rotor of section 25.9.1 have a symmetric stiffness matrix \(\mat K\) and a symmetric positive definite mass matrix \(\mat M\) of order \(N\), with bearings with the law (25.43) at the components \(v_1\) and \(v_5\). Let \(\vek d_0\) be an equilibrium (25.44) with \(v_{1,0} > 0\) and \(v_{5,0} > 0\). Let \(k_{\mathrm{b}}(v) = \tfrac32\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\sqrt v\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) the diagonal matrix with \(k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{1,0})\) and \(k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{5,0})\) at \(v_1\) and \(v_5\) and zeros elsewhere. Then:

  1. The equilibrium \(\vek d_0\) is a stationary point of the potential (25.47), its matrix of second derivatives at \(\vek d_0\) is \(\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\), and the motion \(\vek x = \vek d - \vek d_0\) satisfies \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek x} + (\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}})\,\vek x = \vek R\) with a remainder \(\vek R\) that has nonzero components only at the bearings.
  2. For \(|x_{\mathrm{b}}| \le v_{\mathrm{b},0}/2\) we have \(|R_{\mathrm{b}}|\) \le \dfrac{3\sqrt 2}{8},\kappa_b,v_{b,0}^{-1/2},x_b^2\(, so relative to the tangent term \)k_b(v_{b,0}),x_b\( at most \)\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{4},|x_b|/v_{b,0}$.
  3. The matrix \(\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) is symmetric and positive definite. By theorem 10.21 the eigenproblem \((\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}})\,\vek\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi\) has \(N\) positive eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the natural circular frequencies of the linear model are \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}\).
  4. Let the bearings be replaced by springs of stiffness \(c\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\) and let \(0 < c_1 \le c_2\). Then every natural frequency at \(c_2\) is at least as large as at \(c_1\).
Idea

The equations of motion follow from the potential (theorem 10.3), which is smooth enough as long as the displacements of the bearings are positive. We subtract the equilibrium from the motion and what remains is the difference of the bearing force, which we estimate with Taylor's theorem in one variable, because each bearing depends on one component. The positivity of the matrix we show by the energy.

Proof
  1. Let \(U\) be the set of columns \(\vek d\) with \(v_1 > 0\) and \(v_5 > 0\). It is open, and on it \(\max(v_{\mathrm{b}}, 0)^{5/2} = v_{\mathrm{b}}^{5/2}\), which is three times continuously differentiable at \(v_{\mathrm{b}} > 0\). The potential \(V\) is therefore three times continuously differentiable on \(U\), and the kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek d}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek d}\) has a constant matrix. By theorem 10.3 (point 2, constant \(\mat M\), no dampers, \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) because the weight is in the potential) the motion in \(U\) is a solution of \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek d} + \mat K\vek d + \vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d) = \vek F\), since \(\partial V/\partial\vek d = \mat K\vek d + \vek f_{\mathrm{b}} - \vek F\). At \(\vek d_0\) this derivative is zero. The matrix of second derivatives of the potential is \(\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\), since \(\partial^2 V/\partial v_{\mathrm{b}}^2 = \tfrac32\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\sqrt{v_{\mathrm{b}}}\) and the mixed second derivatives of the bearing terms are zero. For \(\vek d = \vek d_0 + \vek x\) we subtract the equilibrium: \(\mat M\,\ddot{\vek x} + \mat K\vek x + \big(\vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d_0 + \vek x) - \vek f_{\mathrm{b}}(\vek d_0)\big) = \vek 0\). For each bearing the difference is \(f_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{b},0} + x_{\mathrm{b}}) - f_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{b},0}) = k_{\mathrm{b}}\,x_{\mathrm{b}} - R_{\mathrm{b}}\) with \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{b},0})\) and \(R_{\mathrm{b}} = k_{\mathrm{b}}\,x_{\mathrm{b}} - \big(f_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{b},0} + x_{\mathrm{b}}) - f_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{\mathrm{b},0})\big)\) for \(f_{\mathrm{b}}(v) = \kappa_{\mathrm{b}} v^{3/2}\). This is the equation of the claim. In figure 25.80 \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\,x_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the increase of force along the tangent, the difference in the bracket the increase along the curve, and \(|R_{\mathrm{b}}|\) the vertical distance between them.
  2. By theorem 8.68 we have \(R_{\mathrm{b}} = -\tfrac12 f_{\mathrm{b}}''(c)\,x_{\mathrm{b}}^2\) with \(c\) between \(v_{\mathrm{b},0}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{b},0} + x_{\mathrm{b}}\). At \(|x_{\mathrm{b}}| \le v_{\mathrm{b},0}/2\) we have \(c \ge v_{\mathrm{b},0}/2\) (the departure in the figure is exactly at this limit). From \(f_{\mathrm{b}}'' = \tfrac34\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,v^{-1/2}\) follows \(|R_{\mathrm{b}}| \le \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac34\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,(v_{\mathrm{b},0}/2)^{-1/2}x_{\mathrm{b}}^2 = \tfrac{3\sqrt 2}{8}\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,v_{\mathrm{b},0}^{-1/2}x_{\mathrm{b}}^2\). We divide by \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\,|x_{\mathrm{b}}| = \tfrac32\,\kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,v_{\mathrm{b},0}^{1/2}|x_{\mathrm{b}}|\): the quotient is \(\tfrac{3\sqrt 2/8}{3/2}\,|x_{\mathrm{b}}|/v_{\mathrm{b},0} = \tfrac{\sqrt 2}{4}\,|x_{\mathrm{b}}|/v_{\mathrm{b},0}\).
  3. Symmetry follows from the symmetry of \(\mat K\) and the diagonality of \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\). The energy is \(\vek y^\T(\mat K + \mat K_{\mathrm{b}})\vek y = \int_0^L EI\,(v_{\mathrm{h}}'')^2\,\mathrm{d}x + k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{1,0})\,y_1^2 + k_{\mathrm{b}}(v_{5,0})\,y_5^2 \ge 0\) for every column \(\vek y\) (point 3 of theorem 12.9, the field \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) from \(\vek y\)). If it is zero, then \(v_{\mathrm{h}}'' = 0\), so \(v_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a linear function, and \(y_1 = y_5 = 0\) gives \(v_{\mathrm{h}}(0) = v_{\mathrm{h}}(L) = 0\), so \(v_{\mathrm{h}} = 0\). The Hermite functions are linearly independent (definition 12.3), so \(\vek y = \vek 0\). The matrix is therefore positive definite, and by theorem 10.21 the eigenvalues are real and, by the minimum of the quotient, positive.
  4. The difference \((\mat K + c_2\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}) - (\mat K + c_1\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}) = (c_2 - c_1)\,\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) is diagonal with nonnegative entries, so positive semidefinite, and therefore by corollary 10.46 (point 1) no eigenvalue decreases. A frequency is the root of an eigenvalue, so every frequency is nondecreasing as well.

Source: The theorem is ours, from theorems 10.3, 8.68 and 10.21. FPGL (PDF p. 214 to 215) describes adding the stiffness of a bearing to the assembled matrix, and FPGL (PDF p. 216) says that bearing stiffnesses may depend on the spin speed, which we do not consider here.

What did the theorem show? In vibration about a state the bearing is replaced by a spring with the tangent stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\), and the error of this replacement is estimated by the departure \(x_{\mathrm{b}}\) relative to the static displacement \(v_{\mathrm{b},0}\), whatever the frequency. For example: a departure of \(10\,\%\) of the static displacement, that is, \(0{,}5\) µm at \(4{,}98\) µm, gives an error of at most \(3{,}5\,\%\) of the change of force. The computation: the force of the bearing at \(v_0 = 4{,}98\) µm is \(283{,}71\) N, at a \(10\,\%\) larger displacement \(327{,}32\) N, and the linear approximation \(326{,}27\) N, so \(1{,}05\) N of error at a change of \(42{,}56\) N, that is, \(2{,}5\,\%\). At \(50\,\%\), the departure of figure 25.80, the error of the approximation is \(-4{,}74\,\%\) of the force, which is \(11{,}6\,\%\) of the change, and the estimate of the theorem is \(17{,}7\,\%\). The bound was exceeded in no case. If in vibration the bearing departs upward by more than the static displacement, \(x_{\mathrm{b}} < -v_{\mathrm{b},0}\), the bearing lets the shaft go (it does not pull) and the vector \(\vek d\) leaves the set \(U\) of the theorem: the linear model does not hold there.

We test the order of magnitude of the frequency with a model with one mass. Let a massless shaft carry the disk \(m_{\mathrm{d}} = 50\) kg at the middle. Under a force \(P\) at the middle the shaft on rigid pins (togi členki) bends by \(P/k\) with the stiffness \(k = 48EI/L^3 = 2{,}309\cdot 10^6\) N/m (equation (5.60)). The bearings add compliance: each carries \(P/2\) and yields by \(P/(2k_{\mathrm{b}})\). The bending of the shaft and the settling of the bearings add up at the disk, because the same force \(P\) passes first through the shaft and then through the bearings, so the compliance of the whole is \(1/k + 1/(2k_{\mathrm{b}})\). The frequency \(\sqrt{k_{\text{c}}/m_{\mathrm{d}}}/(2\pi)\) with the stiffness \(k_{\text{c}} = k\) for pins and \(k_{\text{c}} = \big(1/k + 1/(2k_{\mathrm{b}})\big)^{-1}\) for bearings gives \(34{,}20\) Hz for the pins and \(33{,}97\) Hz for the bearings (num-09.py). The mass of the shaft (\(7{,}84\) kg) is missing in this model, so the numbers are higher than the \(32{,}97\) and \(32{,}74\) Hz of the finite element model below, but the difference between pins and bearings is \(0{,}7\,\%\) in both. So the first frequency is determined mainly by the bending stiffness of the shaft, and the bearings lower it only a little.

Example 25.52 Natural frequencies of the rotor (lastne frekvence rotorja)

The rotor of section 25.9.1, static state \(v_1 = v_5 = 4{,}9847\) µm, \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 8{,}5375\cdot 10^7\) N/m, which is \(37\) times more than \(48EI/L^3 = 2{,}309\cdot 10^6\) N/m. NumPy solves the eigenproblem of theorem 25.51.

We draw the first mode. The horizontal grey line is the shaft at rest, the blue curve above it its shape at the largest displacement, normalized to \(1\) at the middle. The disk moves the most, the ends of the shaft hardly at all, and the nodal displacements are \(-0{,}014,\ -0{,}693,\ -1{,}000,\ -0{,}693,\ -0{,}014\) (the sign is arbitrary). The frequency beside the curve is \(32{,}74\) Hz. The grey dashed curve is the same mode with rigid pins, where the ends of the shaft stay at zero, and has \(32{,}97\) Hz, which is \(0{,}7\,\%\) more. In the second mode the middle is at rest and the two halves of the shaft move in opposite directions, the nodal displacements are \(-0{,}137,\ -1{,}000,\ 0,\ 1{,}000,\ 0{,}137\). Rigid pins (dashed curve) give \(494{,}07\) Hz, the bearings \(472{,}24\) Hz, so \(4{,}4\,\%\) less. Here the ends of the shaft move noticeably at the bearings, in the first mode they do not: an elastic bearing allows a displacement at the support that a rigid pin prevents, and the second mode uses it more (\(0{,}137\)) than the first (\(0{,}014\)). So the bearing lowers the second frequency more than the first. The second mode holds for a point disk (section 25.9.1): with the rotary inertia of a disk of diameter \(0{,}3\) m it would lie at \(164\) Hz.

Bearings \(f_1\) (Hz) \(f_2\) (Hz)
rigid pins \(32{,}97\) \(494{,}07\)
tangent stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) \(32{,}74\) \(472{,}24\)
\(0{,}5\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\) \(32{,}51\) \(451{,}30\)
\(1{,}5\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\) \(32{,}81\) \(479{,}44\)
\(0{,}01\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\) \(21{,}13\) \(125{,}97\)
\(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) at \(1000\) N per bearing \(32{,}82\) \(479{,}65\)

With four elements the frequencies are \(32{,}74\) and \(472{,}24\) Hz, with eight \(32{,}74\) and \(470{,}62\) Hz (rigid pins \(32{,}97\) and \(492{,}26\) Hz). The higher mode drops by \(0{,}3\,\%\) with the finer mesh. This is expected, because the strain energy of the shaft and the energy of the springs are terms of the potential, so the Ritz solution is an upper bound, as in corollary 13.83 for a beam without springs. At \(0{,}01\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\), \(0{,}5\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\), \(k_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(1{,}5\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\) the frequencies grow, as theorem 25.51 (point 4) requires.

The last row of the table shows what the theorem does not promise. The tangent stiffness depends on the load: a bearing with \(1000\) N instead of \(283{,}7\) N has \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 1{,}2993\cdot 10^8\) N/m, which is \(52\,\%\) more, and the second frequency \(479{,}65\) instead of \(472{,}24\) Hz. It moves the first frequency by only \(0{,}08\) Hz. So the linear model is not independent of statics: it always requires a previously computed static state. When the bearing is without load and without preload, \(k_{\mathrm{b}} = 0\) and the bearing does not support the shaft, as at the start at zero (example 25.48). The row \(0{,}01\,k_{\mathrm{b}}\) is not that case, it only illustrates how fast the frequencies fall (\(f_2\) to \(125{,}97\) Hz) when the bearing softens.

The two steps of the section are therefore the following. Statics (equation (25.44)) is nonlinear, and we solve it by Newton's method (definition 25.46), in which the stiffness matrix of the bearing enters as the tangent term, and each step is a linear system of the same look as in chapter 12. Vibration about the solution (theorem 25.51) uses the same tangent matrix and gives the eigenproblem of chapter 10. Statics with bearings that have no closed solution, and vibration with gyroscopic terms and spin speeds we do not solve here, but chapter 24 will carry them over to the same matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\).

25.10 Connections

The course abbreviations are the same as in section 1.19. The chapter took three steps: the spring of a foundation under a beam, a half-space loaded at a point and the Hertz contact that follows from it, and then the bearing as a set of such contacts. For each notion we say where we will need it again, and then what the chapter did not prove.

  • The foundation under a beam (podlaga): the equation \(EI\,v'''' + k\,v = q\) of theorem 25.2 is a fourth-order equation with constant coefficients, of the kind solved in section 9.4.7, and its solutions with roots \(\beta(\pm 1 \pm \mathrm{i})\) received boundary conditions in theorem 25.3 (VT, MK, DSK). The foundation pulls the beam back even where the beam has moved away from it (lemma 25.5), so the Winkler spring is a model of a foundation that is glued to the beam and both pushes and pulls it, not of a foundation that merely supports it. Where the lift-off and the contact length have to be found, we need the contact conditions of definition 25.19. The same equation holds for a cylindrical shell under an axisymmetric load, where the ring stiffness of the shell takes the role of the foundation (MK, AK, chapter 22). For a plate on a foundation the foundation is the force \(k\,w\) per unit area and \(w\) is a function of two variables (MK, AK, chapter 18).
  • The foundation in vibration and in the finite element method: by lemma 25.8 the foundation matrix is \(k/(\rho A)\) times the consistent mass matrix of lemma 12.43, so for a simply supported beam every mode is kept and the frequency rises by theorem 25.7. In assembly we add it like any element by theorem 12.9, and the deflection under one force is underestimated by corollary 25.10 (AK, DSK, chapters 12 and 13). For a shortened model of a beam on a foundation we keep only a few modes (DSK, chapter 21).

We compare three laws of the force between two bodies, the Winkler foundation, the penalty of chapter 12 and the Hertz contact, in figure 25.82. Horizontally we measure the approach \(\delta\) (the displacement by which the bodies press together, negative means a gap), vertically the force \(F\) between them. All three laws give the force \(1\) at \(\delta = 1\) so that they are comparable.

On the left is the Winkler foundation, which by definition 25.1 is a spring of stiffness \(k\) per unit length. It is a straight line through the origin, so the force changes sign with the displacement and the foundation also pulls. The penalty term \(\tfrac12\,\alpha\,|\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g|^2\) of definition 12.27 has the same form, since the force \(-\alpha\,(\mat C\,\vek d - \vek g)\) is two-sided. The Winkler foundation therefore has the form of a penalty on the constraint \(v = 0\) along the whole length of the beam with the penalty number \(k\). The purpose is different, though: we choose \(\alpha\) large so that the constraint is nearly satisfied, while \(k\) is the stiffness of the real foundation that we describe, and we may not increase it without changing the foundation. In contact the bodies must not pull on each other, so the middle law is zero for \(\delta < 0\) and for \(\delta > 0\) a linear spring with \(\alpha\). With this the pressure of definition 25.19 is always non-negative, and the product of pressure and gap is zero only in the limit \(\alpha \to \infty\), while for finite \(\alpha\) the bodies penetrate by \(F/\alpha\). That the penetration goes to zero as \(\alpha \to \infty\) is proved by theorem 12.28 (claim 2) for equality constraints, for one-sided constraints the book does not prove it. The right law is the Hertz law: the force is zero as long as the bodies do not touch, then grows as \(\delta^{3/2}\) by theorem 25.27 and corollary 25.28. Penetration here is not an error of the method. It is the approach by which the bodies really come closer, because they are compressed around the contact, and \(K = \tfrac43\,E^*\sqrt R\) is given by the material and the radius (\(E^*\) and \(R\) from section 25.6), not chosen. Into the right panel we also draw two straight lines through the orange point at \(\delta = 1\). The grey dashed secant joins the origin to this point, the orange tangent only touches the curve there and is steeper. What the two lines mean we show on the Hertz law in real units, on the left for one ball and on the right for a whole bearing.

A penalty number chosen for one load does not hold for another. The left panel shows the law \(F = K\,\delta^{3/2}\) of a steel ball of diameter \(12{,}7\) mm on a steel flat body, with the approach in micrometres horizontally and the force in newtons vertically. At the force \(100\) N the approach is \(4{,}24\) µm and the tangent has the slope \(35\,353\) N/mm. At the force \(1000\) N the approach is \(19{,}69\) µm and the slope \(76\,167\) N/mm (section 25.6). The force is ten times larger, the tangent stiffness only \(2{,}15\) times. The reason is the power: from \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = \tfrac32\,K\,\delta^{1/2}\) and \(\delta = (F/K)^{2/3}\) it follows that \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = \tfrac32\,K^{2/3}\,F^{1/3}\), and \(10^{1/3} = 2{,}15\). A linear spring with the penalty number \(\alpha\) has a single slope, so it agrees with the curve at one force only.

What are the secant and the tangent for the Hertz law? The right panel shows the law of the bearing of section 25.9, which at zero clearance is the power \(3/2\), \(F = \kappa_{\mathrm{b}}\,\delta^{3/2}\) (equation (25.43)). The orange point is its state under the static load \(283{,}7\) N, where the approach is \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}} = 4{,}98\) µm. The secant joins the unloaded state at the origin to this state, so its slope \(k_{\mathrm{s}} = F/\delta\) measures the whole approach under the whole force: the static approach is computed from the secant, \(\delta = F/k_{\mathrm{s}}\). A small additional force moves the state along the curve, which close to the point hardly differs from its tangent, so a small vibration about the state is described by the tangent \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\) (theorem 25.51, which uses theorem 8.68). For the power \(F = K\,\delta^{3/2}\) we have \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = \tfrac32\,K\,\delta^{1/2} = \tfrac32\,F/\delta = \tfrac32\,k_{\mathrm{s}}\), because the derivative of the power is \(\tfrac32\,K\,\delta^{1/2}\). The tangent stiffness of the bearing is \(8{,}538 \cdot 10^7\) N/m. If we divided the force by it, we would follow the dotted line through the origin that has the slope of the tangent and reach the height \(283{,}7\) N already at \(283{,}7/(8{,}538 \cdot 10^7)\) m \(= 3{,}32\) µm instead of at \(4{,}98\) µm. The difference \(1{,}66\) µm is a third of the true approach, because \(F/k_{\mathrm{t}} = \tfrac23\,F/k_{\mathrm{s}}\). From the rounded numbers \(283{,}7\) N and \(4{,}98\) µm we get \(k_{\mathrm{s}} = 5{,}697 \cdot 10^7\) N/m and the ratio \(k_{\mathrm{t}}/k_{\mathrm{s}} = 1{,}499\), and from the exact \(283{,}71\) N and \(4{,}9847\) µm of section 25.9 \(1{,}500\), as it must be for the power \(3/2\). The ratio therefore only checks the computation and does not prove the law, since the law of the bearing is a power already by equation (25.43). A spring with one stiffness must therefore use the secant in statics and the tangent in vibration.

The law \(F = K\,\delta^{3/2}\) also allows a computation of impact.

From history

Hertz presented the solution of the compression of two elastic bodies to the Physical Society in Berlin in January 1881, applied it to special cases and extended it to impact, for which he derived formulas for the duration of the impact of two spheres and for the stresses during it (TIMO, PDF p. 287).

The computation of impact thus follows from the force law: the force is a known function of the approach, so we insert it into Newton's law.

In LOVE the force law \(F = K\,\delta^{3/2}\) is equation (61), \(P = k\,\alpha^{3/2}\), where \(k\) and \(\alpha\) mean our \(K\) and \(\delta\) (LOVE, PDF p. 218). It holds only if the duration of the impact is a large multiple of the longest natural period of that vibration of either body which compresses the place of contact, because only then does the compression at the contact behave as a static phenomenon (LOVE, PDF pp. 217-218). Here we show only what we get when this is satisfied. We send a ball of mass \(m\) with speed \(v\) against a flat body that we take to be at rest. This is an idealization: for a movable body the reduced mass of both bodies, \(m_1 m_2/(m_1 + m_2)\), would appear in place of \(m\) (LOVE, PDF p. 218). For a body much heavier than the ball it is almost equal to \(m\). For two equal balls it would be \(m/2\). Then \(K\) changes as well, because the second surface is curved: by equation (25.23) \(R\) is half the radius of the ball, so \(K = \tfrac43\,E^*\sqrt R\) is smaller by the factor \(\sqrt2\). The largest approach is by the formula below proportional to \((m/K)^{2/5}\), so at the same speed of approach it would be \(\big(\tfrac12\sqrt2\big)^{2/5} = 2^{-1/5} = 0{,}87\) times ours. In the middle panel we draw the approach \(\delta\) in time, in the right one the force \(K\,\delta^{3/2}\) against the approach.

At time \(t = 0\) the bodies touch and \(m\,\ddot\delta = -K\,\delta^{3/2}\) holds. The sign is minus because the force of the flat body on the ball points against the motion and slows the ball down. The weight of the ball is not in the equation. We may leave it out, because for the ball below \(m g = 0{,}082\) N is only \(0{,}012\) % of the largest contact force \(684\) N. For a very slow impact this does not hold: the largest force grows with the speed as \(v^{6/5}\) and equals the weight already at \(v = 0{,}54\) mm/s. We multiply the equation by \(\dot\delta\), write both sides as a derivative, \(\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\tfrac12\,m\,\dot\delta^2\big) = -\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\big(\tfrac25\,K\,\delta^{5/2}\big)\), and integrate from \(t = 0\), where \(\delta = 0\) and \(\dot\delta = v\):

\[\tfrac12\,m\,\dot\delta^2 + \tfrac25\,K\,\delta^{5/2} = \tfrac12\,m\,v^2 . \tag{25.48}\]

The equation is a balance of energy. The first term is the kinetic energy of the ball. The second is the area under the force curve from \(0\) to \(\delta\), because \(\int_0^\delta K\,s^{3/2}\,\mathrm{d}s = \tfrac25\,K\,\delta^{5/2}\), so it is the work that the ball has done against the contact force and that is stored in the compressed bodies. The sum of the two stays equal to the initial kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\,m\,v^2\), which for the ball below is \(4{,}18\) mJ.

At the largest approach \(\dot\delta = 0\) and all the energy is in the area, so \(\delta_{\max} = \big(5\,m\,v^2/(4K)\big)^{2/5}\). From (25.48) it follows that \(\dot\delta^2 = v^2\big(1 - (\delta/\delta_{\max})^{5/2}\big)\). During the approach \(\dot\delta > 0\), so there \(\dot\delta = v\sqrt{1 - (\delta/\delta_{\max})^{5/2}}\). Then \(\delta\) is an increasing function of time and has an inverse function \(t(\delta)\) with the derivative \(1/\dot\delta\). The time of approach is therefore \(\int_0^{\delta_{\max}} \frac{1}{\dot\delta}\,\mathrm{d}\delta\), and with the substitution \(x = \delta/\delta_{\max}\) it is \(\frac{\delta_{\max}}{v}\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{5/2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x\). The rebound is the approach reversed, because the force is a function of \(\delta\) only, so the duration of the impact is twice the time of approach:

\[T = \frac{2\,\delta_{\max}}{v}\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{5/2}}}\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{25.49}\]

The integral is improper, because the integrand is unbounded at \(x = 1\): at the top of the curve of the approach the speed \(\dot\delta\) is zero, so \(1/\dot\delta\) grows beyond all bounds there. We draw this in figure 25.85.

On the axes we have \(x\) from \(0\) to \(1\) horizontally and the value of the integrand vertically. The orange curve is the integrand \(1/\sqrt{1 - x^{5/2}}\), which rises beyond all bounds at the vertical line \(x = 1\). We therefore understand the integral as the limit of the integrals from \(0\) to \(1 - h\) as \(h > 0\) goes to \(0\), just as definition 9.21 takes the limit of the integrals up to \(T\). The integral up to \(1 - h\) is the orange area up to the cut at \(1 - h\), for \(h = 0{,}1\) it is \(1{,}067\).

Do the areas grow beyond all bounds as \(h\) decreases, like the integrand? No. Since \(x^{5/2} \le x\) on \([0, 1]\), we have \(1 - x^{5/2} \ge 1 - x\), so the positive integrand is at most \(1/\sqrt{1 - x}\), the grey dashed curve. At \(x = 0{,}8\) this is shown by two vertical distances, \(1{,}53\) to the orange and \(2{,}24\) to the grey curve. The integral of the grey curve from \(0\) to \(1 - h\) is \(2 - 2\sqrt h < 2\). On the right are the orange bars, the integrals up to \(1 - h\) for \(h = 0{,}2\), \(0{,}1\) and \(0{,}01\), that is \(0{,}891\), \(1{,}067\) and \(1{,}345\). Each is lower than the grey dashed bar \(2 - 2\sqrt h\) next to it, that is \(1{,}106\), \(1{,}368\) and \(1{,}800\), and all are below the dashed line at \(2\). The integrals up to \(1 - h\) therefore grow as \(h\) decreases and are bounded by \(2\), so they have a limit (the proof is the same as for theorem 1.52). Its value is \(1{,}4716\) (NumPy, num-10.py).

Take a steel ball of diameter \(12{,}7\) mm and density \(7800\) kg/m³, so \(m = 8{,}37\) g, hitting a steel flat body with speed \(1\) m/s, which is the speed after a fall from a height of \(51\) mm. We get \(\delta_{\max} = 15{,}29\) µm, \(F_{\max} = 684\) N and \(T = 45{,}0\) µs. The duration is inversely proportional to the fifth root of the speed (LOVE, PDF p. 219): in formula (25.49) \(\delta_{\max}\) is proportional to \(v^{4/5}\), and divided by \(v\) it gives \(v^{-1/5}\). An impact ten times faster is therefore only \(10^{1/5} = 1{,}58\) times shorter. The contact radius is then \(a = 311{,}6\) µm and \(a/R = 0{,}049\), so much smaller than the radius of the ball, as the idealization of a non-conforming contact requires (section 25.5). For the period of vibration of the ball the book has no expression. LOVE (PDF p. 219) gives for it only the order of magnitude, the reciprocal of the product of the curvature \(A\) and the speed \(V_1\) of compression waves, where \(V_1^2 = (\lambda + 2\mu)/\rho\) with the Lamé constants of definition 3.18. For a ball on a plane \(A = 1/(2R) = 1/D\) (LOVE (69)), so this order is the time in which the wave crosses the diameter. With the wave along a rod, whose speed \(c = \sqrt{E/\rho} = 5013\) m/s is given by lemma 13.35, this time is \(D/c = 2{,}53\) µs, the short orange piece at the origin of the time axis. With \(V_1 = 5816\) m/s of our steel it would be \(2{,}18\) µs, which is the same order of magnitude. The duration \(T\) is \(17{,}8\) times longer than \(D/c\) and \(20{,}6\) times longer than \(D/V_1\), so the condition from LOVE is satisfied with a large margin. Since the period is given only as an order of magnitude, the margin tells only that the two times are an order of magnitude apart, not the exact factor. The largest pressure \(p_0 = 3364\) MPa is beyond the elastic limit of mild steel (section 25.6), so the computation holds for the hardened steel of bearings and not for the steel of the book.

  • The half-space and contact in FEM: the solutions of Flamant (theorem 25.13) and Boussinesq (theorem 25.15) were promised in chapter 11. By corollary 25.16 the displacement of the half-space falls only as \(1/r\), so a truncated body in a finite element model loses part of the displacement that the half-space has far from the contact. How much, the book does not compute (AK, chapter 15). The displacement under a point force is infinite, also for a plane body, where chapter 17 shows it by energy (AK). Contact in finite elements needs elements that look for the gap and the pressure by the conditions 25.19, and these are outside this chapter (AK, chapter 15). The uniqueness of the contact problem itself, which chapter 11 left to this chapter, is not proved here either. The reason is that the contact conditions are inequalities and the contact area is an unknown.
  • The bearing in a rotor model: the tangent stiffness matrix of the bearing \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) of theorem 25.40 is added into the diagonal of the system like a spring, as in theorem 7.13, and the natural frequencies are by theorem 10.3 and theorem 10.21 the eigenvalues of the corresponding problem. Chapter 24 (DSK) adds the rotation of the shaft with gyroscopic terms and critical speeds, where the matrix \(\mat K_{\mathrm{b}}\) enters as data. Our two bearings have no speed terms (centrifugal forces and the gyroscopic effect neglected, section 25.7).
  • Bearing damping: FPGL states that damping in rolling bearings is small and that the coefficient \(c\) is typically \((0{,}25 \text{ to } 2{,}5) \cdot 10^{-5}\) s times a typical stiffness \(k\) of the bearing (FPGL, PDF p. 203). For the stiffness \(8{,}538 \cdot 10^7\) N/m of our bearing this gives \(213\) to \(2134\) N s/m, but this is a datum of the source and not our computation. Chapter 20 (DSK) shows how \(c\) enters the equations of motion.
  • Limits of the chapter: the idealizations are named in the sections. The Winkler foundation is a force per length with no coupling between points, the half-space is linearly elastic, isotropic and frictionless, the Hertz contact is non-conforming and frictionless, the bearing has rigid rings, is at rest and is not loaded by speed forces. Elastohydrodynamic lubrication, friction and shear on the contact surface, crowning and edge loading of rollers, service life and combined axial loads are only named by the chapter. Stated without proof are: the quadratic form of the Hertz displacement away from the centre (from the sources and checked numerically), the elliptic contact, the uniqueness of the half-space and of contact problems, Palmgren's formula for \(\delta_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the law \(n = 10/9\) for rollers (both empirical), the convergence of Newton's iteration for systems and the stiffness ratios of Kramer.
